title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: The study aimed to investigate how t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex (t‑PAIC) concentrations vary across severity levels in hantaan virus‑induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and to evaluate its predictive value for disease severity.
analysis.methods: A total of 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls were enrolled; t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay, routine labs (WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, PT) were performed, HFRS‑specific antibodies were detected by colloidal gold, and statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve analysis.
analysis.results: t‑PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; significant positive correlations were found with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), Cr (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), UA (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997); significant inverse correlations with PLT (r=−0.6177), HDL (r=−0.3074), ALB (r=−0.4790); ROC analysis showed good predictive performance (AUC=0.796, 95% CI: 0.724–0.867).
analysis.contribution: t‑PAIC levels closely reflect HFRS severity and associated clinical features such as renal dysfunction and coagulation abnormalities, indicating its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study aimed to investigate how t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex concentrations vary across severity levels in hantaan virus‑induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and to evaluate its predictive value for disease severity. Methods: 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls were enrolled; t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay, routine labs were performed, HFRS‑specific antibodies were detected by colloidal gold, and statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve analysis. Results: t‑PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; significant positive correlations were found with leukocyte count, Cr, urea, UA, APTT, PT; inverse correlations with PLT, HDL, ALB; ROC analysis showed good predictive performance (AUC=0.796). title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening pathology in children worldwide and in Ukraine.

analysis.contribution: The report urges clinicians to include hantavirus in the differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic signs, and thrombocytopenia regardless of age or region, and showcases serologic testing as a useful diagnostic tool.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease causing hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening condition in children worldwide and in Ukraine. Methods: A case report of a 14‑year‑old from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, diagnosed by IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting. Results: The child developed hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, showing how the infection can mimic other inflammatory diseases and is hard to diagnose due to rarity. Contribution: Highlights the need to consider hantavirus in differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia in any age or region and demonstrates serologic testing utility. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: Recent work has advanced understanding of virology, ecology, transmission, immunopathogenesis, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine development, yet major challenges persist in surveillance, diagnostics, treatment, and vaccine pipelines. (A2)
analysis.current_state: The review collates current evidence on hantavirus taxonomy, reservoir ecology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, and existing diagnostic and therapeutic tools. (A3)
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited surveillance in South Asia and Africa, incomplete knowledge of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms. (A8)
analysis.future_research: Priorities are One Health‑based surveillance, predictive modeling of climate‑driven spillover, accelerated validation of point‑of‑care diagnostics, development of broadly effective antivirals and vaccines, and studies of human‑to‑human transmission dynamics. (A9)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. Main directions: Recent advances cover virology, ecology, transmission, immunopathogenesis, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines, but surveillance, diagnostics, treatment, and vaccine development remain challenging. Current state: The review synthesizes evidence on taxonomy, reservoir ecology, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and existing diagnostic/therapeutic tools. Gaps: Surveillance is inadequate in South Asia and Africa, Andes virus human‑to‑human spread is poorly understood, rapid diagnostics lack validation, and immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms are unresolved. Future research: Emphasize One Health surveillance, climate‑driven spillover modeling, rapid diagnostic validation, broad‑spectrum antivirals and vaccines, and investigation of human‑to‑human transmission.

title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting a review of their risk in Europe amid climate change and global mobility.
analysis.main_directions: The review examines European hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness, emphasizing endemic PUUV, DOBV, SEOV and the imported ANDV relevance for travel medicine and maritime response.
analysis.current_state: PUUV and DOBV cause most recognised European disease, SEOV is important in ports and urban settings, and imported ANDV infections are rare but can cause severe HCPS with documented person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius cruise‑ship cluster highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness, notably uneven molecular diagnostic capacity.
analysis.future_research: Preparedness should prioritize PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV through rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS, driving a review of European risk in the context of climate change and mobility. Main directions: The review covers epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness for PUUV, DOBV, SEOV, and imported ANDV. Current state: PUUV and DOBV dominate European cases, SEOV is relevant in urban ports, and ANDV, though rare, can cause severe disease with person‑to‑person spread. Gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship outbreak exposed critical preparedness gaps, especially uneven molecular testing. Future research: Strengthen rodent biomonitoring, harmonise surveillance, enhance molecular diagnostics, and develop locally calibrated early‑warning for PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV.

title: Hantavirus infection: global overview and current situation in Spain.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses with worldwide distribution and the capacity to cause severe human disease, motivating a global overview and a focus on Spain (A1, A5).
analysis.main_directions: The review addresses hantavirus taxonomy, reservoirs, transmission routes, epidemiology, clinical syndromes (HFRS vs HCPS), laboratory diagnosis, treatment, prognosis and prevention, emphasizing Spanish data (A5, A2, A3, A4).
analysis.current_state: More than 40 species are known, >20 pathogenic; Old World viruses cause HFRS, New World cause HCPS; infection is mainly via inhalation of contaminated rodent aerosols; many infections are asymptomatic leading to underdiagnosis; serology and molecular methods are primary diagnostics; no universally effective antiviral exists and care is supportive; Spain shows confirmed circulation in rodents and humans despite few recognized cases (A2, A3, A4, A6, A7, A8, A9, A10).
analysis.gaps: Underdiagnosis, lack of specific antiviral therapy, limited diagnostic awareness, and insufficient longitudinal surveillance hinder control (A6, A8, A11).
analysis.future_research: Enhanced national surveillance, improved diagnostic capacity and awareness, and development of effective preventive and therapeutic strategies are highlighted as priorities (A11, A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses with worldwide distribution and severe disease potential, prompting a review of global knowledge and the specific situation in Spain. Main directions: The review covers hantavirus taxonomy, reservoirs, transmission (including aerosol exposure and rare person‑to‑person), epidemiology, clinical syndromes (HFRS vs HCPS), diagnostics, treatment, prognosis and prevention, with focus on Spanish data. Current state: Over 40 species are known, >20 pathogenic; Old World viruses cause HFRS, New World cause HCPS; infection occurs mainly via inhaled rodent excreta; many cases are asymptomatic or nonspecific leading to underdiagnosis; serology and molecular tests are standard; no universally effective antivirals exist, care is supportive; Spain shows confirmed circulation in rodents and humans despite low clinical case numbers. Gaps: Underrecognition of cases, lack of specific antiviral therapy, limited public‑health awareness, and insufficient longitudinal surveillance data. Future research: Strengthen national surveillance, improve diagnostic capacity and awareness, and develop effective preventive (e.g., vaccines) and therapeutic interventions.

title: Maintenance of Hokkaido virus, a genotype of Orthohantavirus puumalaense, in the rodent host Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae under natural conditions.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic viruses that persist in natural rodent hosts; the mechanisms of maintenance and transmission in the field are poorly understood (A1, A2, A13).
analysis.methods: Field surveys were conducted in a forest in Tobetsu, Hokkaido, Japan, between 2022 and 2025, capturing 199 gray red‑backed voles (Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae) and testing for HOKV RNA and antibodies (A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8, A9).
analysis.results: 23 of 199 voles were HOKV positive; 5 showed acute infection markers (RNA+, IgG‑negative, low neutralizing titers, low IgG avidity ≤26%) and 18 were persistently infected (RNA+, high antibody titers, IgG avidity ≥64%) (A4, A5, A6, A7). Viral RNA and antigens were abundant in lungs, kidneys, and spleen, and infectious virus was recovered from oral swabs (8/8), urine (3/6), and feces (4/6) (A8, A9, A10).
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that HOKV establishes both acute and persistent infections in its natural host without major pathology, and that saliva, urine, and feces serve as multiple shedding routes, informing hantavirus ecology and spillover risk assessment (A10, A14, A15, A16, A17, A18).
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence (A2).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses persist in rodent hosts, but field maintenance mechanisms are unclear. Methods: Field surveys in Tobetsu, Hokkaido (2022‑2025) captured 199 gray red‑backed voles, testing for HOKV RNA and antibodies. Results: 23 voles were HOKV positive; 5 acute (RNA+, IgG‑negative, low neutralizing titers, IgG avidity ≤26%) and 18 persistent (RNA+, high antibody titers, IgG avidity ≥64%). Viral RNA and antigens were abundant in lungs, kidneys, spleen; infectious virus recovered from oral swabs (8/8), urine (3/6), feces (4/6). Contribution: HOKV establishes acute and persistent infections without major pathology, with saliva, urine, and feces as shedding routes, enhancing understanding of hantavirus ecology and spillover risk. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi‑country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in 2026.
analysis.methods: The authors sequenced complete ANDV small (S), medium (M), and large (L) genome segments from Chile together with outbreak‑associated and publicly available sequences and performed phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses.
analysis.results: Across all three segment phylogenies the outbreak virus clustered in ANDV Clade III spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia and was most closely related to a 2012 human isolate from Los Ríos, Chile; phylogeography showed the distinct Clade V from central Chile was unrelated, reducing the likelihood of spillover in the Maule Region; the geographic origin was traced to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Neuquén (Argentina) with Los Ríos and La Araucanía (Chile).
analysis.contribution: The study identifies a cross‑border ANDV lineage and pinpoints the likely geographic source of the cruise‑ship outbreak, informing surveillance and public‑health strategies for hantavirus emergence.
analysis.limitations: Limited rodent‑derived sequences mean broader unsampled regional diversity may exist, constraining the certainty of the inferred source.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus caused a multi‑country HPS outbreak on a cruise ship in 2026. Methods: Researchers sequenced complete S, M, and L segments from Chilean and outbreak‑associated samples plus public genomes and applied phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses. Results: The outbreak virus fell within ANDV Clade III of southern Chile/northern Patagonia, closest to a 2012 human isolate from Los Ríos; Clade V from central Chile was unrelated, lowering spillover likelihood in Maule; origin traced to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Neuquén (Argentina) with Los Ríos and La Araucanía (Chile). Contribution: This delineates the cross‑border lineage and geographic source, aiding surveillance and public‑health response. Limitations: Sparse rodent sequences indicate unsampled regional diversity, limiting source certainty.

title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: The study investigates how t-PAIC concentrations change across severity levels in HFRS patients to assess its potential as a biomarker.
analysis.methods: 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls were enrolled; t-PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay, routine labs (WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, PT) were performed, HFRS antibodies were detected by colloidal gold, and Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC analyses were applied.
analysis.results: t-PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; significant positive correlations were found with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), Cr (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), UA (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997); inverse correlations with PLT (r=−0.6177), HDL (r=−0.3074), ALB (r=−0.4790); ROC analysis yielded AUC=0.796 (95% CI 0.724–0.867).
analysis.contribution: t-PAIC closely reflects HFRS severity and associated renal dysfunction and coagulation abnormalities, indicating its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study investigates how t-PAIC concentrations change across severity levels in HFRS patients to assess its potential as a biomarker. Methods: 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls were enrolled; t-PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay, routine labs (WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, PT) were performed, HFRS antibodies were detected by colloidal gold, and Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC analyses were applied. Results: t-PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; significant positive correlations were found with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), Cr (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), UA (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997); inverse correlations with PLT (r=−0.6177), HDL (r=−0.3074), ALB (r=−0.4790); ROC analysis yielded AUC=0.796 (95% CI 0.724–0.867). Contribution: t-PAIC closely reflects HFRS severity and associated renal dysfunction and coagulation abnormalities, indicating its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are a globally distributed genus of negative‑sense RNA viruses (A1) and their rising public‑health impact under climate change motivates a comprehensive review (A15).
analysis.main_directions: The review covers the two major zoonoses—HFRS and HPS/HCPS (A2)—their endothelial infection and immune‑mediated vascular leakage (A7), and emerging therapeutic and vaccine strategies such as monoclonal antibodies and mRNA candidates (A13).
analysis.current_state: Transmission occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta (A3); HFRS causes 100‑150 k cases annually in Asia/Europe (A5) while HPS has a 25‑40 % fatality rate in the Americas (A6). Diagnosis relies on ELISA serology and RT‑PCR (A8), with sequencing aiding strain tracking (A9). Licensed vaccines exist only for HTNV/SEOV in limited regions (A10), and ribavirin shows benefit only for early HFRS (A12).
analysis.gaps: Human‑to‑human spread is rare, documented only for Andes virus (A4); there is no globally licensed vaccine (A10) or approved antiviral therapy (A11), and critical knowledge gaps remain regarding ecological drivers and immune evasion (A15).
analysis.future_research: Priorities include advancing monoclonal antibody, mRNA, and subunit vaccine candidates (A13) and investigating climate‑driven ecological changes that may alter hantavirus emergence (A15).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed RNA viruses and their increasing threat under climate change warrants review (A1, A15). Main directions: The article discusses HFRS and HPS/HCPS, endothelial pathogenesis, and new therapeutics/vaccines such as monoclonal antibodies and mRNA platforms (A2, A7, A13). Current state: Transmission is via aerosolised rodent excreta; HFRS causes 100‑150k cases yearly, HPS has 25‑40% mortality; diagnosis uses ELISA and RT‑PCR; only limited regional vaccines exist and ribavirin benefits early HFRS (A3, A5, A6, A8, A10, A12). Gaps: Human‑to‑human transmission is rare, no global vaccine or approved antiviral, and ecological knowledge gaps persist (A4, A10, A11, A15). Future research: Develop monoclonal antibody, mRNA, and subunit vaccines and study climate‑driven ecological factors influencing emergence (A13, A15).

title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure (A1) and belongs to a group of severe, potentially life‑threatening pathologies in children worldwide and in Ukraine (A2).
analysis.methods: The authors present a case report of a 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine (A6) aiming to demonstrate diagnostic stages (A5); diagnosis used detection of hantavirus‑specific IgM and IgG antibodies by ELISA and immunoblotting (A10) after ethical approval (A11) and parental informed consent (A12).
analysis.results: The case highlighted that hantavirus infection can mimic other inflammatory diseases (A7), that diagnosis is complicated by its rarity and symptom overlap (A8), and that it should be considered in patients with fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic signs, and thrombocytopenia (A9); serological testing confirmed infection (A10).
analysis.contribution: The report raises clinical awareness of hantavirus as a differential diagnosis in pediatric hemorrhagic‑renal presentations (A9), illustrates diagnostic challenges (A7), and demonstrates the utility of IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting for confirmation (A10).
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease causing hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening condition in children worldwide and in Ukraine. Methods: A case report of a 14‑year‑old from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, aimed to illustrate diagnostic steps; diagnosis relied on IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting after ethical approval and parental consent. Results: The case showed hantavirus can mimic other diseases, diagnosis is difficult due to rarity, clinicians should consider it in febrile patients with renal failure, hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia, and serology confirmed infection. Contribution: The report raises awareness for differential diagnosis in pediatric cases and demonstrates serological testing utility. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: Recent work has advanced virology, ecology and clinical aspects, yet major challenges remain in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccine development. (A2)
analysis.current_state: The review collates current evidence on hantavirus taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and existing diagnostic and preventive measures. (A3)
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited surveillance in South Asia and Africa, incomplete understanding of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms. (A8)
analysis.future_research: Priorities are to strengthen One Health surveillance, improve outbreak prediction, and accelerate development and validation of point‑of‑care diagnostics, effective antivirals, and globally approved vaccines. (A9)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. Main directions: Recent advances are offset by major challenges in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics and vaccine development. Current state: Evidence now covers taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features and existing diagnostic/preventive tools. Gaps: Surveillance gaps in South Asia/Africa, unclear Andes virus human‑to‑human spread, limited rapid‑test validation, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology persist. Future research: Strengthen One Health surveillance, enhance outbreak prediction, and fast‑track point‑of‑care diagnostics, effective antivirals and globally approved vaccines.

title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for two severe human diseases: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40% (A2). Single‑layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics have advanced understanding, but true multi‑omics integration remains scarce (A3). Genomic studies clarified viral diversity, evolution and reassortment, while transcriptomics identified regulatory networks governing endothelial and innate immune responses (A6). Proteomics revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation and endothelial dysfunction, and metabolomics indicated substantial metabolic reprogramming during infection, though dedicated studies are limited (A7). AI‑based approaches are increasingly applied to outbreak prediction, surveillance and risk modeling (A8).
analysis.contribution: High‑throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus–host interactions (A4). This review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and AI‑enabled approaches in hantavirus research (A5) and discusses opportunities to improve biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development and precision‑medicine strategies (A9).
analysis.limitations: The abstract notes a scarcity of true multi‑omics integration (A3) and, as only an abstract is provided, detailed methodological and quantitative data are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses causing HFRS and HCPS, severe diseases with high mortality. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Case fatality rates range 1%–40% (A2); single‑layer omics have expanded knowledge but integrated multi‑omics studies are rare (A3); genomics clarified diversity and reassortment, transcriptomics identified endothelial and innate immune networks (A6); proteomics uncovered host immune and endothelial proteins, metabolomics showed metabolic reprogramming though few studies exist (A7); AI tools are applied to outbreak prediction and risk modeling (A8). Contribution: High‑throughput omics have markedly advanced hantavirus‑host interaction research (A4); this review compiles current omics and AI approaches (A5) and outlines future opportunities for biomarkers, surveillance, therapeutics and precision medicine (A9). Limitations: Scarcity of true multi‑omics integration (A3) and only an abstract is available, so detailed data are not reported.

title: Paparan hantavirus ditemukan pada peternak satwa liar di Vietnam: Alarm bagi negara lain di Asia Tenggara

analysis.background: The study addresses hantavirus exposure among wildlife farmers in Vietnam, a setting where close human‑wildlife contact creates a zoonotic spillover risk (F8).
analysis.methods: A cross‑sectional survey enrolled 210 wildlife farmers from Lao Cai and Dong Nai provinces and tested serum by ELISA for hantavirus antibodies (F14; F36).
analysis.results: 8.7 % of participants had hantavirus antibodies, indicating past exposure, and 1.9 % showed evidence of recent infection; farmers solely managing wildlife farms had markedly higher risk (F15; F16; F17).
analysis.contribution: The findings serve as a surveillance alert for other Southeast Asian nations with wildlife markets, highlighting a potential public‑health threat (F12).
analysis.limitations: The study could not determine the hantavirus species involved and the exact source of infection remains unclear (F21; F35).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study addresses hantavirus exposure among wildlife farmers in Vietnam, where close human‑wildlife contact creates zoonotic spillover risk. Methods: A cross‑sectional survey of 210 farmers in Lao Cai and Dong Nai provinces used ELISA to detect hantavirus antibodies. Results: 8.7 % were seropositive and 1.9 % showed recent infection; those only managing farms had higher risk. Contribution: Provides a surveillance alert for other Southeast Asian countries with wildlife markets. Limitations: Virus species were not identified and the infection source remains unclear.

title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review addresses heterogeneous European epidemiology, reservoir ecology, climate‑driven rodent dynamics, diagnostic capacity, and the distinct threat of imported Andes virus (A8).
analysis.current_state: In Europe, Puumala virus and Dobrava virus cause most recognised disease, while Seoul virus is important in ports and urban settings (A2).
analysis.gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius cruise‑ship Andes virus outbreak exposed urgent gaps in preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus infections (A4).
analysis.future_research: Preparedness should focus on rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems for PUUV, DOBV and SEOV (A12).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS (A1). Main directions: The review covers heterogeneous European epidemiology, reservoir ecology, climate effects, diagnostics, and imported Andes virus risk (A8). Current state: Puumala and Dobrava viruses dominate European cases, with Seoul virus relevant in urban ports (A2). Gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship Andes virus cluster highlighted major preparedness deficiencies (A4). Future research: Prioritise rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, better molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning for PUUV, DOBV and SEOV (A12).

title: Bile acid signaling at the gut–vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown.
analysis.methods: The authors re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) with standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines to assess endothelial gene expression and bile acid transporter changes.
analysis.results: Infected endothelial cells showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation, NF‑κB suppression, and downregulation of bile acid transporters (e.g., ABCC3), with TGR5 undetectable; quantitative log2 fold changes and p‑values were reported.
analysis.contribution: The study proposes that hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and cholesterol‑metabolism disruption deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving NF‑κB inhibition and promoting vascular leakage, highlighting a repurposable therapeutic axis.
analysis.limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile acid signaling to vascular damage is absent; conclusions are hypothesis‑driven and require further validation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown. Methods: The authors re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) with standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines to assess endothelial gene expression and bile acid transporter changes. Results: Infected endothelial cells showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation, NF‑κB suppression, and downregulation of bile acid transporters (e.g., ABCC3), with TGR5 undetectable; quantitative log2 fold changes and p‑values were reported. Contribution: The study proposes that hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and cholesterol‑metabolism disruption deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving NF‑κB inhibition and promoting vascular leakage, highlighting a repurposable therapeutic axis. Limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile acid signaling to vascular damage is absent; conclusions are hypothesis‑driven and require further validation.

title: Hantavirus infection: global overview and current situation in Spain.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses with a worldwide distribution and the capacity to cause severe human disease.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers >40 hantavirus species, of which >20 are pathogenic, distinguishes Old World (HFRS) from New World (HCPS) clinical syndromes, describes aerosol transmission from rodent reservoirs and the rare person‑to‑person spread of Andes virus, and outlines biology, epidemiology, diagnosis, treatment and prevention, especially for Spain.
analysis.current_state: Hantavirus infections remain underdiagnosed due to asymptomatic or nonspecific cases; diagnosis relies on serology and molecular methods; no universally effective antiviral exists and care is supportive; evidence over three decades confirms circulation of hantaviruses in Spanish animal reservoirs and humans.
analysis.gaps: Surveillance is limited, diagnostic awareness is insufficient, and effective preventive or therapeutic strategies are lacking, highlighting gaps in epidemiologic data and treatment options.
analysis.future_research: Enhanced national surveillance, increased diagnostic capacity, and development of targeted antivirals or vaccines, together with public‑health interventions to reduce rodent exposure, are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses worldwide causing severe disease. Main directions: The review discusses >40 species, Old World HFRS vs New World HCPS, aerosol transmission (including Andes virus), and Spain‑focused biology, epidemiology, diagnosis, treatment and prevention. Current state: Infections are underdiagnosed, diagnosed by serology/molecular tests, lack effective antivirals, and are confirmed in Spanish reservoirs and humans. Gaps: Limited surveillance, low diagnostic awareness, and no proven preventive or therapeutic measures. Future research: Strengthen surveillance, improve diagnostics, and develop antivirals/vaccines and public‑health strategies to limit rodent exposure.

title: Maintenance of Hokkaido virus, a genotype of Orthohantavirus puumalaense, in the rodent host Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae under natural conditions.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are zoonotic viruses that persist in natural rodent hosts, but the mechanisms of maintenance and transmission in the field remain unclear.
analysis.methods: Field surveys were conducted in a forest in Tobetsu, Hokkaido, Japan, between 2022 and 2025, capturing 199 gray red‑backed voles (Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae). Viral RNA, antibody responses (ELISA, IFA, neutralization), IgG avidity, quantitative PCR, immunohistochemistry, and virus isolation from oral swabs, urine, and feces were performed.
analysis.results: 23 of 199 rodents were HOKV positive; 5 showed viral RNA but no IgG (acute infection), while 18 had viral RNA and high antibody titers and avidity (persistent infection). Viral RNA and antigens were abundant in lungs, kidneys, and spleen, and infectious virus was recovered from all oral swabs, 3/6 urine, and 4/6 feces of 2024 captures.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that HOKV establishes both acute and persistent infections in its natural host without major pathology, and that saliva is a predominant shedding route, informing hantavirus ecology and spill‑over risk assessment.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses persist in rodent hosts, yet field maintenance mechanisms are unclear. Methods: Field surveys in Tobetsu, Hokkaido (2022‑2025) captured 199 gray red‑backed voles; viral RNA, antibody profiles, IgG avidity, qPCR, IHC, and virus isolation from swabs, urine, and feces were performed. Results: 23/199 voles were HOKV positive; 5 acute (RNA+, IgG‑negative) and 18 persistent (RNA+, high antibody titers and avidity). Viral RNA/antigen were abundant in lungs, kidneys, spleen; infectious virus recovered from all oral swabs, 3/6 urine, 4/6 feces. Contribution: HOKV establishes acute and persistent infections without major pathology, with saliva as a key shedding route, enhancing understanding of hantavirus ecology and spill‑over risk. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi‑country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in 2026.
analysis.methods: Complete S, M, and L genome segment sequences from Chilean isolates and outbreak‑associated samples were analyzed together with publicly available ANDV sequences.
analysis.results: Across all three segment phylogenies the outbreak virus clustered in ANDV Clade III spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia, most closely related to a 2012 human isolate (p1236) from Los Ríos, Chile; phylogeographic analysis showed the distinct Clade V from central Chile was unrelated, reducing the likelihood of spillover in the Maule Region; the geographic origin was traced to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Neuquén (Argentina) with Los Ríos and La Araucanía (Chile).
analysis.contribution: The work identifies a cross‑border corridor as the likely source of the cruise‑ship outbreak, informing surveillance and public‑health strategies for hantavirus emergence.
analysis.limitations: Specific study limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence; conclusions rely on available genomic data without extensive rodent sampling, and only abstract/partial text is provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus caused a multi‑country HPS outbreak on a cruise ship in 2026. Methods: Researchers sequenced complete S, M, and L segments from Chilean and outbreak samples and compared them with public ANDV genomes. Results: Phylogenies placed the outbreak virus in Clade III, closest to a 2012 Los Ríos isolate; Clade V from central Chile was unrelated, lowering spillover likelihood in Maule; origin traced to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Argentina and Chile. Contribution: Pinpoints a cross‑border corridor as the outbreak source, aiding surveillance and public‑health response. Limitations: No explicit limitations reported; analysis based on available genomes without extensive rodent sampling and only abstract/partial text available.

title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus–induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) lacks reliable biomarkers for early severity assessment, prompting investigation of t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex (t‑PAIC) levels.
analysis.methods: t‑PAIC concentrations were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve analyses were performed to evaluate associations and predictive performance.
analysis.results: t‑PAIC levels increased progressively with disease severity, peaking in critically ill patients; they correlated positively with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), creatinine (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), uric acid (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182) and PT (r=0.2997), and inversely with platelet count (r=-0.6177), HDL (r=-0.3074) and albumin (r=-0.4790); ROC analysis gave an AUC of 0.796 (95% CI 0.724‑0.867, p<0.001).
analysis.contribution: The findings suggest t‑PAIC could serve as a biomarker for monitoring HFRS severity and related renal and coagulation abnormalities.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed methodology, patient demographics, and external validation are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS caused by hantaan virus lacks reliable severity biomarkers, leading to study of t‑PAIC. Methods: t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 patients and 37 controls; correlations, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC analysis were applied. Results: t‑PAIC rose with severity, showed strong positive correlations with leukocytes, creatinine, urea, uric acid, APTT, PT and negative correlations with platelets, HDL, albumin; ROC AUC was 0.796. Contribution: t‑PAIC may be a useful biomarker for HFRS severity and associated renal/coagulation dysfunction. Limitations: Only abstract information is provided, lacking detailed methods, demographics, and validation.

title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses causing severe zoonotic diseases (HFRS and HPS/HCPS).
analysis.main_directions: The review covers epidemiology, pathogenesis, diagnostics, and emerging therapeutics, highlighting rodent reservoirs, aerosol transmission, and immune dysregulation.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge confirms aerosol spread, high HFRS burden in Asia/Europe, lower HPS incidence in the Americas, limited licensed vaccines, and supportive care with ribavirin effective only for early HFRS.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include scarce licensed vaccines, lack of approved antivirals, limited evidence for ribavirin in HPS, and rare but documented human‑to‑human transmission.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on vaccine development, antiviral trials, next‑generation sequencing for outbreak tracing, and climate‑driven surveillance of rodent hosts.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting a global review of their impact.
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights major challenges in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine development, emphasizing immunopathogenesis, environmental drivers, and One‑Health approaches.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge integrates virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission dynamics, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, and existing diagnostic and treatment options.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited surveillance in South Asia and Africa, unclear mechanisms of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology.
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize One‑Health surveillance, predictive modeling of climate and land‑use impacts, validation of point‑of‑care diagnostics, development of broad‑spectrum antivirals, and vaccine candidates.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing severe renal and pulmonary syndromes, warranting a comprehensive review. Main directions: The review outlines challenges in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines, focusing on immunopathogenesis, environmental drivers, and One‑Health strategies. Current state: Knowledge now spans virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and existing diagnostic/treatment tools. Gaps: Surveillance gaps in South Asia/Africa, uncertain Andes virus human‑to‑human spread, limited rapid test validation, and unresolved immune‑mediated mechanisms remain. Future research: Priorities include One‑Health surveillance, climate‑driven risk modeling, point‑of‑care diagnostic validation, broad‑spectrum antiviral development, and vaccine advancement.

title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir

analysis.background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environments, and accidental human hosts, causing severe disease without licensed antivirals.
analysis.methods: The authors formulate a coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model linking a rodent reservoir with chronic shedding, an environmental viral compartment, and a dead‑end human SEIR population.
analysis.results: They derive a basic reproduction number R0 = R0_dir + R0_ind separating direct and environmental transmission (A3), prove R0 is the exact threshold with globally stable disease‑free and endemic equilibria (A4), show the system remains globally positive under multiplicative Brownian noise (A5), demonstrate that the usual Ito‑corrected threshold is insufficient (A6) and introduce a variational exponent Λ that guarantees almost‑sure extinction when Λ<0 (A7), quantify small‑noise deviations from endemic equilibrium (A8), and reproduce observed winter peaks of HFRS incidence using temperature forcing (A10) with a periodic reproduction number ≈2.15 (A11).
analysis.contribution: The work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for hantavirus dynamics, clarifies thresholds under stochasticity, and links environmental drivers to observed epidemiological patterns.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; empirical validation and parameter estimation are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environments, and humans, causing severe disease without antivirals. Methods: A coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model links rodent, environmental, and human compartments. Results: The model yields an additive R0 separating direct and environmental routes, proves R0 as the exact threshold with globally stable equilibria, remains positive under noise, shows the classic Ito correction is insufficient, introduces a variational exponent Λ for extinction, quantifies small‑noise deviations, and reproduces winter HFRS peaks with temperature forcing, giving a periodic R≈2.15. Contribution: Provides a rigorous stochastic framework linking environmental drivers to hantavirus epidemiology. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; no empirical validation or detailed parameter data are reported.

title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with a hemorrhagic syndrome and the development of renal failure.
analysis.methods: The paper presents a clinical case of a 14‑year‑old child residing in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, describing the course of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; diagnosis was based on detection of IgM and IgG antibodies to hantavirus using ELISA and immunoblotting.
analysis.results: The case demonstrates that hantavirus infection can mimic other inflammatory diseases and was confirmed by serological testing in the pediatric patient.
analysis.contribution: The report highlights that hantavirus infection should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic manifestations, and thrombocytopenia regardless of age or region.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease causing hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure. Methods: A 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, was evaluated for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, with diagnosis confirmed by IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting. Results: The case shows hantavirus can mimic other inflammatory diseases and was serologically confirmed. Contribution: The authors argue hantavirus should be included in differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic signs, and thrombocytopenia in any age or region. Limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both severe human diseases.
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Worldwide case fatality rates vary from 1% to 40%; single‑layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have advanced understanding of hantavirus biology, but true multi‑omics integration remains scarce; genomics clarified viral diversity and evolution, transcriptomics identified regulatory networks in endothelial and innate immune responses, proteomics revealed host proteins involved in immune regulation and endothelial dysfunction, metabolomics indicated substantial metabolic reprogramming, and AI‑based approaches are being applied to outbreak prediction and risk modeling.
analysis.contribution: High‑throughput omics technologies have greatly advanced the study of hantavirus–host interactions; the review summarizes genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI‑enabled approaches and outlines opportunities for biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and precision‑medicine strategies.
analysis.limitations: Multi‑omics integration is limited; the article is a review with only abstract information, providing no primary data or detailed methods.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses causing HFRS and HCPS, severe human diseases. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Case fatality rates range 1%–40%; single‑layer omics have advanced knowledge, but true multi‑omics integration is scarce; genomics clarified diversity, transcriptomics identified regulatory networks, proteomics revealed host immune and endothelial proteins, metabolomics showed metabolic reprogramming, and AI aids outbreak prediction. Contribution: High‑throughput omics have greatly advanced hantavirus‑host interaction studies; the review summarizes these approaches and highlights opportunities for biomarkers, surveillance, therapeutics, and precision medicine. title: Paparan hantavirus ditemukan pada peternak satwa liar di Vietnam: Alarm bagi negara lain di Asia Tenggara

analysis.background: Hantavirus exposure among wildlife farm workers in Vietnam raises concern because close human‑wildlife contact in these farms creates a zoonotic spillover risk, and recent outbreaks (e.g., Andes virus on a cruise ship) highlight the public‑health threat.
analysis.methods: The 2025 study sampled 210 wildlife‑farmers in Lao Cai and Dong Nai provinces and screened serum using ELISA for hantavirus antibodies.
analysis.results: Eight point seven percent of participants had hantavirus antibodies, indicating past exposure, and 1.9% showed evidence of recent infection; farmers who only managed wildlife farms had a markedly higher exposure risk.
analysis.contribution: The findings provide surveillance evidence of hantavirus exposure in Vietnamese wildlife‑farm workers and serve as an alarm for other Southeast Asian countries with similar wildlife‑trade practices.
analysis.limitations: The study could not determine the specific hantavirus species involved and relied solely on ELISA serology, limiting pathogen characterization.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus exposure among wildlife farm workers in Vietnam poses a zoonotic spillover risk, underscored by recent severe outbreaks. Methods: In 2025, 210 farmers from Lao Cai and Dong Nai were tested with ELISA for hantavirus antibodies. Results: 8.7% were seropositive and 1.9% showed recent infection, with higher risk among those solely managing wildlife farms. Contribution: This surveillance alerts other Southeast Asian nations to potential hantavirus threats linked to wildlife farming. Limitations: The study could not identify the hantavirus type and used only antibody testing.

title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting a review of European risk amid climate change and global mobility.
analysis.main_directions: The review concentrates on endemic Puumala, Dobrava, and Seoul viruses and imported Andes virus, addressing epidemiology, reservoir ecology, climate effects, diagnostic capacity, and travel‑medicine implications.
analysis.current_state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, shaped by biome‑specific rodent dynamics, variable clinical awareness, and uneven diagnostic preparedness.
analysis.gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius cruise‑ship Andes virus cluster highlighted urgent gaps in European preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease.
analysis.future_research: Preparedness should be enhanced through rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing HFRS and HCPS, prompting a review of European risk amid climate change and mobility. Main directions: The review focuses on endemic PUUV, DOBV, SEOV and imported ANDV, covering epidemiology, reservoir ecology, climate influences, diagnostics, and travel‑medicine. Current state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, driven by biome‑specific rodent dynamics, variable clinical awareness, and uneven diagnostic capacity. Gaps: The 2026 MV Hondius Andes virus cruise‑ship outbreak exposed critical preparedness gaps for endemic and imported disease. Future research: Strengthen preparedness via rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi‑country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in 2026.
analysis.methods: The study analyzed complete ANDV small (S), medium (M), and large (L) genome segment sequences from Chile, including outbreak‑associated and publicly available genomes.
analysis.results: Phylogenetic analysis showed the outbreak virus clustered within ANDV Clade III spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia, and was most closely related to a 2012 human‑derived ANDV (p1236) from Los Ríos Region.
analysis.contribution: Phylogeographic analysis identified the Hua Hum Pass corridor as the geographic origin of the outbreak‑associated virus, reducing the likelihood of zoonotic spillover in the Maule Region.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi‑country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among passengers and crew of a cruise ship in 2026. title: Bile acid signaling at the gut–vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome through endothelial barrier breakdown; clinical severity varies with undefined host regulators and no targeted endothelial‑protective treatments exist; recent data link hantaviruses to gut microbiome remodeling and bile acid receptors FXR/TGR5 inhibit NF‑κB‑mediated endothelial inflammation.
analysis.methods: Authors re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) with standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines, examining endothelial cell expression of VCAM1/ICAM1, NF‑κB components, BA transporters, and receptor expression, and reviewed metagenomic reports of gut/lung microbiota in rodent reservoirs.
analysis.results: SEOV‑infected human/rat lung ECs showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log2FC=+1.17, P=0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC=+0.32, padj=0.016) with unchanged FXR; SEOV suppressed Nfkb1 (P<0.05) and downregulated Slc10a2 (P=0.028); PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation (log2FC=+1.22, P=3.1×10⁻⁸) and reduced BA transporter ABCC3 (log2FC=−1.44, P=7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells; FXR/TGR5 agonists repressed NF‑κB inflammation and mitigated lung vascular injury; HTNV upregulated CH25H, blocking HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis and depleting BA precursors.
analysis.contribution: The study proposes a gut microbiota–BA–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus diseases and outlines tiered testable predictions for clinical cohorts, in vitro assays, and in vivo interventions.
analysis.limitations: Direct causal evidence linking BA signaling to viral vascular damage is absent; the analysis relies on re‑analysis of public datasets and metagenomic reports and is hypothesis‑driven.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome through endothelial barrier breakdown; clinical severity varies with undefined host regulators and no targeted endothelial‑protective treatments exist; recent data link hantaviruses to gut microbiome remodeling and bile acid receptors FXR/TGR5 inhibit NF‑κB‑mediated endothelial inflammation. Methods: Authors re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets with standardized pipelines, examining endothelial cell expression of VCAM1/ICAM1, NF‑κB components, BA transporters, and receptor expression, and reviewed metagenomic reports of gut/lung microbiota in rodent reservoirs. Results: SEOV‑infected human/rat lung ECs showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log2FC=+1.17, P=0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC=+0.32, padj=0.016) with unchanged FXR; SEOV suppressed Nfkb1 (P<0.05) and downregulated Slc10a2 (P=0.028); PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation (log2FC=+1.22, P=3.1×10⁻⁸) and reduced BA transporter ABCC3 (log2FC=−1.44, P=7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells; FXR/TGR5 agonists repressed NF‑κB inflammation and mitigated lung vascular injury; HTNV upregulated CH25H, blocking HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis and depleting BA precursors. title: Hantavirus infection: global overview and current situation in Spain.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses with worldwide distribution and capacity to cause severe disease, prompting a review of their biology and impact, especially in Spain.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers >40 hantavirus species, >20 pathogenic to humans, distinguishes Old World HFRS from New World HCPS, outlines rodent‑to‑human aerosol transmission (including rare person‑to‑person for Andes virus), and discusses reservoirs, epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, and prevention.
analysis.current_state: Old World hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, while New World strains cause cardiopulmonary syndrome; infections are often underdiagnosed due to asymptomatic or nonspecific presentations; serology and molecular assays remain the main diagnostic tools; and no universally effective antiviral exists, with care largely supportive.
analysis.gaps: Underdiagnosis persists, therapeutic options are limited, and the true burden in Spain remains unclear despite serological and ecological evidence, highlighting gaps in surveillance, diagnostic awareness, and preventive measures.
analysis.future_research: Enhanced surveillance, increased diagnostic awareness, and development of effective preventive and antiviral strategies are identified as priority research and public‑health actions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic RNA viruses with global spread and severe disease potential, motivating a review focused on Spain. Main directions: The article surveys >40 species, pathogenicity, Old World HFRS vs New World HCPS, transmission (including Andes virus), reservoirs, epidemiology, clinical picture, diagnostics, treatment, prognosis, and prevention. Current state: Old World strains cause renal syndrome, New World cause cardiopulmonary syndrome; many cases are missed, serology/molecular tests are primary diagnostics, and no universally effective antiviral exists. Gaps: Underdiagnosis, lack of therapy, and uncertain disease burden in Spain reveal surveillance and diagnostic shortcomings. Future research: Priorities include stronger surveillance, better diagnostic awareness, and development of preventive and therapeutic interventions.

title: Maintenance of Hokkaido virus, a genotype of Orthohantavirus puumalaense, in the rodent host Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae under natural conditions.

analysis.background: Ort­hohantaviruses typically have preferred natural rodent hosts and are thought to spread by direct contact or inhalation of contaminated excreta, but the mechanisms of maintenance and transmission in wild populations remain unclear.
analysis.methods: Field surveys were carried out from 2022 to 2025 in a forest in Tobetsu, Hokkaido, Japan, capturing 199 gray red‑backed voles (Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae); infection was evaluated by viral RNA detection, ELISA, IFA, neutralization tests, IgG avidity indexes, quantitative PCR and immunohistochemistry.
analysis.results: Twenty‑three voles (11.6%) were HOKV‑positive; five lacked anti‑HOKV IgG and had low avidity (≤26%) indicating acute infection, while eighteen showed high antibody titers and avidity (≥64%) consistent with persistent infection; high viral RNA loads were present in lung, kidney and spleen, and infectious virus was recovered from oral swabs (8/8), urine (3/6) and feces (4/6).
analysis.contribution: The study shows HOKV can persist at high loads in host organs and be shed via saliva, urine and feces, revealing multiple shedding routes and enhancing understanding of orthohantavirus ecology, persistence, and spill‑over risk.
analysis.limitations: No explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Ort­hohantaviruses have preferred rodent hosts and unclear natural maintenance mechanisms. Methods: Field surveys (2022‑2025) in Tobetsu, Hokkaido captured 199 Myodes rufocanus bedfordiae voles; infection assessed by RNA detection, ELISA, IFA, neutralization, IgG avidity, qPCR and immunohistochemistry. Results: 23 voles (11.6%) were HOKV‑positive; 5 acute (no IgG, ≤26% avidity) and 18 persistent (high antibodies, ≥64% avidity); high viral loads in lung, kidney, spleen; infectious virus recovered from oral swabs (8/8), urine (3/6), feces (4/6). Contribution: Demonstrates high‑load persistence and multiple shedding routes, informing hantavirus ecology and spill‑over risk. Limitations: No explicit limitations reported.

title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: The study addresses the need for biomarkers that reflect disease severity in hantaan virus‑induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), because severity assessment guides clinical management.
analysis.methods: t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex (t‑PAIC) concentrations were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; routine laboratory parameters and HFRS‑specific antibodies were also assessed, and statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve analysis. Location and demographic details were not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: t‑PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; t‑PAIC correlated positively with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), creatinine (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), uric acid (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182) and PT (r=0.2997), and inversely with platelet count (r=-0.6177), HDL (r=-0.3074) and albumin (r=-0.4790); ROC analysis gave an AUC of 0.796 for predicting severe disease.
analysis.contribution: The findings suggest that t‑PAIC may serve as a biomarker for monitoring HFRS severity and associated renal and coagulation disturbances, offering potential clinical utility.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed methodology, patient demographics, and external validation are not reported; the reported associations do not establish causation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study seeks biomarkers for hantaan virus‑induced HFRS severity. Methods: t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 patients and 37 controls; routine labs, antibodies, and statistical analyses (Spearman, logistic regression, ROC) were performed (location not reported). Results: t‑PAIC increased with severity, showed positive correlations with leukocytes, creatinine, urea, uric acid, APTT, PT and negative correlations with platelets, HDL, albumin; ROC AUC=0.796 for severity prediction. Contribution: t‑PAIC may be a useful biomarker for monitoring disease severity and related renal/coagulation abnormalities. Limitations: Abstract‑only data limit detail on methods and validation; associations are not causal.

title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses causing severe zoonotic diseases HFRS and HPS/HCPS, with significant morbidity and mortality worldwide.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers aerosol transmission from rodent excreta, diverse rodent reservoirs, endothelial infection and cytokine storm pathogenesis, serologic and RT‑PCR diagnostics, and emerging vaccines and antivirals.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge confirms aerosol transmission, >50 rodent hosts, limited licensed vaccines for HTNV/SEOV, supportive care as standard, and early ribavirin reducing mortality in HFRS but not proven for HPS.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include absence of licensed vaccines for most hantaviruses, lack of approved antivirals, limited evidence for ribavirin in HPS, and incomplete understanding of immune evasion mechanisms.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on broad‑spectrum vaccine candidates, randomized antiviral trials, improved diagnostic assays, genomic surveillance, and ecological studies linking climate change to hantavirus emergence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses causing severe zoonotic diseases HFRS and HPS/HCPS, with significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. Main directions: The review covers aerosol transmission from rodent excreta, diverse rodent reservoirs, endothelial infection and cytokine storm pathogenesis, serologic and RT‑PCR diagnostics, and emerging vaccines and antivirals. Current state: Current knowledge confirms aerosol transmission, >50 rodent hosts, limited licensed vaccines for HTNV/SEOV, supportive care as standard, and early ribavirin reducing mortality in HFRS but not proven for HPS. Gaps: Key gaps include absence of licensed vaccines for most hantaviruses, lack of approved antivirals, limited evidence for ribavirin in HPS, and incomplete understanding of immune evasion mechanisms. Future research: Future work should focus on broad‑spectrum vaccine candidates, randomized antiviral trials, improved diagnostic assays, genomic surveillance, and ecological studies linking climate change to hantavirus emergence.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting a need to review their impact.
analysis.main_directions: Recent decades have yielded advances, yet major challenges persist in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine development.
analysis.current_state: The review collates current knowledge on hantavirus virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and One Health surveillance.
analysis.gaps: Identified gaps include limited surveillance in South Asia and Africa, incomplete understanding of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms.
analysis.future_research: Priorities are to strengthen One Health surveillance, improve outbreak prediction, and accelerate development and validation of diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, warranting a comprehensive review. Main directions: Despite recent progress, major challenges remain in surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine development. Current state: The review synthesizes current evidence on hantavirus virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission dynamics, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and One Health surveillance. Gaps: Key gaps include inadequate surveillance in South Asia and Africa, limited understanding of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved mechanisms of immune‑mediated endothelial pathology. Future research: Priorities are to enhance One Health surveillance, improve outbreak prediction, and accelerate development and validation of effective diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines.

title: Host hybridization enabled the emergence of a reassorted hantavirus lineage.

analysis.background: Genetic exchange drives evolution across life; reassortment in segmented viruses can generate strains with broader infection ranges or higher virulence, yet natural examples beyond influenza are rare.
analysis.methods: The authors investigated Tula orthohantavirus in a hybrid zone of its reservoir, the common vole (Microtus arvalis), sampling 58 trapping sites over a 12.5 km contact area and analyzing 127 infected voles; phylogenomic analyses were applied to detect reassortment events.
analysis.results: They detected 27 TULV reassortants, indicating three independent reassortment events, with a single dominant strain carrying a reassorted M‑segment; five residues in the glycoprotein N‑terminal region differed between clades, two showing positive selection, and in silico 3D modeling revealed this region as uniquely structured for each clade.
analysis.contribution: The work presents the first example of host‑virus co‑hybridization, demonstrating that hybrid zones can act as hotspots for the emergence of novel hantavirus lineages potentially adapted to hybrid hosts, informing viral evolution and surveillance.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Genetic exchange drives evolution; reassortment can create broader or more virulent strains, but natural examples beyond influenza are rare. Methods: Researchers sampled 58 sites (12.5 km) and 127 infected common voles in a hybrid zone, using phylogenomic analysis to identify reassortments. Results: Twenty‑seven reassortants were found, representing three independent events, with one dominant strain carrying a reassorted M‑segment and specific glycoprotein N‑terminal changes under positive selection. Contribution: This is the first host‑virus co‑hybridization example, showing hybrid zones as hotspots for novel hantavirus lineages adapted to hybrid hosts. Limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure.
analysis.methods: The study formulates an SIR–SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations, extends it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects, and evaluates the model using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite difference methods.
analysis.results: Analysis shows hantavirus persistence is primarily governed by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote disease extinction; numerical simulations confirm consistent solutions across methods and superior stability of the SNSFD scheme at larger time steps.
analysis.contribution: The stochastic delay model provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for studying hantavirus dynamics, emphasizing that controlling infection in the rodent reservoir is the most effective way to reduce persistence and limit human spillover, and demonstrates the SNSFD method’s suitability for simulating stochastic epidemic systems with delays.
analysis.limitations: The work is limited to theoretical modeling and numerical simulation without empirical validation; only an abstract is provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease where humans acquire infection through spillover exposure. Methods: An SIR–SIR framework for rodent and human populations was extended with stochastic perturbations, discrete delays, and delay‑survival effects, and solved using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and SNSFD methods. Results: Persistence is driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human cases arise from spillover, and stochastic/delay effects can lower the reproduction threshold and promote extinction; simulations show consistent results and superior stability of SNSFD at larger steps. Contribution: The model offers a rigorous, realistic tool for hantavirus dynamics, highlighting reservoir control as key to limiting human spillover and validating SNSFD for stochastic epidemic simulations. Limitations: The study is purely theoretical with no empirical data; only an abstract is available.

title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir

analysis.background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environmental substrates, and accidental human hosts, causing two severe syndromes for which no licensed antiviral therapy exists.
analysis.methods: The authors formulate and rigorously analyse a coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model linking a rodent reservoir with chronic lifelong shedding, an environmental viral compartment, and a dead‑end human SEIR population.
analysis.results: They establish well‑posedness, derive an additive R0 separating direct and indirect routes, prove R0 as the exact threshold with globally stable disease‑free and endemic equilibria, show global positivity under multiplicative Brownian noise, expose limits of the classical Itô‑corrected threshold, introduce a computable variational exponent Λ (Λ<0 forces extinction), and show temperature‑ and rainfall‑driven forcing reproduces observed seasonal and interannual HFRS peaks (periodic R≈2.15 vs R0 = 1.63).
analysis.contribution: The study provides a rigorous stochastic framework for hantavirus dynamics, refines threshold criteria beyond traditional Ito corrections, and links environmental drivers to incidence, offering tools for surveillance and risk assessment.
analysis.limitations: Persistence is only documented numerically and not proved, and the abstract offers no empirical validation of the model predictions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environments, and humans, causing severe syndromes with no licensed antiviral. Methods: A coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model links a rodent reservoir, environmental viral pool, and dead‑end human SEIR population. Results: The model is well‑posed, yields an additive R0 separating direct and indirect transmission, proves R0 as the exact threshold with globally stable equilibria, remains globally positive under Brownian noise, identifies shortcomings of the classic Ito‑corrected threshold, introduces a variational exponent Λ (<0 forces extinction), and reproduces observed seasonal and interannual HFRS peaks (periodic R≈2.15 vs R0 = 1.63). Contribution: Provides a rigorous stochastic framework, refines threshold criteria, and connects environmental drivers to incidence for surveillance. Limitations: Persistence is only shown numerically, not proved, and the abstract lacks empirical validation.

title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure, and it belongs to the group of severe, potentially life‑threatening pathologies in children worldwide and in Ukraine.
analysis.methods: The authors present a clinical case of a 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, aiming to illustrate diagnostic stages and challenges; diagnosis used detection of IgM and IgG antibodies to hantavirus by ELISA and immunoblotting, with ethical approval and parental consent obtained.
analysis.results: The case describes the course of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in the child, showing that hantavirus infection can mimic other inflammatory diseases and that its rarity complicates diagnosis.
analysis.contribution: The report advises that hantavirus infection be considered in the differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic manifestations, and thrombocytopenia regardless of age or region, and it highlights serologic testing (ELISA, immunoblot) as essential diagnostic tools.
analysis.limitations: No explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; the article is a single case report without broader epidemiological data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease causing hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening condition in children worldwide and in Ukraine. Methods: A 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, was described; diagnosis relied on IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting, with ethical approval and parental consent. Results: The case documented hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, illustrating that hantavirus can mimic other inflammatory diseases and is hard to diagnose due to rarity. Contribution: The authors recommend considering hantavirus in differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia and emphasize serologic testing as key. Limitations: No explicit limitations are reported; the study is a single case report.

analysis.methods: The review synthesizes findings from genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI‑enabled studies of hantavirus–host interactions.

analysis.limitations: Multi‑omics integration is limited and dedicated metabolomics studies are scarce; the review is based solely on the abstract, restricting depth of analysis.
