title: Paparan hantavirus ditemukan pada peternak satwa liar di Vietnam: Alarm bagi negara lain di Asia Tenggara

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a zoonotic pathogen that can cause severe disease, and wildlife farms in Vietnam create close human‑wild animal contact that facilitates spillover risk.
analysis.methods: In 2025 the authors surveyed 210 wildlife‑farm workers in Lao Cai and Dong Nai provinces, collecting blood between August 2023 and March 2024 and testing for hantavirus antibodies with ELISA.
analysis.results: 8.7 % of workers had hantavirus antibodies, indicating past exposure, and 1.9 % showed evidence of recent infection; workers who only managed farms had a higher exposure risk despite not handling, hunting, or consuming animals.
analysis.contribution: The study provides the first serological evidence of hantavirus exposure among Vietnamese wildlife‑farm workers and warns other Southeast Asian nations with similar markets to strengthen biosecurity and surveillance.
analysis.limitations: The study could not identify the hantavirus species, the infection source remains unclear, and reliance on ELISA limits confirmation of active infection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a zoonotic pathogen and wildlife farms in Vietnam create close human‑animal contact, raising spillover risk. Methods: In 2025, 210 wildlife‑farm workers in Lao Cai and Dong Nai were sampled (Aug 2023–Mar 2024) and tested for antibodies by ELISA. Results: 8.7 % were seropositive and 1.9 % showed recent infection; farm‑only workers had higher risk despite no hunting or consumption. Contribution: First serological evidence of exposure among Vietnamese wildlife‑farm workers, alerting other SE Asian countries to improve biosecurity and surveillance. Limitations: Virus species not identified, source of infection unclear, and ELISA alone cannot confirm active infection.

title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on European hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness, emphasizing Puumala, Dobrava, and Seoul viruses and the imported Andes virus.
analysis.current_state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, driven by reservoir ecology, rodent dynamics, and variable diagnostic capacity, with climate effects mediated by mast years and land use.
analysis.gaps: Preparedness gaps include uneven molecular diagnostics, limited surveillance harmonisation, and the rare but high‑consequence risk of imported Andes virus with documented person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritise rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems for PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Main directions: The review focuses on European hantavirus epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness, emphasizing Puumala, Dobrava, and Seoul viruses and the imported Andes virus. Current state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, driven by reservoir ecology, rodent dynamics, and variable diagnostic capacity, with climate effects mediated by mast years and land use. Gaps: Preparedness gaps include uneven molecular diagnostics, limited surveillance harmonisation, and the rare but high‑consequence risk of imported Andes virus with documented person‑to‑person transmission. Future research: Future work should prioritise rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems for PUUV, DOBV, and SEOV.

title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak

title: Bile acid signaling at the gut–vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening HFRS and HCPS by inducing severe endothelial barrier breakdown and systemic capillary leakage (A1). Clinical severity is highly variable and no endothelial‑protective therapies exist (A2). Recent work links hantavirus infection to gut microbiome remodeling and shows that bile‑acid receptors FXR and TGR5 can inhibit NF‑κB‑driven endothelial inflammation (A3).
analysis.methods: The authors synthesized four lines of evidence: (i) metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota changes in rodent reservoirs (A5); (ii) re‑analysis of three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines to assess endothelial gene expression (A6‑A10); (iii) literature on FXR/TGR5 agonists suppressing NF‑κB inflammation and reducing lung vascular injury (A11); and (iv) reports that HTNV up‑regulates CH25H, impairing cholesterol‑derived bile‑acid precursors (A12).
analysis.results: Re‑analysis showed conserved up‑regulation of VCAM1 (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023) and ICAM1 (rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016) without FXR change (A6‑A7); sustained Nfkb1 suppression and Slc10a2 down‑regulation (P = 0.028) in infected rat lung (A8); strong IL6 elevation (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and loss of BA transporter ABCC3 (log2FC −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²) in PUUV‑infected vessel chips (A9); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells (A10). FXR/TGR5 agonists reduced NF‑κB activity and mitigated vascular injury (A11), and HTNV‑induced CH25H up‑regulation blocked HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis (A12).
analysis.contribution: The paper proposes a unified pathogenic model linking hantavirus‑driven gut dysbiosis and impaired cholesterol metabolism to depletion of FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, thereby releasing inhibition of endothelial NF‑κB and monocyte NLRP3 inflammasomes (A13). It outlines tiered, testable predictions for multi‑omics clinical cohorts, in‑vitro receptor assays, and in‑vivo pharmacologic interventions (A14). The gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis is highlighted as a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus disease (A15).
analysis.limitations: The authors acknowledge that direct causal evidence linking bile‑acid signaling to hantavirus‑induced vascular damage is absent (A15); the work is a hypothesis‑driven synthesis relying on re‑analysis of existing datasets rather than new experimental data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus causes severe HFRS/HCPS via endothelial barrier breakdown, with variable severity and no targeted treatments; gut microbiome changes and bile‑acid receptors FXR/TGR5 can modulate inflammation (A1‑A3). Methods: The study synthesizes metagenomic reports, re‑analyzes three GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) for endothelial gene expression, reviews FXR/TGR5 agonist effects, and examines HTNV‑induced CH25H up‑regulation (A5‑A12). Results: VCAM1/ICAM1 are up‑regulated (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023; rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016), Nfkb1 is suppressed, Slc10a2 down‑regulated (P = 0.028), IL6 elevated (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸), BA transporter ABCC3 reduced (log2FC −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²), TGR5 absent, and FXR/TGR5 agonists mitigate NF‑κB inflammation (A6‑A12). Contribution: Proposes a model where gut dysbiosis and cholesterol‑metabolism disruption deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, enhancing NF‑κB/NLRP3 activity, and suggests this axis as a therapeutic target with testable predictions (A13‑A15). Limitations: No direct causal evidence is provided; conclusions are based on re‑analysis and hypothesis rather than new experimental data (A15).

title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: The study investigates whether t-PAIC concentrations vary with HFRS severity and could serve as a severity biomarker.
analysis.methods: t-PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; routine labs (WBC, PLT, Cr, UA, urea, HDL, ALB, APTT, PT) and HFRS-specific antibodies (colloidal gold) were assessed; Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve analyses were performed.
analysis.results: t-PAIC levels rose progressively with HFRS severity, peaking in critically ill patients; significant positive correlations were found with WBC (r=0.6082), Cr (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), UA (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997); significant inverse correlations with PLT (r=-0.6177), HDL (r=-0.3074), ALB (r=-0.4790); ROC analysis showed good predictive value (AUC=0.796, 95% CI: 0.724-0.867).
analysis.contribution: t-PAIC levels closely reflect HFRS severity and associated clinical features, indicating its potential as a biomarker for monitoring disease status.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study examines whether t-PAIC concentrations correlate with HFRS severity and could serve as a biomarker. Methods: t-PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; routine labs and HFRS-specific antibodies were assessed; statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curves. Results: t-PAIC increased with severity, peaking in critically ill patients; it positively correlated with WBC, Cr, urea, UA, APTT, PT and inversely with PLT, HDL, ALB; ROC analysis yielded AUC=0.796. Contribution: t-PAIC reflects HFRS severity and clinical features, suggesting utility as a monitoring biomarker. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses, and rising ecological change heightens their public‑health relevance.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers the two major zoonoses (HFRS and HPS/HCPS), endothelial infection and immune dysregulation, and emerging therapeutic approaches such as monoclonal antibodies and vaccine candidates.
analysis.current_state: Transmission occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta; HFRS causes ~100‑150 k cases annually in Asia/Europe while HPS has 25‑40 % mortality in the Americas. Diagnosis relies on ELISA serology and RT‑PCR; licensed vaccines exist only for HTNV and SEOV in limited regions and no approved antivirals are available, with ribavirin showing benefit only for early HFRS.
analysis.gaps: Human‑to‑human transmission is documented only for Andes virus, ribavirin lacks efficacy for HPS, and broader gaps in vaccine availability, antiviral options, and ecological drivers remain.
analysis.future_research: Priorities include development and clinical testing of monoclonal antibodies, mRNA and subunit vaccines, and surveillance of climate‑driven spillover to inform public‑health interventions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses, and rising ecological change heightens their public‑health relevance. Main directions: The review covers the two major zoonoses (HFRS and HPS/HCPS), endothelial infection and immune dysregulation, and emerging therapeutic approaches such as monoclonal antibodies and vaccine candidates. Current state: Transmission occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta; HFRS causes ~100‑150 k cases annually in Asia/Europe while HPS has 25‑40 % mortality in the Americas. Diagnosis relies on ELISA serology and RT‑PCR; licensed vaccines exist only for HTNV and SEOV in limited regions and no approved antivirals are available, with ribavirin showing benefit only for early HFRS. Gaps: Human‑to‑human transmission is documented only for Andes virus, ribavirin lacks efficacy for HPS, and broader gaps in vaccine availability, antiviral options, and ecological drivers remain. Future research: Priorities include development and clinical testing of monoclonal antibodies, mRNA and subunit vaccines, and surveillance of climate‑driven spillover to inform public‑health interventions.

title: The Natural Killer Cell Landscape in the Natural History of Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome in a Chilean Cohort.

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes Orthohantavirus (ANDV) has case‑fatality rates up to 40%, and the innate immune determinants of disease severity remain poorly defined.
analysis.methods: Multiparameter flow cytometry and unsupervised UMAP‑based clustering were performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 13 HCPS patients (stratified by severity) and nine healthy donors.
analysis.results: Severe HCPS exhibited a coordinated disruption of the CD56dim NK cell compartment, including reduced frequencies of the terminally differentiated NKG2C+CD57+ adaptive‑like pool and intrinsic impairment of IFN‑γ production and degranulation, deficits absent in mild patients and partially persisting after recovery; CD56dimCD16+ NK cell frequencies correlated negatively with viral load across all acute patients, independent of clinical severity.
analysis.contribution: These findings establish that severe HCPS is characterized by selective functional impairment of the most cytotoxically competent NK cell population during the early acute phase of ANDV infection, advancing immunopathogenic insight.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence; only an abstract was available.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by ANDV has up to 40% fatality and innate immune drivers of severity are unclear. Methods: Flow cytometry and UMAP clustering were applied to PBMCs from 13 Chilean HCPS patients (by severity) and nine healthy donors. Results: Severe disease showed reduced CD56dim NK cells, especially the NKG2C+CD57+ adaptive subset, with impaired IFN‑γ production and degranulation; CD56dimCD16+ NK frequencies inversely correlated with viral load regardless of severity. Contribution: The work reveals selective functional loss of the most cytotoxic NK cells early in ANDV infection, informing disease immunopathogenesis. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence; abstract only.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease of considerable public health importance.

title: Differentiated Contact Tracing for Emerging Zoonotic Hantavirus and Ebolavirus Infections: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus (MV Hondius) and Bundibugyo Virus Outbreaks.

analysis.background: In May 2026, simultaneous outbreaks of Andes virus aboard the MV Hondius expedition cruise ship and Bundibugyo virus in Central Africa highlighted the need for tailored contact‑tracing strategies.
analysis.methods: Passengers and crew from 23 countries were traced across 32 countries and territories; contact‑tracing and active‑surveillance protocols were applied to the Andes virus outbreak.
analysis.results: The Andes virus outbreak involved 13 cases (12 laboratory‑confirmed, 1 probable), 3 deaths, and more than 600 contacts; the Bundibugyo virus outbreak had over 1,000 laboratory‑confirmed cases and more than 250 confirmed deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus can sustain multiple generations, whereas Bundibugyo virus lacks pre‑symptomatic transmission, informing differentiated contact‑tracing intensity and timing.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Person-to-Person Transmission of Andes Virus (ANDV): A Systematic Review of Transmission Dynamics, Viral Shedding, and Public Health Implications.

analysis.background: ANDV is the only hantavirus with documented person‑to‑person transmission, prompting a focused review.
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights incomplete knowledge of transmission timing, viral shedding, exposure contexts, and public‑health management.
analysis.current_state: Thirty‑three studies covering 17,204 individuals identified 2,221 laboratory‑confirmed cases and 135 secondary cases, establishing a median incubation of ~21 days and a median serial interval of ~22 days.
analysis.gaps: Recommendations on post‑discharge counselling, especially regarding sexual transmission, remain provisional due to limited evidence.
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize prospective contact‑tracing studies, standardized virological sampling, and genomic confirmation of infectious virus.

title: The 2026 Andes Hantavirus Outbreak: A Comparative Analysis and Strategic Roadmap

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS and remain a continuous global public health threat, motivating a review of the 2026 Andes orthohantavirus outbreak.
analysis.main_directions: The article reviews epidemiology, molecular virology, endothelial injury mechanisms, person‑to‑person transmission, current treatments, investigational therapeutics, vaccine development, and preparedness strategies.
analysis.current_state: The 2026 ANDV cluster had a 38% case‑fatality rate, sustained transmission chains in crowded environments without major genetic adaptation, driven by high viral loads and super‑spreading events, with endothelial dysfunction causing rapid cardiogenic shock.
analysis.gaps: Current outbreak management is reactive; proactive bio‑surveillance and early detection in travel networks are insufficient.
analysis.future_research: Develop systematic bio‑surveillance, test antiviral candidates, accelerate vaccine pipelines, and create policies for rapid containment of person‑to‑person hantavirus spread.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS and remain a continuous global public health threat, motivating a review of the 2026 Andes orthohantavirus outbreak. title: Gen-YSD: An Experiment-Aware Generative AI Pipeline for Closing the Sim-to-Real Gap in Pan-Hantavirus Antibody Design

analysis.background: Generative AI has accelerated structural biology, yet designed antibodies almost never become functional therapeutics (A1).
analysis.methods: Gen‑YSD is a three‑stage computational pipeline: Stage 1 generates antibodies with an SE(3)‑equivariant diffusion backbone enforcing developability constraints; Stage 2 simulates yeast surface‑display flow cytometry with stochastic expression, photon‑counting noise, optical effects, and gating thresholds; Stage 3 uses Pareto optimization to balance binding affinity, solution viscosity, expression yield, and epitope diversity (A8).
analysis.results: Candidates emerging from the pipeline have already survived virtual testing that mirrors the physics and chemistry of real experiments (A15).
analysis.contribution: The pipeline targets pan‑hantavirus immunity by designing broadly neutralizing antibodies against Gn and Gc glycoproteins, aiming to close the sim‑to‑real gap and reduce wet‑lab attrition (A12).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; no experimental validation, quantitative performance data, or real‑world testing are reported (A3).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Generative AI speeds structural biology but designed antibodies rarely become functional therapeutics. Methods: Gen‑YSD is a three‑stage pipeline—SE(3)‑equivariant diffusion generation with developability constraints, full‑fidelity yeast surface‑display simulation, and Pareto optimization of affinity, viscosity, yield, and epitope diversity. Results: Virtual candidates have already passed in‑silico testing that mirrors real experimental physics and chemistry. Contribution: The approach seeks to close the simulation‑to‑real gap for pan‑hantavirus broadly neutralizing antibody design, potentially lowering wet‑lab attrition. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; no experimental validation or quantitative results are reported.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Hantavirus Outbreak Risk Prediction: A Multisource Early Warning Framework for Tourism, Hospitality, and Public Health Systems

analysis.background: Hantavirus infections are relatively rare but can cause severe clinical outcomes, involve rodent‑linked environmental exposure, and occasionally form travel‑associated clusters, creating a complex risk problem for tourism, hospitality, and public‑health systems.
analysis.methods: Using a design‑science and conceptual modeling approach, the authors propose the Hantavirus Risk Prediction AI (HRP‑AI) framework that integrates rodent, environmental, syndromic, laboratory, travel, digital weak‑signal, and business vulnerability data, and applies anomaly detection, spatiotemporal forecasting, natural language processing, ensemble learning, and explainable AI.
analysis.results: Quantitative results or empirical validation are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.contribution: The article contributes a publishable AI risk architecture, feature taxonomy, model‑selection logic, validation metrics, and governance controls, intended to support earlier detection, risk stratification, targeted prevention, transparent communication, and operational preparedness in high‑contact travel and hospitality environments.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; no empirical evaluation is presented, and the framework does not replace public‑health decision‑makers, leaving performance and real‑world applicability untested.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infections are rare but cause severe outcomes and involve rodent exposure and travel‑linked clusters, posing complex risks for tourism, hospitality, and public health. Methods: A design‑science, conceptual modeling study proposes the HRP‑AI framework that fuses rodent, environmental, syndromic, laboratory, travel, digital weak‑signal, and business data, using anomaly detection, spatiotemporal forecasting, NLP, ensemble learning, and explainable AI. Results: No quantitative results or validation are reported. Contribution: The paper delivers an AI risk architecture with a feature taxonomy, model‑selection logic, validation metrics, and governance controls to aid early detection, risk stratification, prevention, communication, and preparedness in high‑contact travel settings. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided; empirical performance is untested and the system does not replace public‑health decision‑makers.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome.
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes immunopathogenic endothelial dysfunction, climate‑driven ecological drivers of spillover, diagnostic and therapeutic limitations, and a One‑Health framework for surveillance and intervention.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge integrates virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission dynamics, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and existing diagnostics such as serology, RT‑PCR, and sequencing.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include sparse surveillance in South Asia and Africa, limited understanding of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms.
analysis.future_research: Priority actions are expanded One‑Health surveillance, validation of point‑of‑care diagnostics, development of broadly effective antivirals and vaccines, and studies linking climate and ecological changes to spillover risk.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome. Main directions: The review emphasizes immunopathogenic endothelial dysfunction, climate‑driven ecological drivers, diagnostic and therapeutic gaps, and a One‑Health framework for surveillance and intervention. Current state: Knowledge now integrates virology, taxonomy, reservoir ecology, transmission, global epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical features, and existing diagnostics (serology, RT‑PCR, sequencing). Gaps: Surveillance is limited in South Asia and Africa, Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission is poorly understood, rapid diagnostics lack validation, and immune‑mediated pathology mechanisms remain unresolved. Future research: Priorities include expanded One‑Health surveillance, validation of point‑of‑care tests, development of effective antivirals and vaccines, and studies linking climate and ecology to spillover risk.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe and often fatal zoonotic disease primarily caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review summarizes the roles and alterations of monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells and B cells during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: These immune cells are necessary for viral clearance but also contribute to immunopathological tissue damage, reflecting a central immunological duality.
analysis.gaps: The detailed temporal dynamics, phenotypic changes, and functional profiles of each immune subset across disease stages remain poorly understood.
analysis.future_research: Integrating clinical and mechanistic insights to map immune cell trajectories and identify therapeutic targets is highlighted as a priority.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a severe zoonotic disease caused mainly by HTNV. Main directions: The review covers monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T and B cells in HTNV infection. Current state: These cells clear virus yet drive immunopathology, showing a dual role. Gaps: Precise dynamics and functional profiles of immune subsets across disease stages are insufficiently defined. Future research: Mapping immune trajectories and pinpointing therapeutic targets through integrated clinical‑mechanistic studies is needed.

title: Host hybridization enabled the emergence of a reassorted hantavirus lineage.

analysis.background: Reassortment of segmented viruses can generate new strains with altered host range and virulence, yet concrete natural examples beyond influenza are scarce.
analysis.methods: The authors sampled 58 sites and 127 infected common voles in a 12.5‑km hybrid zone, performed phylogenomic analyses to identify reassortment events, and used in silico 3D modeling of the glycoprotein.
analysis.results: They detected 27 reassortants, three independent reassortment events, and a dominant strain with a reassorted M‑segment; glycoprotein N‑terminal variation of five residues, two under positive selection, showed clade‑specific structural differences.
analysis.contribution: The study provides the first evidence that host hybridization zones can drive the emergence of reassorted hantavirus lineages with potentially novel host adaptation, highlighting hybrid zones as viral evolution hotspots.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure, representing an ongoing public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: An SIR–SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations was formulated, then extended with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays and exponential delay‑survival effects, and numerical simulations were performed using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta and stochastic nonstandard finite‑difference (SNSFD) methods.
analysis.results: The analysis showed that hantavirus persistence is primarily driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold under certain conditions and promote disease extinction.
analysis.contribution: The paper provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic stochastic delay model for hantavirus risk assessment, emphasizes that controlling infection within the rodent reservoir is the most effective strategy to reduce persistence and human spillover, and demonstrates the superior numerical stability of the SNSFD scheme for such simulations.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease with human infection occurring via spillover from rodent reservoirs, posing ongoing public‑health concerns. Methods: The authors formulated an SIR–SIR transmission model for interacting rodent and human populations, extended it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete delays and exponential delay‑survival effects, and performed numerical simulations using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta and stochastic nonstandard finite‑difference methods. Results: Analysis indicated that virus persistence is driven mainly by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human cases arise from spillover, and that stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote extinction. Contribution: The study provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic stochastic delay framework for hantavirus risk assessment and highlights that controlling infection in rodent reservoirs is the most effective way to reduce persistence and human spillover; it also demonstrates superior stability of the SNSFD scheme for such simulations. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir

analysis.background: Hantaviruses circulate in an ecological web linking rodent population dynamics, contaminated environmental substrates and the accidental human host, causing two severe syndromes for which no licensed antiviral therapy exists.
analysis.methods: The authors formulate and rigorously analyse a coupled SEIR‑SEIV model joining a rodent reservoir with chronic lifelong shedding, an environmental viral compartment V, and a dead‑end human SEIR population.
analysis.results: They derive a basic reproduction number R0 = R_dir0 + R_ind0 separating direct rodent‑to‑rodent and indirect environmental routes, prove R0 is the exact threshold with disease‑free and endemic equilibria globally asymptotically stable, show the stochastic system remains globally positive under multiplicative Brownian noise, demonstrate that the usual Ito‑corrected threshold Rs < R0 is insufficient, introduce a variational exponent Λ (<0 forces almost‑sure extinction), find that small noise keeps solutions within O(∑σ_i^2) of the endemic equilibrium, and that temperature forcing reproduces the documented winter HFRS peak with a periodic reproduction number ≈2.15 versus R0 = 1.63, while rainfall forcing captures interannual peaks (2005‑2016).
analysis.contribution: The work provides rigorous threshold theory and global stability proofs for a hantavirus model, introduces a new stochastic extinction criterion (Λ), and links environmental drivers to observed incidence patterns, advancing theoretical and ecological understanding of hantavirus transmission.
analysis.limitations: Persistence is only documented numerically and not proved analytically; the paper is abstract‑only, so empirical validation beyond the described forcings is not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, contaminated environments and humans, causing severe disease with no licensed antivirals. Methods: A coupled SEIR‑SEIV model links a rodent reservoir with chronic shedding, an environmental viral compartment, and a dead‑end human SEIR population. Results: The basic reproduction number R0 = R_dir0 + R_ind0 separates direct and environmental transmission; R0 is the exact threshold with globally stable disease‑free and endemic equilibria; the stochastic system stays positive under Brownian noise; the usual Ito‑corrected threshold Rs < R0 is insufficient; a variational exponent Λ (<0) ensures almost‑sure extinction; small noise keeps solutions within O(∑σ_i^2) of the endemic equilibrium; temperature forcing reproduces winter HFRS peaks (periodic R ≈2.15 vs R0=1.63) and rainfall forcing captures interannual peaks 2005‑2016. Contribution: Provides rigorous threshold and stability theory, a new stochastic extinction criterion, and demonstrates environmental drivers of hantavirus incidence. Limitations: Persistence is only shown numerically, not analytically, and the work is limited to abstract‑level description without empirical validation.

title: Omics Approaches in Hantavirus Research: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives

analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Single‑layer genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have each advanced understanding of hantavirus biology, but true multi‑omics integration remains scarce, leaving systems‑level mechanisms of disease severity unresolved; omics have identified viral diversity, host regulatory networks, immune‑related host proteins, and metabolic reprogramming; AI approaches are being applied to outbreak prediction and risk modeling.
analysis.contribution: The review synthesizes current genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and AI‑enabled studies, highlights gaps in multi‑omics integration, and proposes opportunities for biomarker discovery, surveillance, therapeutic development, and precision medicine for hantavirus infections.
analysis.limitations: The article is an abstract‑only review, providing no primary data or detailed methodology; the scarcity of integrated multi‑omics studies limits concrete conclusions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe HFRS and HCPS with case fatality rates of 1%–40%. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Single‑omics studies have advanced knowledge of viral diversity, host responses, and metabolic changes, but integrated multi‑omics analyses are scarce, and AI tools are emerging for prediction. Contribution: This review compiles current omics and AI approaches, identifies gaps, and suggests future directions for biomarkers, surveillance, and therapeutics. Limitations: Abstract‑only review with no primary data or detailed methods, and limited multi‑omics integration.

title: Hantavirus risk and preparedness in Europe in an era of climate change and global mobility.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, motivating a review of European risk and preparedness.
analysis.main_directions: The review addresses endemic Puumala, Dobrava, and Seoul viruses and imported Andes virus, focusing on epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness.
analysis.current_state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous and driven by reservoir ecology and climate‑mediated rodent dynamics, while diagnostic capacity, especially molecular testing, remains uneven.
analysis.gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship Andes virus cluster exposed urgent gaps in surveillance harmonisation, molecular diagnostics, and overall preparedness for both endemic and imported hantavirus disease.
analysis.future_research: Recommendations call for rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, improved molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonoses causing HFRS and HCPS, prompting a review of European risk and preparedness. Main directions: The review examines endemic PUUV, DOBV, SEOV and imported ANDV, covering epidemiology, ecology, clinical recognition, diagnostics, and preparedness. Current state: European hantavirus epidemiology is heterogeneous, shaped by reservoir ecology and climate‑mediated rodent dynamics, while diagnostic capacity, especially molecular testing, is uneven. Gaps: The 2026 cruise‑ship ANDV outbreak highlighted urgent gaps in surveillance harmonisation, molecular diagnostics, and overall preparedness for endemic and imported infections. Future research: Prioritise rodent biomonitoring, harmonised surveillance, enhanced molecular diagnostics, and locally calibrated early‑warning systems.

title: A historical cross-border Andes virus lineage reveals the origin of a cruise ship hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) caused a multi‑country outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome among cruise‑ship passengers and crew in 2026, highlighting a cross‑border public‑health threat.
analysis.methods: Complete ANDV small (S), medium (M), and large (L) genome segment sequences from Chile were analyzed together with outbreak‑associated and publicly available genome sequences.
analysis.results: Phylogenies of all three segments placed the outbreak virus within ANDV Clade III spanning southern Chile and northern Patagonia and identified it as most closely related to a 2012 human‑derived isolate (p1236) from Los Rios, Chile; phylogeographic analysis showed the distinct Clade V in central Chile was not related, reducing the likelihood of spillover in the Maule Region; the geographic origin was traced to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Neuquén Province (Argentina) with Los Rios and La Araucanía (Chile).
analysis.contribution: The work delineates the evolutionary lineage and geographic source of the cruise‑ship outbreak, informing surveillance and control measures for cross‑border hantavirus transmission.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; sample size, detailed methods, quantitative results, and broader epidemiologic context are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus caused a multi‑country HPS outbreak on a cruise ship in 2026, raising cross‑border health concerns. Methods: Complete ANDV S, M, and L genome segments from Chile were compared with outbreak‑associated and public sequences. Results: Phylogenies placed the outbreak virus in Clade III, closely related to a 2012 human isolate from Los Rios, Chile; Clade V was unrelated, lowering spillover likelihood in Maule Region; phylogeography traced the source to the Hua Hum Pass corridor linking Argentina and Chile. Contribution: The study clarifies the outbreak’s evolutionary origin and geographic source, aiding surveillance and control. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; sample numbers, detailed methods, and quantitative analyses are not reported.

title: t-PA/PAI-1 complex expression correlates with the severity in hantaan virus-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: The study addresses the need for biomarkers to assess severity in hantaan virus‑induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS).
analysis.methods: t‑PA/PAI‑1 complex (t‑PAIC) concentrations were measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 HFRS patients and 37 healthy controls; routine laboratory indices and HFRS‑specific antibodies were also obtained, and statistical analyses included Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC curve assessment.
analysis.results: t‑PAIC levels rose progressively with disease severity, peaking in critically ill patients; t‑PAIC correlated positively with leukocyte count (r=0.6082), creatinine (r=0.3567), urea (r=0.4376), uric acid (r=0.3201), APTT (r=0.6182), PT (r=0.2997) and inversely with platelet count (r=-0.6177), HDL (r=-0.3074), and albumin (r=-0.4790) (all p<0.01); ROC analysis gave AUC=0.796 (95% CI 0.724‑0.867, p<0.001) for predicting severity.
analysis.contribution: The findings suggest t‑PAIC may serve as a useful biomarker for monitoring HFRS severity and associated renal and coagulation disturbances.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed methodological and cohort information, as well as any authors‑stated limitations, are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study seeks biomarkers for hantaan virus‑induced HFRS severity. Methods: t‑PAIC was measured by chemiluminescence immunoassay in 156 patients and 37 controls, with routine labs, antibody testing, Spearman correlation, ordinal logistic regression, and ROC analysis performed. Results: t‑PAIC increased with severity, showed strong positive correlations with leukocytes, creatinine, urea, uric acid, APTT, PT and negative correlations with platelets, HDL, albumin (all p<0.01); ROC AUC=0.796 for severity prediction. Contribution: t‑PAIC appears a promising biomarker for HFRS severity and related renal/coagulation changes. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; detailed methods, sample characteristics, and explicit limitations are not reported.

title: Prevalence and Genetic Diversity of Zoonotic Leptospira and Hantavirus in Rodents, Lanxi City, 2023-2025.

analysis.background: Leptospirosis and hantavirus disease are important zoonoses with rodents as the main reservoirs (A1).
analysis.methods: Rodents were trapped in rural Lanxi City from April 2023 to August 2025 (A2, A6); liver and kidney tissues were aseptically collected (A7) and screened by real‑time fluorescent PCR, with positive samples subjected to gene sequencing and phylogenetic analysis (A8).
analysis.results: Among 350 rodents (80% Rattus norvegicus) the Leptospira carriage was 7.14% (25/350) and hantavirus carriage 1.43% (5/350) with no coinfections (A9‑A11, A13); 12 Leptospira isolates were L. interrogans and 2 were L. borgpetersenii forming a unique local phylogenetic cluster (A14, A5); all hantavirus isolates were Seoul virus showing only 86.08‑86.81% nucleotide identity to vaccine strains, indicating high genetic divergence (A4, A16); rodents exhibited a higher Leptospira carriage than the national average (A3).
analysis.contribution: The study documents elevated Leptospira prevalence and SEOV dominance in local rodents, reveals novel genetic variants that may reduce vaccine match, and highlights the need for targeted surveillance and control measures (A4, A5, A19, A20).
analysis.limitations: The authors note that serological validation of vaccine mismatch is required, and the findings are limited to rodent samples from a single city over a defined period (A20).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Leptospirosis and hantavirus disease are important rodent‑borne zoonoses (A1). Methods: Rodents were trapped in rural Lanxi City (Apr 2023‑Aug 2025), liver/kidney tissues collected, and screened by real‑time PCR with sequencing of positives (A2, A6‑A8). Results: Of 350 rodents (80% R. norvegicus), Leptospira prevalence was 7.14% and hantavirus 1.43% with no coinfections; 12 Leptospira were L. interrogans, 2 L. borgpetersenii formed a unique local cluster, and all hantavirus isolates were SEOV showing 86.08‑86.81% identity to vaccine strains (A3‑A11, A13‑A16). Contribution: The work reveals higher local Leptospira rates, SEOV dominance, and genetic divergence that may affect vaccine efficacy, informing surveillance and control (A4, A5, A19, A20). Limitations: Serological validation is lacking and results apply only to rodents from one city during the study period (A20).

title: The 2026 Andes Hantavirus Outbreak: A Comparative Analysis and Strategic Roadmap

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, representing an ongoing global public‑health threat.
analysis.main_directions: The paper surveys epidemiology, molecular virology, endothelial injury mechanisms, person‑to‑person transmission, treatment options, investigational therapeutics, vaccine development, and preparedness strategies for Andes orthohantavirus.
analysis.current_state: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak showed a 38 % case‑fatality rate and confirmed sustained human‑to‑human transmission in crowded settings without major viral genetic adaptation.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited knowledge of factors driving super‑spreading during the prodromal phase and insufficient proactive surveillance in travel networks.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on proactive bio‑surveillance, viral load dynamics, targeted antivirals and vaccines, and travel‑related containment policies.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS, a continuous global health threat. Main directions: The review covers epidemiology, molecular virology, endothelial injury, person‑to‑person spread, treatments, investigational drugs, vaccines, and preparedness for Andes virus. Current state: The 2026 outbreak had a 38% fatality rate and proved sustained human transmission without major genetic change. Gaps: Understanding of super‑spreading drivers and proactive travel‑network surveillance is limited. Future research: Priorities are proactive bio‑surveillance, viral load studies, antiviral and vaccine development, and travel‑related containment policies.

title: Gen-YSD: An Experiment-Aware Generative AI Pipeline for Closing the Sim-to-Real Gap in Pan-Hantavirus Antibody Design

analysis.background: Generative AI has accelerated structural biology, yet designed antibodies rarely become functional therapeutics because current models optimize only for binding affinity and ignore physical constraints, leading to failures in synthesis, expression, solubility, and screening.
analysis.methods: The study proposes Gen‑YSD, a three‑stage computational pipeline: Stage 1 uses an SE(3)‑equivariant diffusion model with hard constraints on developability, charge, hydrophobicity, and glycosylation; Stage 2 simulates yeast surface display with realistic flow‑cytometry noise and gating; Stage 3 applies Pareto optimization across binding affinity, viscosity, yield, and epitope diversity; AlphaFold2, ESMFold, and RFdiffusion provide predicted structures at scale.
analysis.results: Candidates emerging from the pipeline have already survived virtual testing that mirrors the physics and chemistry of real experiments, but no quantitative performance metrics are reported.
analysis.contribution: The pipeline targets pan‑hantavirus immunity by designing broadly neutralizing antibodies against Gn and Gc glycoproteins, addressing the difficulty of expressing these glycoproteins and shifting failure detection from wet‑lab to in silico to reduce attrition.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; empirical validation, experimental data, and quantitative outcomes are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Generative AI speeds structural biology but designs often fail because models ignore physical constraints, causing synthesis and expression problems. Methods: Gen‑YSD is a three‑stage pipeline using SE(3) diffusion with developability constraints, realistic yeast surface‑display simulation, and Pareto optimization, leveraging AlphaFold2, ESMFold, and RFdiffusion. Results: Virtual candidates passed in‑silico testing, though no quantitative results are given. Contribution: The approach aims to create broadly neutralizing pan‑hantavirus antibodies, reducing wet‑lab attrition. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; experimental validation and detailed data are not reported.

title: Climate change as an amplifier of hantavirus risk in South Asia: a neglected nexus.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is serologically documented in South Asian humans and rodent reservoirs, with antibodies found in occupational risk groups in India, an independent association with chronic kidney disease reported in Sri Lanka, and co‑infection with leptospirosis observed in more than one‑fifth of hospitalized leptospirosis patients (A1).
analysis.methods: Methods are not reported in the supplied evidence (A2).
analysis.results: Seroprevalence in humans and rodents is established; occupational groups in India show anti‑hantavirus antibodies; Sri Lankan data show an independent link to chronic kidney disease; >20% of hospitalized leptospirosis patients are co‑infected with hantavirus (A1).
analysis.contribution: The letter highlights the neglected climate‑hantavirus nexus, identifies structural vulnerabilities that may amplify transmission risk, and calls for integrated flood‑response surveillance and One Health coordination across South Asia (A3).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract/letter is available; no primary data, study design, or detailed methods are provided, and the interaction with monsoon floods, urbanization, and climate‑driven rodent ecology remains unexamined (A2).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus seroprevalence is documented in South Asian humans and rodents, with occupational antibodies in India, an association with chronic kidney disease in Sri Lanka, and >20% co‑infection in leptospirosis patients. Methods: Not reported. Results: Established seroprevalence, occupational risk, CKD link, and notable co‑infection rates. Contribution: The letter emphasizes the climate‑hantavirus nexus, structural vulnerabilities, and urges integrated flood‑response surveillance and One Health coordination. Limitations: Only an abstract/letter is available; no primary data or methods, and climate‑related intersections remain unexamined.

title: Hantavirus disease: A review of global epidemiology, immunopathogenesis, clinical management, and future research priorities

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome, motivating a comprehensive review.
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes immunopathogenic endothelial dysfunction, climate variability, land‑use change, biodiversity loss, and rodent dynamics that shape spillover risk and geographic expansion.
analysis.current_state: Current diagnostic tools comprise serology, RT‑PCR and next‑generation sequencing, with emerging point‑of‑care technologies being critically evaluated.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include inadequate surveillance in South Asia and Africa, limited understanding of Andes virus human‑to‑human transmission, insufficient validation of rapid diagnostics, and unresolved mechanisms of immune‑mediated pathology.
analysis.future_research: A One‑Health framework is proposed to strengthen global preparedness through enhanced surveillance, outbreak prediction, and accelerated development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe hemorrhagic fever and pulmonary syndromes, prompting a global review. Main directions: The review focuses on immunopathogenic endothelial injury and ecological drivers such as climate and land‑use change that influence spillover. Current state: Diagnostics rely on serology, RT‑PCR and sequencing, with point‑of‑care tests under evaluation. Gaps: Surveillance gaps in South Asia/Africa, unclear Andes virus human transmission, limited rapid test validation, and unresolved immune pathology persist. title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge shows immune cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine release correlating with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: Detailed temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined, limiting therapeutic targeting.
analysis.future_research: Future studies should longitudinally profile immune subsets, dissect signaling pathways driving dual roles, and evaluate interventions that modulate immune responses without compromising viral clearance.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV). Main directions: The review examines dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells during HTNV infection. Current state: Immune cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine release correlating with disease severity. Gaps: Detailed temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined. Future research: Longitudinal profiling of immune subsets, dissection of signaling pathways, and evaluation of interventions that modulate immune responses without compromising viral clearance.

title: Host hybridization enabled the emergence of a reassorted hantavirus lineage.

analysis.background: Reassortment of segmented viruses can generate novel strains, but concrete examples of adaptive advantages in nature apart from influenza are rare (A1).
analysis.methods: The study sampled 58 trapping sites across a 12.5 km hybrid zone of the common vole (Microtus arvalis), sequencing Tula orthohantavirus from 127 infected voles and conducting phylogenomic analyses (A4, A5).
analysis.results: Twenty‑seven reassortant viruses were detected, representing three independent reassortment events, with a dominant strain carrying a reassorted M‑segment; five N‑terminal residues showed clade‑specific variation, two under positive selection, and structural modeling confirmed a unique glycoprotein conformation (A5, A6, A7, A8).
analysis.contribution: The findings illustrate the first example of host‑virus co‑hybridization, indicating that hybrid zones can act as hotspots for the emergence of transgressive hantavirus lineages potentially adapted to hybrid hosts (A9).
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: Reassortment of segmented viruses can generate novel strains, but concrete examples of adaptive advantages in nature apart from influenza are rare. Methods: The study sampled 58 sites across a 12.5 km hybrid zone of common voles (Microtus arvalis), sequencing Tula orthohantavirus from 127 infected voles and performed phylogenomic and in‑silico glycoprotein analyses. Results: Twenty‑seven reassortants were found, representing three independent events, with a dominant strain carrying a reassorted M‑segment; five N‑terminal residues showed clade‑specific variation, two under positive selection, and a unique structural conformation. Contribution: This provides the first example of host‑virus co‑hybridization, showing hybrid zones can foster emergence of transgressive hantavirus lineages potentially adapted to hybrid hosts. Limitations: No explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir, while humans acquire infection through spillover exposure.
analysis.methods: The study develops a stochastic delay differential model using an SIR–SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations, incorporating Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; numerical simulations are performed with Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite difference methods.
analysis.results: The analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, with human infections arising from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote disease extinction; all three numerical methods yield consistent solutions for small time steps, while the SNSFD scheme preserves positivity and shows superior stability under larger steps and stronger perturbations.
analysis.contribution: The model provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing hantavirus transmission risk, highlighting that controlling infection within the rodent reservoir is the most effective strategy for reducing disease persistence and limiting human spillover, and demonstrating the suitability of the SNSFD method for simulating stochastic epidemic systems with delays.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir, while humans acquire infection through spillover exposure. Results: The analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, with human infections arising from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote disease extinction; all three numerical methods yield consistent solutions for small time steps, while the SNSFD scheme preserves positivity and shows superior stability under larger steps and stronger perturbations. title: A Stochastic Hantavirus Model with Environmental Reservoir

analysis.background: Hantaviruses circulate in an ecological web linking rodent dynamics, contaminated environmental substrates and accidental human hosts, causing two severe syndromes for which no licensed antiviral therapy exists (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors formulate and rigorously analyse a coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model that joins a rodent reservoir with chronic lifelong shedding, an environmental viral compartment, and a dead‑end human SEIR population (A2).
analysis.results: The deterministic system yields a basic reproduction number R₀ that decomposes additively into direct and indirect components (A3); disease‑free and endemic equilibria are globally asymptotically stable with R₀ as the exact threshold (A4); a variational exponent Λ is introduced, with Λ < 0 guaranteeing almost‑sure exponential extinction even when R₀ > 1 (A7); forcing the environmental decay rate with Shaanxi temperature reproduces the winter peak of HFRS and gives a periodic reproduction number Rₚₑᵣ₀ ≈ 2.15 versus R₀ = 1.63 (A10, A11).
analysis.contribution: The work provides a rigorous theoretical threshold for hantavirus persistence (A4), introduces a novel extinction criterion based on Λ (A7), and demonstrates that realistic climatic forcing can reproduce observed seasonal and interannual incidence patterns (A10‑A12).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed parameter values, data sources, and empirical validation beyond the reported numerical illustrations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses circulate among rodents, environment, and humans, causing severe disease with no licensed antivirals (A1). Methods: A coupled SEIR‑SEIV stochastic model linking rodent, environmental, and human compartments was formulated and analysed (A2). Results: R₀ splits into direct and indirect parts (A3); equilibria are globally stable with R₀ as the threshold (A4); a variational exponent Λ predicts extinction even if R₀>1 (A7); temperature forcing reproduces winter peaks and yields a periodic Rₚₑᵣ₀≈2.15 versus R₀=1.63 (A10‑A11). Contribution: Provides a rigorous threshold, a new extinction criterion, and links model dynamics to observed seasonal patterns (A4, A7, A10‑A12). Limitations: Only abstract provided; detailed data and validation are not reported.

title: Hantavirus infection in a child: diagnostic challenges and clinical case

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease that manifests with hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening pathology in children worldwide and in Ukraine.
analysis.methods: The authors present a case report of a 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine; diagnosis relied on detection of IgM and IgG antibodies to hantavirus using ELISA and immunoblotting.
analysis.results: The child experienced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, demonstrating that hantavirus infection can mimic other inflammatory diseases and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhagic signs, and thrombocytopenia.
analysis.contribution: The report illustrates diagnostic challenges and raises clinical awareness of hantavirus infection in the pediatric population.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare zoonotic disease causing hemorrhagic syndrome and renal failure and is a severe, potentially life‑threatening condition in children worldwide and in Ukraine. Methods: A case report of a 14‑year‑old child from Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, diagnosed by IgM/IgG ELISA and immunoblotting. Results: The child developed hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome, showing that hantavirus can mimic other inflammatory diseases and should be considered in differential diagnosis of fever, renal failure, hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia. Contribution: The report highlights diagnostic challenges and raises clinical awareness in pediatrics. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus: A Comprehensive Narrative Review of Virology, Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations, Diagnostics, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses causing severe zoonotic diseases (HFRS and HPS/HCPS) with significant morbidity and mortality.
analysis.main_directions: Transmission occurs via aerosolised rodent excreta, with over 50 rodent species as reservoirs; pathogenesis involves endothelial infection and cytokine storm; diagnosis relies on ELISA and RT‑PCR, while therapeutic options are limited to supportive care and early ribavirin for HFRS.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge confirms the two major clinical syndromes, aerosol transmission, limited regional vaccines for HTNV/SEOV, and ribavirin’s benefit in HFRS but not in HPS.
analysis.gaps: Human‑to‑human spread is rare, licensed vaccines are scarce, antiviral therapies are lacking, and efficacy of ribavirin in HPS remains unproven, highlighting critical knowledge gaps.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on next‑generation sequencing for outbreak tracking, development of monoclonal antibodies, mRNA and subunit vaccines, and surveillance of ecological drivers linked to climate change.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed negative‑sense RNA viruses causing severe zoonotic diseases (HFRS and HPS/HCPS) with significant morbidity and mortality. Main directions: Transmission occurs via aerosolised rodent excreta, with over 50 rodent species as reservoirs; pathogenesis involves endothelial infection and cytokine storm; diagnosis relies on ELISA and RT‑PCR, while therapeutic options are limited to supportive care and early ribavirin for HFRS. Current state: Current knowledge confirms the two major clinical syndromes, aerosol transmission, limited regional vaccines for HTNV/SEOV, and ribavirin’s benefit in HFRS but not in HPS. Gaps: Human‑to‑human spread is rare, licensed vaccines are scarce, antiviral therapies are lacking, and efficacy of ribavirin in HPS remains unproven, highlighting critical knowledge gaps. Future research: Future work should focus on next‑generation sequencing for outbreak tracking, development of monoclonal antibodies, mRNA and subunit vaccines, and surveillance of ecological drivers linked to climate change.

title: The Natural Killer Cell Landscape in the Natural History of Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome in a Chilean Cohort.

analysis.background: HCPS caused by Andes Orthohantavirus has case‑fatality rates up to 40% and the innate immune determinants of disease severity are poorly defined.
analysis.methods: Multiparameter flow cytometry and unsupervised UMAP clustering were performed on PBMCs from 13 Chilean HCPS patients stratified by severity and nine healthy donors.
analysis.results: Severe HCPS showed coordinated disruption of the CD56dim NK cell compartment, with reduced subset frequencies, loss of the NKG2C+CD57+ adaptive‑like pool, and impaired IFN‑γ production and degranulation; these deficits were absent in mild patients and persisted partially after recovery. CD56dimCD16+ NK cell frequencies correlated negatively with viral load across all acute patients, independent of severity.
analysis.contribution: The work establishes severe HCPS as a state of selective functional impairment of the most cytotoxically competent NK cells during the early acute phase, advancing understanding of HCPS immunopathogenesis.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based on abstract‑only data with a limited sample size and lack detailed methodological and longitudinal information.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by Andes Orthohantavirus has case‑fatality up to 40% and innate immune determinants of severity are poorly defined. Methods: Multiparameter flow cytometry and unsupervised UMAP clustering were applied to PBMCs from 13 Chilean HCPS patients (stratified by severity) and nine healthy donors. Results: Severe HCPS showed coordinated disruption of the CD56dim NK cell compartment, including reduced frequencies, loss of the NKG2C+CD57+ adaptive‑like subset, and impaired IFN‑γ production and degranulation, whereas mild cases were unaffected; deficits persisted partially after recovery. CD56dimCD16+ NK cell frequencies correlated negatively with viral load across all acute patients, independent of severity. Contribution: The study demonstrates that severe HCPS is characterized by selective functional impairment of the most cytotoxically competent NK cells during the early acute phase, advancing understanding of HCPS immunopathogenesis. Limitations: Findings are based on abstract‑only data with a limited sample size and lack detailed methodological and longitudinal information.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease of considerable public health importance.
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights evolving epidemiological patterns, interactions among environmental factors, rodent reservoirs, and human exposure, and discusses pathogenesis, clinical spectrum, diagnostics, and supportive management.

analysis.gaps: Key gaps are limited effective therapies, insufficient surveillance, and need for timely diagnosis and preventive measures.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rodent‑borne zoonosis of public health importance. Current state: Knowledge of virology and clinical features is consolidated, but treatment remains largely supportive with research into new diagnostics and therapies. Gaps: Effective antivirals, robust surveillance, and rapid diagnosis are lacking. Future research: Priorities include stronger surveillance, specific antiviral development, rapid point‑of‑care tests, and preventive measures such as rodent control and vaccination.

title: Differentiated Contact Tracing for Emerging Zoonotic Hantavirus and Ebolavirus Infections: Lessons from the 2026 Andes Virus (MV Hondius) and Bundibugyo Virus Outbreaks.

analysis.background: The May 2026 simultaneous outbreaks of Andes virus on the MV Hondius cruise ship and Bundibugyo virus in Central Africa underscore the need to understand and optimize contact‑tracing for emerging zoonotic hemorrhagic fevers (A1, A5).
analysis.methods: ANDV cases involved passengers and crew from 23 countries with >600 contacts traced across 32 territories, while BDBV involved >1000 laboratory‑confirmed cases in the DRC and Uganda; the paper compares the contact‑tracing and active‑surveillance protocols applied to each pathogen (A2, A3, A10).
analysis.results: ANDV produced 13 cases (12 confirmed, 1 probable) and 3 deaths, with transmission sustained across three generations and one asymptomatic PCR‑positive contact later developing symptoms; BDBV caused >1000 confirmed cases and >250 deaths, with no documented major pre‑symptomatic transmission (A1, A3, A6, A7).
analysis.contribution: The perspective synthesizes epidemiologic, molecular, diagnostic, therapeutic (favipiravir, tocilizumab, Icatibant) and vaccine (USAMRIID DNA) data to guide differentiated tracing strategies for these distinct pathogens (A8, A10).
analysis.limitations: The abstract provides limited methodological detail, and the infectiousness of pre‑symptomatic ANDV RNA remains uncertain (A6, A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The May 2026 simultaneous outbreaks of Andes virus on the MV Hondius cruise ship and Bundibugyo virus in Central Africa underscore the need to optimize contact‑tracing for emerging zoonotic hemorrhagic fevers. Methods: ANDV involved passengers and crew from 23 countries with >600 contacts traced across 32 territories, while BDBV involved >1000 laboratory‑confirmed cases in the DRC and Uganda; protocols for contact‑tracing and active surveillance were compared. Results: ANDV caused 13 cases (12 confirmed, 1 probable) and 3 deaths, with transmission across three generations and one asymptomatic PCR‑positive contact later symptomatic; BDBV caused >1000 cases and >250 deaths, with no major pre‑symptomatic transmission. Contribution: The paper integrates epidemiologic, molecular, diagnostic, therapeutic and vaccine information to inform differentiated tracing strategies. title: Person-to-Person Transmission of Andes Virus (ANDV): A Systematic Review of Transmission Dynamics, Viral Shedding, and Public Health Implications.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus with documented person-to-person transmission, yet key parameters of transmission timing, viral shedding, and public health management remain incompletely defined.
analysis.main_directions: The review identified 33 studies (17,204 individuals, 2,221 confirmed cases, 135 secondary cases) showing person-to-person transmission as primary or co-occurring in 20 papers, with median incubation 20.8 days and serial interval 21.8 days; secondary attack rates were higher among sexual and close contacts, and ANDV RNA was detected in blood, saliva, respiratory secretions, urine, breast milk, and semen, with rare culture-confirmed replication-competent virus.
analysis.current_state: Current evidence confirms biological plausibility of close-contact transmission and supports prolonged monitoring and risk-stratified follow-up of high-risk contacts, but recommendations such as post-discharge counselling remain provisional.
analysis.gaps: Uncertainties persist regarding the infectiousness of RNA-positive samples, the precise timing and magnitude of viral shedding, and the effectiveness of current public health interventions, highlighting methodological limitations and the need for standardized virological sampling.
analysis.future_research: Prospective contact studies, standardized virological sampling, and genomic confirmation are needed to refine transmission dynamics and inform preparedness in endemic and non-endemic regions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus with documented person-to-person transmission, yet key parameters of transmission timing, viral shedding, and public health management remain incompletely defined. Main directions: The review identified 33 studies (17,204 individuals, 2,221 confirmed cases, 135 secondary cases) showing person-to-person transmission as primary or co-occurring in 20 papers, with median incubation 20.8 days and serial interval 21.8 days; secondary attack rates were higher among sexual and close contacts, and ANDV RNA was detected in blood, saliva, respiratory secretions, urine, breast milk, and semen, with rare culture-confirmed replication-competent virus. Current state: Current evidence confirms biological plausibility of close-contact transmission and supports prolonged monitoring and risk-stratified follow-up of high-risk contacts, but recommendations such as post-discharge counselling remain provisional. Gaps: Uncertainties persist regarding the infectiousness of RNA-positive samples, the precise timing and magnitude of viral shedding, and the effectiveness of current public health interventions, highlighting methodological limitations and the need for standardized virological sampling. Future research: Prospective contact studies, standardized virological sampling, and genomic confirmation are needed to refine transmission dynamics and inform preparedness in endemic and non-endemic regions.

title: Potent in vitro antiviral activity of 4'-Fluorouridine against diverse orthohantaviruses including Andes virus.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause severe diseases such as HFRS and HPS and lack FDA‑approved antivirals.
analysis.methods: The authors used a Seoul virus minigenome system to confirm that 4'-fluorouridine (EIDD-2749) inhibits the hantavirus polymerase, then tested the compound against a panel of 16 hantaviruses from Old and New World lineages.
analysis.results: 4'-fluorouridine showed dose‑dependent inhibition of all tested viruses with EC50 values uniformly in the low‑to sub‑micromolar range.
analysis.contribution: The study identifies 4'-fluorouridine as a highly potent, pan‑hantavirus inhibitor and a promising candidate for further preclinical development.
analysis.limitations: Findings are limited to in‑vitro data presented in an abstract; no in‑vivo efficacy, safety, or pharmacokinetic information is provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe HFRS and HPS and have no approved antivirals. Methods: Using a Seoul virus minigenome system, the study confirmed 4'-fluorouridine targets the polymerase and evaluated it against 16 diverse hantaviruses. Results: The compound inhibited all viruses dose‑dependently with low‑to sub‑micromolar EC50s. Contribution: This establishes 4'-fluorouridine as a potent pan‑hantavirus inhibitor and a candidate for preclinical work. Limitations: Only in‑vitro abstract data are reported; no in‑vivo or safety data are available.

title: First reported case of Andes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome treated with a combination of favipiravir, ribavirin, icatibant and baricitinib.

analysis.background: The paper reports the first documented Andes virus hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) case in Spain and the first worldwide use of a regimen combining two antivirals and two host‑directed drugs.
analysis.methods: A 69‑year‑old Spanish man repatriated after an ANDV outbreak was managed in a high‑level isolation unit; diagnosis was made by RT‑PCR and serology while asymptomatic; under compassionate use he received ribavirin (IV then oral), oral favipiravir, subcutaneous icatibant, and oral baricitinib with serial clinical, laboratory, and radiological monitoring.
analysis.results: Within 24 h of diagnosis the patient developed hypoxaemia, bilateral B‑lines, thrombocytopaenia, lymphopaenia and hyponatraemia; the regimen started on day 0 (baricitinib added day +1) and clinical, laboratory and radiological recovery began from day +2 without invasive ventilation; ribavirin was stopped day +5 for mild diarrhoea and favipiravir on day +8 for severe diarrhoea, while baricitinib completed day +10.
analysis.contribution: The authors claim this is the first combined antiviral and host‑directed therapy for HCPS and the first use of favipiravir in hantavirus infection, suggesting the favourable outcome supports prospective evaluation of such regimens in preparedness protocols.
analysis.limitations: The report is a single‑patient case study presented only as an abstract, providing no comparative data, limited detail on dosing or long‑term follow‑up, and thus limited generalisability.

analysis.summary_en: Background: First documented Andes virus HCPS case in Spain and first worldwide use of combined antivirals and host‑directed drugs. Methods: 69‑year‑old repatriated patient diagnosed by RT‑PCR/serology in a high‑level isolation unit received ribavirin, favipiravir, icatibant, and baricitinib with serial monitoring. Results: Within 24 h he developed hypoxaemia and laboratory abnormalities; treatment began day 0, recovery started day +2 without invasive ventilation; ribavirin stopped day +5 (diarrhoea), favipiravir stopped day +8 (diarrhoea), baricitinib completed day +10. Contribution: First reported combined regimen and favipiravir use for hantavirus, supporting future evaluation. Limitations: Single‑case abstract only, no control or detailed data, limiting generalisability.

title: When rare zoonoses travel: Andes virus, hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, and the preparedness gap.

analysis.background: The perspective highlights a critical preparedness gap revealed by a suspected Andes virus (ANDV) hantavirus cluster on the cruise ship MV Hondius, illustrating challenges of rare zoonoses in mobile, closed, medically limited settings.
analysis.main_directions: It examines the multi‑country outbreak of severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, diagnostic and epidemiological hurdles, and risk factors such as European ethnicity and αVβ3 integrin variation.
analysis.current_state: ANDV is unique among hantaviruses for its documented limited person‑to‑person transmission during close, prolonged contact, with known virology and pathogenesis details.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include the absence of specific antiviral therapy, limited validated severity biomarkers, and incomplete understanding of host genetic susceptibility.
analysis.future_research: The authors call for integrated One Health surveillance, maritime medicine preparedness, and targeted research on diagnostics, biomarkers, and therapeutic options to prevent international spread.

analysis.summary_en: Background: A suspected ANDV cluster on a cruise ship exposed a preparedness gap for rare zoonoses in mobile, closed settings. Main directions: The outbreak highlighted diagnostic, clinical, and epidemiological challenges, plus risk factors like European ethnicity and integrin variation. Current state: ANDV uniquely can transmit person‑to‑person during close contact, with established virology and pathogenesis. Gaps: No specific antivirals, limited severity biomarkers, and uncertain host genetic susceptibility remain. Future research: Integrated One Health surveillance, maritime medicine preparedness, and studies on diagnostics, biomarkers, and therapies are needed.
