title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact, and no FDA‑approved vaccine exists.
analysis.methods: An immunoinformatics workflow was used to predict B‑cell and T‑cell epitopes from the glycoproteins of SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV, assess allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage, build two vaccine constructs with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants, and perform molecular docking to TLR4 and in silico immune simulations.
analysis.results: Molecular docking suggested plausible TLR4 interactions, and immune simulations predicted robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses with strong antibody production and memory cells persisting beyond one year.
analysis.contribution: The work provides a rational framework for designing broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccines, supporting pre‑clinical development of universal vaccine candidates.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on in silico analyses; experimental confirmation is required and only an abstract is available.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat, and no FDA‑approved vaccine exists. Methods: Immunoinformatics predicted B‑ and T‑cell epitopes from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV glycoproteins, evaluated safety and conservation, built two constructs with adjuvants, and performed docking to TLR4 and immune simulations. Results: Docking indicated potential TLR4 interaction; simulations forecast robust, balanced humoral and cellular immunity with antibodies and memory lasting >1 year. Contribution: Provides a rational framework for broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccine design, guiding pre‑clinical development. Limitations: Conclusions are based only on in silico data; experimental validation is needed and only an abstract is provided.

title: Rapid response and surveillance for high-risk contacts during May 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a Northern Italy experience

analysis.background: An outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius prompted international contact tracing and highlighted the need for rapid response to imported infections.
analysis.methods: The Lombardy Region, Northern Italy, notified a contact‑tracing chain involving four individuals (two direct flight‑related contacts and their two accompanying close contacts) who were assessed through regional pathways and referred to Luigi Sacco University Hospital for clinical and public health management.
analysis.results: All four contacts underwent RT‑PCR testing for ANDV, which was negative in each case; they were managed under precautionary measures proportionate to their exposure category.
analysis.contribution: This experience demonstrates how imported pathogens can create complex regional demands even when population‑level risk is low and underscores the value of predefined preparedness frameworks.
analysis.limitations: The authors note that the experience may not be fully generalizable and that evidence on person‑to‑person transmission remains limited.

analysis.summary_en: Background: An outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius prompted international contact tracing and highlighted the need for rapid response to imported infections. Methods: The Lombardy Region, Northern Italy, notified a contact‑tracing chain involving four individuals (two direct flight‑related contacts and their two accompanying close contacts) who were assessed through regional pathways and referred to Luigi Sacco University Hospital for clinical and public health management. Results: All four contacts underwent RT‑PCR testing for ANDV, which was negative in each case; they were managed under precautionary measures proportionate to their exposure category. Contribution: This experience demonstrates how imported pathogens can create complex regional demands even when population‑level risk is low and underscores the value of predefined preparedness frameworks. Limitations: The authors note that the experience may not be fully generalizable and that evidence on person‑to‑person transmission remains limited.

title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding distribution, raising global public health concern. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review examines how ecological disruption, climate variability, urbanization and increased global mobility heighten hantavirus risk in mass‑gathering contexts such as religious events, refugee settlements, cruise tourism, sporting events and temporary accommodations. (A2)
analysis.current_state: Current evidence indicates that transmission occurs primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, while the possibility of human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain. (A5)
analysis.gaps: Controversies persist regarding limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic infection, and the lack of robust diagnostic, reporting and surveillance systems for mass gatherings. (A6)
analysis.future_research: Strengthening integrated One Health frameworks, ecological and genomic surveillance, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems is urged to improve preparedness. (A8)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rod‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding distribution, raising global public health concern. Main directions: The review examines how ecological disruption, climate variability, urbanization and increased global mobility heighten hantavirus risk in mass‑gathering contexts such as religious events, refugee settlements, cruise tourism, sporting events and temporary accommodations. Current state: Transmission is understood to occur primarily via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, while human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain. Gaps: Unresolved issues include possible limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic infection, and inadequate diagnostics and surveillance for mass gatherings. Future research: Strengthening One Health approaches, ecological and genomic monitoring, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems are recommended.

title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses on Cruise Ships: Impact and Prevention

analysis.background: The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and cruise ships creates high‑density, mobile environments that facilitate the emergence and spread of zoonotic diseases, posing a significant global public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: This is a narrative review; specific study design, sample selection, and data sources are not reported in the abstract.
analysis.results: The authors identify hantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, avian influenza) associated with animal reservoirs such as peri‑urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals at ports and tourist destinations; they discuss the influence of climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change on transmission dynamics and highlight epidemiological risks during ecotourism excursions and challenges for maritime surveillance.
analysis.contribution: The review stresses the importance of strengthening integrated One Health surveillance and prevention systems to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed methods, data, and quantitative results are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The growth of maritime tourism and cruise ships creates dense, mobile settings that facilitate zoonotic disease emergence. Methods: This narrative review does not report specific methods in the abstract. Results: Hantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, avian influenza) are linked to reservoirs such as rodents, bats, and migratory birds at ports; climate change and coastal urbanization affect transmission, and ecotourism excursions pose epidemiological risks. Contribution: The authors call for integrated One Health surveillance and prevention to improve maritime tourism safety. Limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed methods and quantitative data are not reported.

title: Transient Andes orthohantavirus RNA detection in an asymptomatic healthcare worker following indirect exposure during hospital care of an imported case, the Netherlands, 2026.

analysis.background: Following an outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infections on a cruise ship in May 2026, a healthcare worker not directly involved in caring for an imported ANDV case in the Netherlands had a single low‑positive ANDV PCR result.

analysis.results: The healthcare worker remained asymptomatic, showed no seroconversion, and all subsequent samples tested negative after the initial low‑positive PCR.
analysis.contribution: The finding may indicate that asymptomatic ANDV infections with low‑level viraemia can occur after indirect exposure.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; details on sample size, timing, and broader context are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, with Shaanxi Province among the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods analyzed spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS and age‑distribution changes in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023.
analysis.results: A total of 34,265 HFRS cases were reported, 25,737 males and 8,528 females; cases were concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, incidence fluctuated markedly, the primary peak occurred from October to January, the proportion of cases in the 15–60 year age group decreased, while the proportion in those > 60 years increased by 150.94 % (from 11.68 % to 29.31 %).
analysis.contribution: The 20‑year surveillance data highlight a significant rise in HFRS among individuals over 60 years, suggesting vaccine coverage limitations and informing potential age‑expanded vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in China, with Shaanxi Province among the most affected. Methods: Descriptive epidemiology examined spatial, temporal, and age distribution from 2004–2023. Results: 34,265 cases reported, mainly in the Guanzhong Plain, with a peak Oct–Jan; the >60 year age group’s proportion rose 150.94 % (11.68 %→29.31 %). Contribution: Findings suggest vaccine coverage gaps and support age‑expanded vaccination. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Bile acid signaling at the gut-vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown (A1). Clinical severity varies widely and no targeted endothelial‑protective therapies exist (A2). Recent data link hantaviruses to gut microbiome remodeling and bile acid receptors FXR/TGR5 that inhibit NF‑κB‑mediated endothelial inflammation (A3).
analysis.methods: The study re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines (A6–A9) and examined metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota reshaping (A5). Endothelial cells were profiled for FXR/TGR5 expression (A10).
analysis.results: SEOV‑infected human/rat lung endothelial cells showed conserved VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log2FC = +1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC = +0.32, padj = 0.016) with unchanged FXR (A6–A7). SEOV infection suppressed Nfkb1 (P < 0.05) and downregulated Slc10a2 (P = 0.028) (A8). PUUV 3D vessel chips exhibited IL6 elevation (log2FC = +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and disrupted BA transporters (ABCC3 log2FC = −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²) (A9). TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells (A10). HTNV upregulated CH25H, blocking HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis and depleting BA precursors (A12).
analysis.contribution: The authors propose a unified pathogenic model in which hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and impaired cholesterol metabolism deplete circulating FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving constitutive inhibition of endothelial NF‑κB and monocyte NLRP3 inflammasomes and exacerbating capillary leakage (A13). They outline tiered testable predictions for clinical multi‑omics cohorts, in‑vitro receptor modulation assays, and in‑vivo pharmacological interventions, positioning the gut microbiota–BA–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus diseases (A14–A15).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection triggers life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown, with variable clinical severity and no targeted endothelial‑protective therapies. Methods: The authors re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines and examined metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota reshaping. Results: SEOV‑infected endothelial cells showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation, NF‑κB suppression, and downregulation of bile acid transporters; PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation and disrupted BA transporters; TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells; HTNV upregulated CH25H, depleting BA precursors. Limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile acid signaling to viral vascular damage is absent; the study is hypothesis‑driven and based on re‑analysis of existing datasets.

title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in the Americas, motivating a review of their emergence in cruise‑ship contexts.
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes Andes virus’s limited person‑to‑person transmission, tiered diagnostic strategies, and the need for integrated One Health maritime surveillance and governance.
analysis.current_state: Clinically, hantavirus infection presents with severe endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and abrupt cardiopulmonary or renal failure after a nonspecific febrile prodrome.
analysis.gaps: There are no curative antivirals or licensed vaccines, and data on transmission dynamics aboard ships remain sparse, limiting effective outbreak control.
analysis.future_research: Future work should establish integrated One Health surveillance on vessels, standardize maritime health protocols, and assess rapid diagnostics and mental‑health protections for crew during isolation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses causing severe renal or cardiopulmonary syndromes, prompting review of cruise‑ship risks. Main directions: Focus on Andes virus person‑to‑person spread, diagnostic tiering, and One Health maritime surveillance. Current state: Disease features severe endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and rapid organ failure after a vague fever. Gaps: No curative antivirals or vaccines and limited shipboard transmission data hinder response. Future research: Deploy integrated One Health vessel surveillance, standardize health governance, and evaluate rapid diagnostics and crew mental‑health safeguards.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health, and current PCR assays for related hantaviruses can yield false negatives and have limited sensitivity.
analysis.methods: The study engineered a light‑activatable magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); detection requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA, with exonuclease III‑driven walking releasing a trigger strand that initiates CHA and produces a fluorescent signal.
analysis.results: The platform displayed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM for DBSV RNA with a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM, and was validated using human serum specimens.
analysis.contribution: This dual‑amplification strategy offers a novel, spatiotemporally controllable approach for ultrasensitive RNA detection, indicating considerable potential for early viral diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract‑level information is available; detailed study design, sample size, population characteristics, and comprehensive clinical performance data are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health, and current PCR assays for related hantaviruses can yield false negatives and have limited sensitivity. Methods: The study engineered a light‑activatable magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); detection requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA, with exonuclease III‑driven walking releasing a trigger strand that initiates CHA and produces fluorescence. Results: The platform showed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM for DBSV RNA with a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM, and was validated using human serum specimens. Contribution: This dual‑amplification strategy provides a novel, spatiotemporally controllable tool for ultrasensitive RNA detection, offering potential for early diagnosis and field monitoring. Limitations: Only abstract‑level information is provided; detailed study design, sample size, and clinical performance data are not reported.

title: Hantavirus Andes: cómo el cambio en el conocimiento nos lleva a un nuevo enfoque en las medidas de intervención para su abordaje. Andes hantavirus: how evolving knowledge is leading to a new approach to intervention measures

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the hantavirus of greatest relevance in Argentina and Chile because it is transmitted both environmentally and intrinsically person‑to‑person, creating a unique public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: This paper is a narrative review that analyzes scientific evidence published between 2020 and 2026 on salivary and respiratory transmission, viral persistence during convalescence, environmental stability, and new epidemiological surveillance protocols in Argentina.
analysis.results: The 2018‑19 outbreak showed a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts during the prodromal period; ultrastructural studies detected ANDV antigens in respiratory epithelium and saliva, with viral RNA found up to ~16 days after symptom onset; a Chilean cohort detected viral RNA up to day 22 in plasma, leukocyte layer, gingival crevicular fluid and saliva, with 42 % of samples containing infected cells and 88.9 % infectivity in Vero E6 culture; environmental experiments showed viability on stainless‑steel surfaces for up to five days, with an estimated half‑life of 23.6 h.
analysis.contribution: The synthesis argues for moving beyond reactive measures toward comprehensive One‑Health preventive strategies and underpins the adoption of selective respiratory isolation (SRI) for close contacts.
analysis.limitations: The article is a non‑systematic review without new primary data, confined to evidence from Argentina/Chile and the 2020‑2026 period, limiting generalizability.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus is the most relevant hantavirus in Argentina and Chile due to its environmental and person‑to‑person transmission, posing a unique public‑health challenge. Methods: This narrative review examines literature from 2020‑2026 on transmission mechanisms, viral persistence, environmental stability, and surveillance in Argentina. Results: The 2018‑19 outbreak yielded a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts in the prodromal phase; studies found viral antigens in respiratory and salivary tissues, RNA up to ~16 days, and persistence up to day 22 in multiple compartments with 42 % infected cells and 88.9 % infectivity in culture; the virus remains viable on steel for up to five days (half‑life ≈23.6 h). Contribution: The review supports a shift to comprehensive One‑Health preventive strategies and justifies selective respiratory isolation for close contacts. Limitations: It is a non‑systematic review lacking primary data and limited to Argentina/Chile evidence from 2020‑2026.

title: Hantavirus: comprender el reservorio para prevenir la enfermedad Hantavirus: Understanding the Reservoir to Prevent the Disease

analysis.background: HCPS in humans represents the final link of a complex chain involving environment, wildlife reservoir, virus, and human activities, making early understanding essential for prevention (A1‑A3).
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Systematic monitoring documented an exceptional increase in rodent numbers and massive dispersal to rural houses during the 2000‑2001 bamboo flowering (F15‑F16); a later 2018‑2019 flowering produced similar rodent surges but no rise in human cases (F18). Capture probability of infected Oligoryzomys longicaudatus is roughly double in peridomestic versus wild habitats (F23), and larger adult male rodents show higher infection prevalence (F31).
analysis.contribution: The paper demonstrates that real‑time ecological data and coordinated inter‑institutional actions enable timely preventive measures, focused risk communication, barriers to rodent entry, and temporary access restrictions, improving public‑health response (F20, F34‑F36).
analysis.limitations: The article offers descriptive observations without detailed methodological description or quantitative risk modeling, limiting causal inference and precise risk estimation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS in humans is the final link of a complex chain of environment, wildlife reservoir, virus, and human activity (A1‑A3). Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Monitoring showed massive rodent population growth and dispersal during the 2000‑2001 bamboo flowering (F15‑F16), but the 2018‑2019 event, despite similar rodent surges, did not increase human cases (F18); infected rodent capture probability is about twice as high in peridomestic settings (F23), and larger adult males have higher prevalence (F31). Contribution: Real‑time ecological information and coordinated inter‑institutional response enabled timely preventive actions, targeted communication, barriers to rodent entry, and temporary access restrictions (F20, F34‑F36). Limitations: No detailed methods or quantitative risk analysis are provided, restricting causal interpretation.

title: Misinformation about the recent hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship.

analysis.background: The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius generated substantial misinformation on social media (A1).
analysis.methods: The editorial addresses six prominent myths concerning pandemic potential, airborne transmission via ventilation, unproven treatments, cruise‑travel risks, influenza‑like transmissibility, and claims the outbreak was fabricated (A2).
analysis.results: Current evidence indicates that ANDV can rarely spread between people after close and prolonged contact, and its transmission differs fundamentally from that of highly contagious respiratory viruses (A3).
analysis.contribution: The outbreak highlights the need for scientists, public‑health authorities, healthcare professionals, and the media to communicate evidence rapidly and transparently (A4).
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: The recent Andes virus outbreak on cruise ship MV Hondius generated substantial misinformation on social media (A1). Methods: The editorial reviews six myths about pandemic potential, airborne spread, unproven treatments, cruise‑travel risk, influenza‑like transmissibility, and claims the outbreak was fabricated (A2). Results: Evidence shows ANDV can rarely spread between people after close, prolonged contact and its transmission differs from that of highly contagious respiratory viruses (A3). Contribution: The event underscores the need for rapid, transparent communication by scientists, public‑health officials, clinicians, and media (A4). Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a fulminant yet potentially reversible respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care.
analysis.methods: The article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system.
analysis.results: Recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA‑ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence.
analysis.contribution: Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology‑guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO‑capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Unmasking Hantavirus: Insights into Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations and Next Generation Therapies

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure and shedding pathways.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers hantavirus history, global burden, virology, morphology, replication cycle, reservoir hosts, transmission dynamics, immunopathology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic approaches, and recent advances in supportive care, antiviral agents, and preventive measures.
analysis.current_state: Hantaviruses cause two severe clinical syndromes—Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome—with high morbidity and mortality, and current knowledge on immunopathology and diagnostics is summarized.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps remain in early diagnosis, effective antiviral therapies, vaccine development, well‑designed clinical trials, and comprehensive global surveillance.
analysis.future_research: Continued scientific investigation and reinforced public‑health initiatives are required to close diagnostic, therapeutic, vaccine, and surveillance gaps.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure and shedding pathways. Main directions: The review covers hantavirus history, global burden, virology, morphology, replication, reservoirs, transmission, immunopathology, clinical syndromes, diagnostics, and recent advances in supportive care, antivirals, and prevention. Current state: HPS and HFRS cause high morbidity and mortality, with current insights into immunopathology and diagnostics summarized. Gaps: Early diagnosis, effective therapies, vaccines, robust trials, and global surveillance remain insufficient. Future research: Ongoing scientific work and strengthened public‑health actions are needed to address these gaps.

title: Hantavirus Infections: A Review of Pathogenesis, Diagnosis,Treatment, and Vaccine Developments

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses causing severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), with high mortality and limited antiviral options, prompting a comprehensive review of their epidemiology, pathogenesis, and emerging countermeasures.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on advances in molecular virology, immunology, and structural biology, highlighting host‑targeted antiviral strategies, TFEB‑mediated lysosomal degradation, monoclonal antibody therapies, mRNA vaccine platforms, and improved molecular diagnostics and metagenomic surveillance.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge identifies >50 hantavirus species, variable mortality (≤1% for Puumala to ~40% for Andes/Sin Nombre), annual global cases of 150–200 k, and a clear endothelial‑mediated pathogenesis driven by cytokines and complement.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include limited diagnostic capacity, asymptomatic infections inflating under‑reporting, lack of specific antivirals, and emerging climate‑driven transmission dynamics.
analysis.future_research: Future work should prioritize host‑targeted therapeutics, TFEB‑based lysosomal pathways, monoclonal antibody development, mRNA vaccine trials, and expanded metagenomic surveillance to monitor ecological drivers and early detection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe HFRS and HCPS with high mortality and limited antivirals, prompting a review of epidemiology, pathogenesis, and countermeasures. Main directions: Advances in molecular virology, host‑targeted antivirals, TFEB pathways, monoclonal antibodies, mRNA vaccines, and improved diagnostics and metagenomic surveillance. Current state: >50 species, variable mortality, 150–200 k annual cases, endothelial‑mediated pathogenesis. Gaps: Diagnostic limitations, asymptomatic under‑reporting, lack of antivirals, climate‑driven transmission. Future research: Host‑targeted therapies, TFEB pathways, monoclonal antibodies, mRNA vaccines, and expanded metagenomic surveillance.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, posing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact, and no FDA‑approved vaccine exists; the viral surface glycoprotein is a key vaccine target but its variability limits conventional approaches, while epitope‑based vaccines are a promising alternative.
analysis.methods: The authors used immunoinformatics to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine, analyzing Gn/Gc glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, and ANDV with B‑cell and T‑cell epitope prediction algorithms, then evaluating predicted epitopes for allergenicity, toxicity, conservation, and population coverage; two constructs incorporating β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants were examined for physicochemical properties, structural stability, and immunogenic potential, and molecular docking screened ectodomain compatibility with TLR4.
analysis.results: In silico docking suggested potential TLR4 interactions (requiring experimental confirmation), and immune‑simulation models predicted robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses with antibody production and memory cell persistence exceeding one year.
analysis.contribution: The study provides a rational framework for designing broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccines, supporting pre‑clinical development of next‑generation universal candidates against genetically diverse hantaviruses.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on abstract‑level in silico analyses; experimental validation of docking and immunogenicity is lacking, and the abstract does not report quantitative data beyond qualitative simulation outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe zoonotic disease, lack an FDA‑approved vaccine, and glycoprotein variability hampers conventional vaccines, but epitope‑based designs are promising. Methods: Immunoinformatics was applied to Gn/Gc from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, ANDV, predicting B/T epitopes, assessing allergenicity, toxicity, conservation, population coverage, and constructing two adjuvanted vaccine candidates evaluated for physicochemical stability and TLR4 docking. Results: Docking indicated possible TLR4 interaction, and simulations forecasted robust humoral and cellular immunity with memory lasting >1 year. Contribution: Offers a rational design platform for broad‑spectrum hantavirus vaccines, guiding preclinical development. Limitations: Conclusions derive from abstract‑only, in silico work without experimental confirmation.

title: Rapid response and surveillance for high-risk contacts during May 2026 Andes hantavirus outbreak: a Northern Italy experience

analysis.background: In May 2026 an outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) linked to the cruise ship MV Hondius triggered international contact tracing because of the severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and uncertain person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.methods: Lombardy Region, Northern Italy, received notification of four high‑risk contacts (two flight‑related exposures and their close contacts) and referred them to Luigi Sacco University Hospital, where they were managed according to exposure category and tested for ANDV by RT‑PCR.
analysis.results: RT‑PCR testing was negative for ANDV in all four individuals.
analysis.contribution: The case illustrates how predefined regional preparedness frameworks can enable rapid coordination of surveillance and clinical management for imported high‑consequence pathogens despite low population risk.
analysis.limitations: The report describes only a single chain of four contacts and the authors note that the experience is not fully generalizable to other settings.

analysis.summary_en: Background: In May 2026 an outbreak of Andes hantavirus linked to a cruise ship prompted international contact tracing due to severe disease and uncertain transmission. Methods: Four high‑risk contacts in Lombardy were referred to Luigi Sacco Hospital, managed by exposure category and tested by RT‑PCR. Results: All four tested negative for ANDV. Contribution: The episode shows the value of predefined preparedness frameworks for rapid response to imported pathogens. title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne pathogens with high mortality and expanding distribution, and recent ecological and mobility changes raise concerns for mass gatherings.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers epidemiology, transmission uncertainty, diagnostics, surveillance, and preparedness in settings such as religious events, refugee camps, cruises, sports, and temporary housing, highlighting the 2026 MV Hondius cruise outbreak.
analysis.current_state: Transmission is mainly via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, but limited interpersonal spread, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic cases create uncertainty.
analysis.gaps: Diagnostic limits, underreporting, inadequate environmental surveillance, and absence of mass‑gathering‑specific frameworks hinder response.
analysis.future_research: Integrated One Health surveillance, genomic monitoring, AI‑driven intelligence, and coordinated international response are needed to strengthen preparedness and policy.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne pathogens with high mortality and expanding distribution, and recent ecological and mobility changes raise concerns for mass gatherings. Main directions: The review covers epidemiology, transmission uncertainty, diagnostics, surveillance, and preparedness in settings such as religious events, refugee camps, cruises, sports, and temporary housing, highlighting the 2026 MV Hondius cruise outbreak. Current state: Transmission is mainly via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, but limited interpersonal spread, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic cases create uncertainty. Gaps: Diagnostic limits, underreporting, inadequate environmental surveillance, and absence of mass‑gathering‑specific frameworks hinder response. Future research: Integrated One Health surveillance, genomic monitoring, AI‑driven intelligence, and coordinated international response are needed to strengthen preparedness and policy.

title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses on Cruise Ships: Impact and Prevention

analysis.background: The rapid growth of international maritime tourism has heightened the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a global public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: This paper is a narrative review; specific search strategy and data sources are not reported in the abstract.
analysis.results: The authors identify hantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, avian influenza) linked to animal reservoirs such as peri‑urban rodents, bats, migratory birds and other mammals; they note that climate change, coastal urbanization and environmental change influence transmission dynamics; they highlight epidemiological risks during cruise‑ship ecotourism excursions and challenges for maritime surveillance; they discuss travel‑medicine, biosecurity and infection‑control measures; and they recommend strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems.
analysis.contribution: The review synthesizes current knowledge on reservoir ecology and transmission risks for maritime tourism, emphasizing a One‑Health approach and informing surveillance and prevention strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed methods, data extraction, and quantitative findings are not reported.

Contribution: The review synthesizes reservoir ecology and transmission risks for maritime tourism, emphasizing a One‑Health approach to guide surveillance and prevention. title: Transient Andes orthohantavirus RNA detection in an asymptomatic healthcare worker following indirect exposure during hospital care of an imported case, the Netherlands, 2026.

analysis.background: An outbreak of Andes orthohantavirus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship in May 2026, and a healthcare worker in the Netherlands who was not directly involved in patient care had a single low‑positive ANDV PCR result.
analysis.methods: The authors performed a retrospective investigation that included detailed reconstruction of potential transmission routes.
analysis.results: The healthcare worker remained asymptomatic, showed no seroconversion, and all subsequent samples were PCR‑negative after the initial low‑positive result.
analysis.contribution: The finding suggests that asymptomatic ANDV infection with low‑level viraemia may occur after indirect exposure.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; details on sample size, testing methods, timing, and broader epidemiological context are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: An outbreak of Andes orthohantavirus on a cruise ship led to a low‑positive PCR in a Dutch healthcare worker not directly caring for the case. Methods: A retrospective investigation with transmission‑route reconstruction was conducted. Results: The worker stayed asymptomatic, did not seroconvert, and subsequent samples were negative. Contribution: This may indicate that asymptomatic ANDV infection with low‑level viraemia can follow indirect exposure. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; many methodological details are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyze spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS cases in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023.
analysis.results: A total of 34,265 HFRS cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, geographically concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, with incidence fluctuating markedly over 20 years and a primary peak from October to January; the proportion of cases in the 15–60 year age group decreased, while cases in persons > 60 years increased 150.94% from 11.68% to 29.31%.
analysis.contribution: The 20‑year surveillance shows a significant rise in elderly cases, possibly due to vaccine coverage limitations, and the findings can guide adjustment of prevention measures and consideration of age‑expanded vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, limiting detail on data sources, analytical techniques, and potential confounders.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas. Methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyze spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS cases in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023. Results: A total of 34,265 HFRS cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, geographically concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, with incidence fluctuating markedly over 20 years and a primary peak from October to January; the proportion of cases in the 15–60 year age group decreased, while cases in persons > 60 years increased 150.94% from 11.68% to 29.31%. Contribution: The 20‑year surveillance shows a significant rise in elderly cases, possibly due to vaccine coverage limitations, and the findings can guide adjustment of prevention measures and consideration of age‑expanded vaccination strategies. title: Bile acid signaling at the gut-vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown and capillary leakage.
analysis.methods: The study re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines and incorporated metagenomic reports confirming hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota remodeling in rodent reservoirs.
analysis.results: SEOV‑infected human/rat lung endothelial cells showed VCAM1/ICAM1 upregulation (human VCAM1 log2FC = +1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC = +0.32, padj = 0.016) with unchanged FXR; sustained Nfkb1 suppression (P < 0.05) and day‑15 Slc10a2 downregulation (P = 0.028); PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation (log2FC = +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and BA transporter disruption (ABCC3 log2FC = −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells.
analysis.contribution: The authors propose a model linking hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and virus‑mediated cholesterol‑metabolism blockade to depletion of FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving NF‑κB inhibition and exacerbating capillary leakage, thereby identifying the gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target.
analysis.limitations: Direct causal evidence connecting bile‑acid signaling to viral vascular damage is absent; the work remains hypothesis‑driven and requires further clinical, in‑vitro, and in‑vivo validation.

title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne pathogens causing severe renal or cardiopulmonary syndromes (A1), and the 2026 Andes virus cluster on a cruise ship highlighted how modern travel can amplify a rare zoonosis (A3).
analysis.main_directions: The review discusses environmental spillover via aerosolized rodent excreta (A2), the unique limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus (A5), and the need for integrated One Health surveillance and maritime health governance (A9).
analysis.current_state: Clinically, hantavirus infection presents with endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and rapid cardiopulmonary or renal failure (A7), while management relies on early field diagnostics and molecular confirmation due to lack of antivirals or vaccines (A8).
analysis.gaps: Evidence gaps include insufficient data on maritime outbreak preparedness and the dynamics of person‑to‑person spread in shipboard settings, compounded by the absence of licensed therapeutics (A9).
analysis.future_research: Future work should develop standardized maritime surveillance protocols, evaluate transmission risk factors on ships, and explore therapeutic and vaccine candidates within a One Health framework (A9, A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne pathogens causing severe disease, and the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship cluster showed travel can magnify this threat. Main directions: The review covers environmental spillover, the unique limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, and calls for One Health surveillance and maritime health governance. Current state: Clinical presentation involves endothelial dysfunction and rapid organ failure; management depends on early field diagnostics and molecular confirmation due to no approved antivirals or vaccines. Gaps: Limited data on shipboard outbreak preparedness and transmission dynamics, plus lack of therapeutics. Future research: Implement standardized maritime surveillance, study shipboard transmission risk, and develop antivirals/vaccines within a One Health approach.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus posing a potential threat to human health; existing PCR assays for related hantaviruses risk false negatives and have low accuracy/sensitivity.
analysis.methods: The study designed a photo‑activatable magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA), requiring UV irradiation and target RNA for dual activation, with exonuclease III‑driven walking releasing a trigger strand that initiates CHA‑mediated fluorescence.
analysis.results: The platform showed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑, and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM for DBSV RNA with a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM, and was validated using human serum specimens.
analysis.contribution: This dual‑amplification, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker strategy offers a novel, ultrasensitive approach for early hantavirus RNA diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: The abstract provides no information on sample size, clinical validation details, or potential cross‑reactivity, and full methodological data are not available (not reported in the supplied evidence).

title: Hantavirus Andes: cómo el cambio en el conocimiento nos lleva a un nuevo enfoque en las medidas de intervención para su abordaje. Andes hantavirus: how evolving knowledge is leading to a new approach to intervention measures

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the hantavirus of greatest relevance in Argentina and Chile because it is transmitted both environmentally and intrinsically person‑to‑person, creating a unique public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: The author conducted a narrative review of scientific evidence published between 2020 and 2026 on salivary and respiratory transmission, viral persistence during convalescence, environmental stability, and new epidemiological surveillance protocols in Argentina.
analysis.results: The 2018‑19 outbreak yielded a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts during the prodromal period; ultrastructural studies detected ANDV antigens in respiratory epithelium and saliva, with viral RNA found up to ~16 days after symptom onset; a Chilean prospective cohort identified RNA in plasma, leukocytes, gingival crevicular fluid and saliva up to day 22, with 42 % of samples containing infected cells and 88.9 % infectivity in Vero E6 culture; environmental testing showed viability on stainless steel for up to five days (half‑life ≈ 23.6 h).
analysis.contribution: The review emphasizes the need for proactive, One‑Health‑based preventive strategies and documents the impact of selective respiratory isolation (SRI) for close contacts as a new intervention measure.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus is the most important hantavirus in Argentina and Chile, notable for both environmental and person‑to‑person transmission, posing a public‑health challenge. Methods: A narrative review of evidence from 2020‑2026 examined salivary/respiratory transmission, viral persistence, environmental stability, and surveillance protocols. Results: The 2018‑19 outbreak showed a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts in the prodromal phase; viral antigens and RNA were detected in respiratory and salivary sites up to ~16 days, RNA persisted to day 22 in multiple compartments with 42 % infected cells and 88.9 % culture infectivity; the virus remained viable on steel for up to five days (half‑life ≈ 23.6 h). Contribution: Highlights proactive One‑Health preventive strategies and the effectiveness of selective respiratory isolation for contacts. Limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus: comprender el reservorio para prevenir la enfermedad Hantavirus: Understanding the Reservoir to Prevent the Disease

analysis.background: When a case of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) is diagnosed, the infection results from a complex chain linking environment, wildlife reservoirs, the virus, and human activities; understanding this chain is essential for anticipating risky situations and guiding prevention strategies (A1‑A3).
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Massive seed‑production events such as the 2000‑2001 bloom in Parque Nacional Lanín caused an exceptional increase in rodent numbers and their dispersal toward rural dwellings, whereas the 2018‑2019 bloom in Villa La Angostura, despite a similar rodent surge, did not produce additional human cases (F14‑F19). Capture probability of an infected Oligoryzomys longicaudatus is roughly double in peri‑domestic rural settings compared with wild habitats (F23), and adult male rodents exhibit higher infection prevalence, likely due to aggressive horizontal transmission (F31).
analysis.contribution: The article emphasizes that integrating ecological monitoring with clinical surveillance and coordinated inter‑institutional actions enables timely risk communication and targeted preventive measures at the rodent‑human interface (F33‑F36).
analysis.limitations: The paper does not provide explicit methodological details or stated limitations; as an editorial, it lacks primary data reporting and formal limitation discussion.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS in humans is the final link of a complex environment‑reservoir‑virus‑human chain, and understanding it is key for risk anticipation (A1‑A3). Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Large seed‑production events (e.g., 2000‑2001 Lanín bloom) led to exceptional rodent population growth and rural dispersal, yet later blooms (2018‑2019 Villa La Angostura) did not increase human cases; peri‑domestic capture of infected O. longicaudatus is about twice that in wild habitats, and adult male rodents show higher infection prevalence (F14‑F19, F23, F31). Contribution: Integrating ecological monitoring with clinical surveillance and coordinated inter‑institutional actions improves timely risk communication and targeted prevention at the rodent‑human interface (F33‑F36). Limitations: No explicit methods or limitation statements are provided; the work is an editorial rather than primary research.

title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU

analysis.background: HCPS due to Andes virus is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care.
analysis.methods: The article addresses eleven practical ICU management questions, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system.
analysis.results: Recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA‑ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence.
analysis.contribution: Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival depends on early suspicion, physiology‑guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO‑capable centres for severe cardiopulmonary failure.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence

title: Unmasking Hantavirus: Insights into Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations and Next Generation Therapies

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis driven by exposure to infected rodents and their shedding pathways.
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights recent refinements in supportive interventions, antiviral therapies, clinical management strategies, and preventive/control measures.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge covers immunopathology, the clinical manifestations of HPS and HFRS, and existing diagnostic approaches.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps remain in early diagnosis, effective therapeutics, vaccine development, well‑designed clinical trials, and global surveillance.
analysis.future_research: The authors call for sustained scientific investigation and robust public‑health initiatives to address diagnostic and therapeutic deficiencies and improve patient outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure. Main directions: Recent advances in supportive care, antivirals, clinical management, and prevention are highlighted. Current state: Immunopathology, HPS/HFRS clinical features, and diagnostics are described. Gaps: Early diagnosis, effective treatments, vaccines, trials, and surveillance are lacking. Future research: Ongoing scientific work and strengthened public‑health actions are needed to close these gaps.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease.
analysis.methods: The authors adapted an existing rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set for Sin Nombre virus to create a pan‑American assay (HantAmeriQ) for both human and rodent surveillance (study design described in A5).
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World hantaviruses with limits of detection from 25 copies/reaction (Blue River virus) to 28,000 copies/reaction (Bayou virus) and identified genetically diverse viruses from North, Central and South America (A6, A7).
analysis.contribution: The assay can be incorporated into public‑health and research laboratories across the Americas and shows strong potential for diagnostic use in clinical laboratories and rodent‑based field studies (A4, A10).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methodology, sample numbers, and field validation are not reported (not reported in the supplied evidence).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Methods: The authors adapted an existing rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set for Sin Nombre virus to create a pan‑American assay (HantAmeriQ) for both human and rodent surveillance (A5). Results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World hantaviruses with limits of detection from 25 to 28,000 copies/reaction and identified diverse viruses from North, Central and South America (A6, A7). Contribution: The assay can be incorporated into public‑health and research labs across the Americas and shows strong potential for diagnostic use in clinical laboratories and rodent‑based field studies (A4, A10). Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methodology, sample numbers, and field validation are not reported.

title: Hantavirus Infections: A Review of Pathogenesis, Diagnosis,Treatment, and Vaccine Developments

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are zoonotic RNA viruses causing hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) with high mortality and emerging public‑health relevance (F4,F5,F6,F16,F17,F18).
analysis.main_directions: Recent advances focus on host‑targeted antivirals, TFEB‑mediated lysosomal degradation, monoclonal antibodies, mRNA vaccines, and improved diagnostics and surveillance (F7,F8,F9,F10).
analysis.current_state: Pathogenesis involves endothelial dysfunction mediated by TNF‑α, IL‑6, VEGF, and complement, with innate and adaptive immunity contributing to clearance and pathology; epidemiology shows 150–200 k annual cases, higher burden in China and Europe, and climate‑driven transmission dynamics (F5,F6,F16,F17,F18,F20,F21,F22,F23,F24,F25,F26,F27,F28,F29,F30,F31,F32,F33,F34).
analysis.gaps: Uncertainty remains regarding person‑to‑person transmission, immune‑mediated endothelial injury mechanisms, and limited specific antiviral therapies (F17,F18,F31).
analysis.future_research: Targeted host‑based therapies, TFEB modulation, monoclonal antibody development, mRNA vaccine platforms, and enhanced molecular diagnostics and metagenomic surveillance should be prioritized (F8,F9,F10).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HCPS with high mortality and growing public‑health importance. Main directions: Host‑targeted antivirals, TFEB‑mediated lysosomal degradation, monoclonal antibodies, mRNA vaccines, and advanced diagnostics and surveillance. Current state: Endothelial dysfunction driven by cytokines and complement underlies disease; epidemiology shows 150–200 k annual cases, high burden in China and Europe, and climate‑driven transmission. Gaps: Uncertainty about person‑to‑person spread, immune‑mediated endothelial injury, and lack of specific antivirals. Future research: Develop host‑based therapies, TFEB modulators, monoclonal antibodies, mRNA vaccines, and strengthen molecular diagnostics and metagenomic surveillance.

title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding distribution, prompting concern for global public health. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on how ecological disruption, climate change, urbanization and global mobility raise hantavirus risk in mass‑gathering settings such as religious events, refugee camps, cruise ships, and sports venues. (A2)
analysis.current_state: Evidence shows that transmission is mainly via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, though the extent of human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain. (A5)
analysis.gaps: Key uncertainties include the possibility of limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic infection, and the lack of robust diagnostic and surveillance systems for mass gatherings. (A6)
analysis.future_research: The authors call for integrated One Health frameworks, enhanced ecological and genomic surveillance, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response mechanisms to improve preparedness. (A8)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding distribution, raising global health concern. Main directions: The review examines how ecological disruption, climate variability, urbanization and increased mobility heighten hantavirus risk in mass‑gathering contexts such as religious festivals, refugee settlements, cruise ships, and sporting events. Current state: Transmission is understood to occur primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, while human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain. Gaps: Unresolved issues include possible limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic infections, and inadequate diagnostic and surveillance capacity for mass gatherings. Future research: Strengthening One Health approaches, ecological and genomic surveillance, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems are recommended to bolster preparedness.

title: Revisiting Animal Reservoirs of Hantavirus and Other Zoonotic Viruses on Cruise Ships: Impact and Prevention

analysis.background: The sustained growth of international maritime tourism and the expansion of the cruise industry have increased the importance of emerging zoonotic diseases as a significant challenge to global public health (A1). Cruise ships create complex epidemiological settings with high density, rapid mobility, and constant human‑animal‑environment interaction that favor introduction and spread of infectious agents (A2).
analysis.methods: The article is a narrative review; specific search strategy, inclusion criteria, and data sources are not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.results: The review identifies hantaviruses and other zoonotic viruses (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, avian influenza) associated with animal reservoirs and vectors in ports, tourist destinations, and tropical ecosystems (A3). It describes the ecology of reservoirs such as peri‑urban rodents, bats, migratory birds, and other mammals (A4). It discusses the impact of climate change, coastal urbanization, and environmental change on viral transmission dynamics (A5). Epidemiological risks linked to international cruises are highlighted, especially exposure during ecotourism excursions and pathogen introduction (A6). The authors address travel medicine, biosecurity, infection control, and a One Health approach (A7).
analysis.contribution: The review emphasizes strengthening integrated surveillance and prevention systems to ensure safer, more sustainable, and resilient maritime tourism (A8).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed methods, data extraction, quantitative results, and full discussion are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The growth of cruise tourism raises zoonotic disease risk due to dense, mobile ship environments (A1, A2). Methods: This is a narrative review; specific methods are not reported. Results: Hantaviruses and other zoonoses (dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, avian influenza) linked to reservoirs (rodents, bats, migratory birds) are highlighted, with climate change and urbanization influencing transmission, and cruise‑related exposure risks emphasized (A3‑A7). Contribution: The authors call for integrated surveillance and prevention to protect maritime tourism (A8). Limitations: Only the abstract is provided, lacking detailed methodology and quantitative data.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, with Shaanxi Province among the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were applied to analyze spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023, using surveillance data and an inactivated bivalent vaccine against Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV).
analysis.results: A total of 34,265 HFRS cases were reported, 25,737 males and 8,528 females; cases were concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, with incidence fluctuating markedly over 20 years and a primary peak from October to January. The proportion of cases in the 15–60 year age group decreased, while the proportion in those > 60 years increased by 150.94 % (from 11.68 % to 29.31 %).
analysis.contribution: The study highlights a significant shift toward older age groups, suggesting potential vaccine coverage limitations and informing adjustments to prevention strategies, including age‑expanded vaccination.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in China, with Shaanxi Province heavily affected. Methods: Descriptive epidemiology analyzed spatial, temporal, and age distribution of HFRS from 2004–2023, using surveillance data and a bivalent HTNV/SEOV vaccine. Results: 34,265 cases reported (25,737 males, 8,528 females); concentrated in Guanzhong Plain, incidence fluctuated, peak Oct–Jan. Proportion in 15–60 yr decreased; > 60 yr increased 150.94 % (11.68 %→29.31 %). Contribution: Findings suggest vaccine coverage gaps and support age‑expanded vaccination strategies. Limitations: Not reported.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) (A1).

Gaps: Detailed dynamics and functional phenotypes of immune subsets across disease stages are still unclear (A2). Future research: Combining clinical and mechanistic insights to map the protective‑pathogenic balance will inform therapeutic target discovery (A5).

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure.
analysis.methods: The study develops a stochastic delay differential SIR–SIR model for interacting rodent and human populations, incorporating Brownian perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; qualitative properties, equilibria, reproduction numbers, and extinction/persistence conditions are derived and examined.
analysis.results: Analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise via spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote disease extinction; numerical simulations with Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and SNSFD methods confirm these findings, with SNSFD offering superior stability at larger time steps.
analysis.contribution: The model provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing hantavirus transmission risk, highlighting that controlling infection within the rodent reservoir is the most effective strategy for reducing human spillover and demonstrating the utility of the SNSFD method for simulating stochastic epidemic systems with delays.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Bile acid signaling at the gut-vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown and capillary leakage, with clinical severity varying widely and no targeted endothelial‑protective therapies.
analysis.methods: The study re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines, complemented by metagenomic reports confirming hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota remodeling in rodent reservoirs.
analysis.results: In SEOV‑infected human/rat lung endothelial cells, VCAM1/ICAM1 were upregulated (human VCAM1 log2FC = +1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC = +0.32, padj = 0.016) with unchanged FXR; SEOV‑infected rat lung showed sustained Nfkb1 suppression (P < 0.05) and day‑15 Slc10a2 downregulation (P = 0.028); PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation (log2FC = +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and BA transporter disruption (ABCC3 log2FC = −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells across all datasets.
analysis.contribution: The authors propose that hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and virus‑mediated cholesterol‑metabolism blockade deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving constitutive NF‑κB inhibition and exacerbating capillary leakage, thereby identifying the gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target and outlining testable predictions for future validation.
analysis.limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile‑acid signaling to hantavirus‑induced vascular damage is absent; the study relies on re‑analysis of existing datasets and metagenomic reports without experimental confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection triggers life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome driven by endothelial barrier breakdown and capillary leakage, with clinical severity varying widely and no targeted endothelial‑protective therapies. Methods: The study re‑analyzed three public GEO datasets (GSE245916, GSE7271, GSE270172) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines, complemented by metagenomic reports confirming hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota remodeling in rodent reservoirs. Results: In SEOV‑infected human/rat lung endothelial cells, VCAM1/ICAM1 were upregulated (human VCAM1 log2FC = +1.17, P = 0.023; rat Icam1 log2FC = +0.32, padj = 0.016) with unchanged FXR; SEOV‑infected rat lung showed sustained Nfkb1 suppression (P < 0.05) and day‑15 Slc10a2 downregulation (P = 0.028); PUUV 3D vessel chips displayed IL6 elevation (log2FC = +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and BA transporter disruption (ABCC3 log2FC = −1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable in endothelial cells across all datasets. Contribution: The authors propose that hantavirus‑induced gut dysbiosis and virus‑mediated cholesterol‑metabolism blockade deplete FXR/TGR5 agonistic bile acids, relieving constitutive NF‑κB inhibition and exacerbating capillary leakage, thereby identifying the gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target and outlining testable predictions for future validation. title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HPS in the Americas, and the 2026 Andes virus cluster on the MV Hondius cruise highlighted how international travel can amplify a rare zoonosis.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on environmental spillover via aerosolized rodent excreta, the unique limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, and the need for One Health surveillance and maritime health governance.
analysis.current_state: Hantavirus infection presents with severe endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and rapid cardiopulmonary or renal failure after a nonspecific febrile prodrome, and diagnosis relies on early field‑ready blood counts followed by molecular confirmation.
analysis.gaps: The narrative review’s methodology may miss unpublished data; the precise exposure timeline before embarkation remains unclear; and integrated maritime biosecurity frameworks are still lacking.
analysis.future_research: Developing rapid point‑of‑care antivirals or vaccines and establishing standardized One Health surveillance and legal protections for crew during outbreaks are priority actions.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses causing HFRS in Eurasia and HPS in the Americas, and the 2026 Andes virus cluster on the MV Hondius cruise highlighted how international travel can amplify a rare zoonosis. Main directions: The review focuses on environmental spillover via aerosolized rodent excreta, the unique limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, and the need for One Health surveillance and maritime health governance. Current state: Hantavirus infection presents with severe endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and rapid cardiopulmonary or renal failure after a nonspecific febrile prodrome, and diagnosis relies on early field‑ready blood counts followed by molecular confirmation. Gaps: The narrative review’s methodology may miss unpublished data; the precise exposure timeline before embarkation remains unclear; and integrated maritime biosecurity frameworks are still lacking. Future research: Developing rapid point‑of‑care antivirals or vaccines and establishing standardized One Health surveillance and legal protections for crew during outbreaks are priority actions.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health, and existing PCR‑based detection for hantaviruses can yield false‑negative results.
analysis.methods: The authors designed a light‑controllable fluorescence assay that combines a photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); activation requires UV irradiation and target RNA, and exonuclease III drives the walker to release a trigger strand that initiates CHA.
analysis.results: The platform showed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM with a linear range from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶ pM, and was validated with human serum specimens.
analysis.contribution: This dual‑amplification strategy demonstrates a novel, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker approach for ultrasensitive RNA detection, offering potential for early hantavirus diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed experimental procedures, sample numbers, and broader performance data are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health, and existing PCR‑based detection for hantaviruses can yield false‑negative results. Methods: The authors designed a light‑controllable fluorescence assay that combines a photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); activation requires UV irradiation and target RNA, and exonuclease III drives the walker to release a trigger strand that initiates CHA. Results: The platform showed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM with a linear range from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶ pM, and was validated with human serum specimens. Contribution: This dual‑amplification strategy demonstrates a novel, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker approach for ultrasensitive RNA detection, offering potential for early hantavirus diagnosis and field monitoring. Limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed experimental procedures, sample numbers, and broader performance data are not reported.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Mortality Risk Stratification in Hantavirus Infection: A Global Study Across Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection remains a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential for timely triage and resource allocation.
analysis.methods: A retrospective supervised learning analysis was performed on 10,000 global hantavirus patient records (both HFRS and HCPS) with demographic, clinical, epidemiological, and treatment variables; mortality was the binary outcome. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models were trained and compared on a held‑out test set using ROC‑AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1‑score, and Brier score after preprocessing that removed identifiers, handled missing values, encoded categories, selected features, and corrected class imbalance.
analysis.results: The cohort included 8,938 recovered and 1,062 deceased cases (mortality rate 10.62%). Logistic regression achieved ROC‑AUC 0.858, recall 0.741, precision 0.321, Brier score 0.119; gradient boosting showed comparable AUC 0.857 with higher precision 0.511 and better calibration (Brier 0.076); random forest had markedly low recall (0.085). Severity, syndrome type, viral load category, age, and geographic setting were the most informative predictors.
analysis.contribution: The findings demonstrate that mortality risk in hantavirus infection can be modeled with routine clinical and epidemiological features, emphasizing sensitivity, calibration, and transparency over raw accuracy for clinical deployment, and support the use of interpretable ML as a practical framework for early risk stratification and external validation.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, making early identification of high‑risk patients crucial for triage. Methods: A retrospective supervised learning study used 10,000 global HFRS and HCPS records with mortality as the outcome; logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were trained and evaluated on a held‑out test set after comprehensive preprocessing. Results: Among 8,938 recoveries and 1,062 deaths (10.62% mortality), logistic regression achieved ROC‑AUC 0.858, recall 0.741, precision 0.321, Brier 0.119; gradient boosting had similar AUC 0.857, precision 0.511, Brier 0.076; random forest showed low recall (0.085); key predictors included severity, syndrome type, viral load, age, and geography. Contribution: The study shows interpretable ML can predict hantavirus mortality, advocating sensitivity, calibration, and transparency for clinical use and supporting external validation. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
