title: Hantavirus Andes: cómo el cambio en el conocimiento nos lleva a un nuevo enfoque en las medidas de intervención para su abordaje. Andes hantavirus: how evolving knowledge is leading to a new approach to intervention measures

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the hantavirus of greatest relevance in Argentina and Chile because it is transmitted both environmentally from rodent excreta and intrinsically person‑to‑person, creating a unique public‑health challenge (A1).
analysis.methods: The paper is a narrative review that collates evidence published between 2020 and 2026 on mechanisms of salivary and respiratory transmission, viral persistence during convalescence, environmental stability, and the impact of new epidemiological surveillance protocols in Argentina (A4).
analysis.results:
The 2018‑19 outbreak analysis yielded a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for infection among close contacts during the pro‑dr

matic period (A23). Prospective data showed viral RNA up to day 22 in plasma, leukocytes, gingival crevicular fluid and saliva, with 42 % of samples containing infected cells and 88.9 % remaining infectious in culture (A33). Environmental studies reported viability on stainless‑steel surfaces for up to five days, with a half‑life of 23.6 h (A36).
analysis.contribution: The review documents how the historic 2018‑19 outbreak led to the implementation of Selective Respiratory Isolation (SRI) for close contacts (A3) and argues that risk mitigation now requires comprehensive One‑Health preventive strategies (A5).
analysis.limitations: The article provides only a synthesis of existing studies; no new primary data were generated, and the scope is limited to evidence from Argentina and Chile up to 2026 (not reported in the supplied evidence).

analysis.summary_en:
Background: Andes hantavirus is the most important hantavirus in Argentina and Chile due to its combined environmental and person‑to‑person transmission, posing a distinct public‑health problem. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes evidence from 2020‑2026 on salivary/respiratory transmission, viral persistence, environmental stability, and new surveillance protocols in Argentina. Results: The 2018‑19 outbreak showed a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts during the pro‑dr

matic phase; viral RNA persisted up to day 22 in multiple compartments, with 42 % of samples containing infected cells and 88.9 % remaining infectious in culture; the virus remained viable on steel for up to five days (half‑life 23.6 h). Contribution: Findings supported the adoption of Selective Respiratory Isolation for close contacts and underscore the need for integrated One‑Health preventive strategies. Limitations: The work is a synthesis of prior studies without new primary data and is confined to Argentine and Chilean contexts up to 2026.

title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) caused by Andes virus is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure that requires timely critical care.
analysis.methods: The article addresses eleven practical ICU‑management questions, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system.
analysis.results: The authors provide recommendations covering early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA‑ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence.
analysis.contribution: Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy consistently improves outcomes, the guidance emphasizes early suspicion, physiology‑guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO‑capable centres to improve survival.
analysis.limitations: The paper is a narrative expert‑opinion piece without original data; specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS due to Andes virus is a fulminant but potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure needing prompt critical care. Methods: The article answers eleven ICU‑management questions based on Chilean clinical experience and research. Results: Recommendations span early recognition, diagnostics, haemodynamic monitoring, fluid/vasoactive strategies, respiratory support, VA‑ECMO referral, daily care, recovery, pitfalls, and low‑evidence therapies. Contribution: With no proven antiviral or immunomodulatory treatment, survival depends on early suspicion, physiology‑guided support, and rapid transfer to ECMO‑capable centres. Limitations: The work is a narrative expert opinion lacking original data; specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Unmasking Hantavirus: Insights into Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations and Next Generation Therapies

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure and shedding pathways.
analysis.main_directions: The review summarizes historical background, global health burden, virology, viral morphology, replication cycle, reservoir hosts, transmission dynamics, immunopathology, clinical manifestations, and diagnostic approaches.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge includes detailed immunopathology, the clinical features of HPS and HFRS, existing diagnostic methods, and recent refinements in supportive care, antiviral therapy, and preventive measures.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps persist in early diagnosis, effective therapeutics, vaccine development, robust clinical trial data, and worldwide surveillance.
analysis.future_research: Addressing these challenges requires sustained scientific investigation and strong public‑health initiatives to develop early diagnostics, novel antivirals, vaccines, and comprehensive surveillance systems.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure. Main directions: The review covers historical background, global burden, virology, morphology, replication, reservoirs, transmission, immunopathology, clinical manifestations, and diagnostics. Current state: Knowledge includes immunopathology, HPS and HFRS clinical features, diagnostics, and recent advances in supportive care, antivirals, and prevention. Gaps: Early diagnosis, effective therapies, vaccine development, trial data, and global surveillance remain insufficient. Future research: Continued scientific work and robust public‑health initiatives are needed to create early diagnostics, novel antivirals, vaccines, and comprehensive surveillance.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease, and their diversity complicates surveillance and diagnostic strategies.
analysis.methods: A pan-America Orthohantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed from an existing rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set originally designed for Sin Nombre virus, enabling use in both human and rodent surveillance.
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection ranging from 25 (Blue River virus) to 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction; it performed as well as or better than a commercial assay for North American hantaviruses and detected diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens across the Americas.
analysis.contribution: The assay offers strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent‑centered field studies, facilitating broader detection of New World hantaviruses.
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease, and their diversity complicates surveillance and diagnostic strategies. Methods: A pan‑America Orthohantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed from an existing rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set originally designed for Sin Nombre virus, enabling use in both human and rodent surveillance. Results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection ranging from 25 (Blue River virus) to 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction; it performed as well as or better than a commercial assay for North American hantaviruses and detected diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens across the Americas. Contribution: The assay offers strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent‑centered field studies, facilitating broader detection of New World hantaviruses. Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors used an immunoinformatics workflow that integrated B‑cell and T‑cell epitope prediction, antigenicity scoring, IFN‑γ induction potential, conservation analysis, and population‑coverage assessment (A6). Viral glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, and ANDV were analyzed (A7), and predicted epitopes were screened for allergenicity, toxicity, conservation, and population coverage (A8). Two vaccine constructs incorporating β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 as adjuvants were evaluated for physicochemical properties, structural stability, and immunogenic potential (A9).
analysis.results: Molecular docking suggested potential compatibility of the constructs with TLR4, indicating possible receptor interaction pending experimental confirmation (A10). In silico immune simulations predicted robust and long‑lasting humoral and cellular responses, with memory cell persistence exceeding one year (A11, A12).
analysis.contribution: The study provides a rational framework for designing broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope vaccines against genetically diverse hantaviruses, supporting pre‑clinical development of universal hantavirus vaccines (A13).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on computational predictions; experimental validation of docking and immune responses is lacking, and the abstract provides no empirical data (A10; abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact. Methods: An immunoinformatics workflow integrated B‑ and T‑cell epitope prediction, antigenicity, IFN‑γ potential, conservation, and population coverage (A6); glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, ANDV were analyzed (A7); epitopes were screened for allergenicity, toxicity, conservation, and coverage (A8); two constructs with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein adjuvants were assessed for physicochemical and structural properties (A9). Results: Docking suggested potential TLR4 compatibility (A10); immune simulations forecasted robust, long‑lasting humoral and cellular immunity with memory >1 year (A11, A12). Contribution: Provides a rational framework for broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccine design (A13). Limitations: Conclusions are based only on in‑silico data; experimental confirmation is required and the abstract offers no empirical evidence (A10).

title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens with high mortality and expanding ecological distribution, prompting global public‑health concern. (A1)
analysis.main_directions: The review examines how ecological disruption, climate variability, urbanization, and increased global mobility heighten hantavirus risk in mass‑gathering settings such as religious events, refugee settlements, cruise tourism, sporting events, and temporary accommodations. (A2)
analysis.current_state: Current evidence indicates that hantavirus transmission occurs primarily through inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, while the possibility of human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain. (A5)
analysis.gaps: Controversies persist regarding limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic infections, complicating risk assessment and preparedness. (A6)
analysis.future_research: Strengthening proactive preparedness via integrated One‑Health approaches, ecological and genomic surveillance, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems is essential. (A8)

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding distribution, raising global concern (A1). Main directions: Ecological change, climate variability, urbanization, and global mobility increase hantavirus risk at mass gatherings such as religious festivals, refugee camps, cruise ships, and sports events (A2). Current state: Transmission is mainly via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, with uncertain human‑to‑human spread (A5). Gaps: Uncertainties about limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic infection hinder risk assessment (A6). Future research: Integrated One‑Health surveillance, genomic monitoring, AI‑driven intelligence, and coordinated international response frameworks are needed (A8).

title: Transient Andes orthohantavirus RNA detection in an asymptomatic healthcare worker following indirect exposure during hospital care of an imported case, the Netherlands, 2026.

analysis.background: An Andes orthohantavirus (ANDV) outbreak occurred on a cruise ship in May 2026, and a Dutch healthcare worker with indirect exposure tested low‑positive by PCR, raising concerns about unnoticed transmission.
analysis.methods: A retrospective investigation was performed in the Netherlands, reconstructing possible transmission routes and testing the worker with PCR and serology; the worker remained asymptomatic and subsequent samples were negative.
analysis.results: The worker had a single low‑positive ANDV PCR result, no symptoms, no seroconversion, and all later specimens tested negative.
analysis.contribution: The report suggests that asymptomatic ANDV infection with low‑level viraemia may follow indirect exposure, informing surveillance and infection‑control considerations.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; details on exposure assessment, sample timing, and broader testing are not reported, limiting inference about infection status and transmission.

analysis.summary_en: Background: An Andes hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship led to a low‑positive PCR detection in a Dutch healthcare worker with indirect exposure, highlighting possible unnoticed transmission. Methods: A retrospective investigation in the Netherlands reconstructed transmission routes and used PCR and serology on the asymptomatic worker; later samples were negative. Results: The worker showed a single low‑positive PCR, no symptoms, and no seroconversion, with subsequent negatives. Contribution: The finding suggests asymptomatic ANDV infection with low‑level viraemia can occur after indirect exposure, informing surveillance and infection‑control. Limitations: Only an abstract is provided; exposure details, timing, and broader testing are not reported, restricting conclusions.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyze spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023.
analysis.results: A total of 34,265 HFRS cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, geographically concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain; incidence fluctuated markedly over 20 years with a primary peak from October to January; the proportion of cases in the 15–60 yr age group decreased, while cases >60 yr increased 150.94% from 11.68% to 29.31%.
analysis.contribution: The 20‑year surveillance shows a significant rise in elderly cases, suggesting possible vaccine‑coverage gaps and supporting age‑expanded vaccination and control measures.
analysis.limitations: No explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence; the study is observational and cannot infer causality.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in mainland China, with Shaanxi Province among the most severely affected areas. Methods: Descriptive epidemiology was applied to surveillance data from Jan 2004–Dec 2023 to assess spatial, temporal, and age distribution. Results: 34,265 cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain; incidence fluctuated, peaking Oct‑Jan; cases 15–60 yr declined, while >60 yr rose 150.94% (11.68%→29.31%). Contribution: The rise in elderly cases may reflect vaccine‑coverage limitations, informing age‑expanded vaccination strategies. Limitations: No explicit limitations are provided; observational design precludes causal inference.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) with high mortality, especially in China.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes of monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T and B cells during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Key immune populations are activated, polarize toward pro‑inflammatory phenotypes, and produce cytokines that correlate with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: While immune cells are essential for viral clearance, they also contribute to immunopathology, yet the precise balance and mechanisms remain unclear.
analysis.future_research: Future studies should integrate clinical and mechanistic data to delineate protective versus pathogenic immune responses and identify therapeutic targets.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV) with high mortality, especially in China. Main directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes of monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T and B cells during HTNV infection. Current state: Key immune populations are activated, polarize toward pro‑inflammatory phenotypes, and produce cytokines that correlate with disease severity. Gaps: While immune cells are essential for viral clearance, they also contribute to immunopathology, yet the precise balance and mechanisms remain unclear. Future research: Future studies should integrate clinical and mechanistic data to delineate protective versus pathogenic immune responses and identify therapeutic targets.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease where rodents act as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure (A1).
analysis.methods: The study formulates an SIR‑SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations (A3), extends it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects (A4), and develops a stochastic delay differential model to capture environmental variability (A2).
analysis.results: Model analysis indicates hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human cases arise from spillover from infected rodents (A9); stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote disease extinction under certain conditions (A10).
analysis.contribution: The stochastic delay model offers a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing reservoir‑driven hantavirus risk and highlights rodent control as the most effective strategy to limit human spillover (A14, A15); the SNSFD numerical scheme provides enhanced stability for simulating such systems (A16).
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is provided; no empirical data, parameter estimation, or field validation is reported (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonosis with human infection via spillover (A1). Methods: An SIR‑SIR model for rodents and humans was built and extended with stochastic noise, discrete delays, and delay‑survival effects (A2‑A4). Results: Persistence is driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human cases stem from spillover, and stochastic/delay effects can lower the reproduction threshold and foster extinction (A9‑A10). Contribution: The model provides a rigorous framework for reservoir‑driven risk assessment and suggests rodent control as key; the SNSFD method offers superior numerical stability (A14‑A16). Limitations: Only an abstract is available; no empirical data or validation are reported (abstract_only).

title: Bile acid signaling at the gut-vascular interface: a novel modulator of hantavirus endothelial barrier dysfunction.

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and cardiopulmonary syndrome by inducing severe endothelial barrier breakdown and systemic capillary leakage; clinical severity varies widely and no endothelial‑protective treatments exist (A1, A2).
analysis.methods: The authors combined metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑driven gut/lung microbiota remodeling in rodent reservoirs (A5) with re‑analysis of three public GEO lung endothelial cell datasets (human and rat) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines (A6‑A9) and evaluated FXR/TGR5 agonists in vitro (A10).
analysis.results: SEOV infection up‑regulated VCAM1 (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023) and ICAM1 (rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016); Nfkb1 was suppressed (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and BA transporter ABCC3 down‑regulated (log2FC ‑1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable; FXR/TGR5 agonists repressed NF‑κB inflammation and mitigated lung vascular injury; HTNV up‑regulated CH25H, blocking HMGCR‑dependent cholesterol synthesis and depleting BA precursors (A6‑A11).
analysis.contribution: The paper proposes a gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target for hantavirus disease and provides a roadmap of testable predictions for multi‑omics cohorts, receptor modulation assays, and pharmacologic interventions (A12‑A15).
analysis.limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile‑acid signaling to hantavirus‑induced vascular damage is absent, and the report is limited to an abstract (A14).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection causes life‑threatening HFRS and HCPS via severe endothelial barrier breakdown and capillary leakage, with variable severity and no endothelial‑protective therapies. Methods: The authors integrated metagenomic reports of hantavirus‑induced gut/lung microbiota changes in rodent reservoirs and re‑analyzed three public GEO lung endothelial cell datasets (human and rat) using standardized RNA‑seq/microarray pipelines; they also tested FXR/TGR5 agonists in vitro. Results: SEOV infection up‑regulated VCAM1 (human log2FC +1.17, P = 0.023) and ICAM1 (rat log2FC +0.32, padj = 0.016); Nfkb1 was suppressed (log2FC +1.22, P = 3.1×10⁻⁸) and BA transporter ABCC3 down‑regulated (log2FC ‑1.44, P = 7.4×10⁻¹²); TGR5 was undetectable; FXR/TGR5 agonists reduced NF‑κB inflammation and lung vascular injury; HTNV induced CH25H, blocking cholesterol synthesis and depleting BA precursors. Contribution: The study proposes a gut‑microbiota–bile‑acid–FXR/TGR5 axis as a repurposable therapeutic target and outlines testable predictions for multi‑omics, receptor assays, and pharmacologic interventions. Limitations: Direct causal evidence linking bile‑acid signaling to hantavirus‑induced vascular damage is absent and the report is limited to an abstract.

title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses that cause severe hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, prompting review of emerging travel‑associated risks.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on environmental spillover via aerosolized rodent excreta, the unique limited person‑to‑person transmission of Andes virus, and the challenges of maritime outbreak preparedness.
analysis.current_state: Andes virus is the only hantavirus with documented limited human‑to‑human spread, especially in close, prolonged contact settings.
analysis.gaps: There is insufficient integrated One Health surveillance and standardized maritime health governance to detect and manage such clusters, and limited data on mental health and labor equity during isolation.
analysis.future_research: Priorities include developing One Health maritime surveillance networks, codifying legal protections for crew, and evaluating rapid field diagnostics and evacuation protocols for hantavirus on ships.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses causing severe hemorrhagic fever or cardiopulmonary syndrome, raising concern over travel‑linked outbreaks. Main directions: The review examines environmental spillover, Andes virus's limited person‑to‑person transmission, and maritime outbreak preparedness. Current state: Andes virus uniquely exhibits limited human‑to‑human spread in close contact. Gaps: Integrated One Health surveillance and standardized maritime health governance are lacking, with scant data on crew mental health and labor equity during isolation. Future research: Build One Health maritime surveillance, legal protections for crew, and assess rapid diagnostics and evacuation strategies for shipboard hantavirus cases.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that poses a potential threat to human health, and existing PCR‑based detection methods for related hantaviruses may produce false negatives.
analysis.methods: The study developed a photoactivated magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); UV irradiation and target RNA activate the walker, Exo III drives the walking process, and the released trigger strand initiates CHA to generate fluorescence; the system was validated in human serum specimens.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Mortality Risk Stratification in Hantavirus Infection: A Global Study Across Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential for timely triage and resource allocation.
analysis.methods: The authors performed a retrospective supervised learning analysis on a global dataset of 10,000 patient records covering Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome, with mortality as the binary outcome; data were preprocessed (identifier removal, missing‑value handling, encoding, feature selection, class‑imbalance correction) and logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models were trained and evaluated on a held‑out test set using ROC‑AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1‑score, and Brier score.
analysis.results: The cohort comprised 8,938 recovered and 1,062 deceased cases (mortality rate 10.62%); logistic regression achieved ROC‑AUC 0.858, recall 0.741, precision 0.321, Brier 0.119; gradient boosting showed ROC‑AUC 0.857, precision 0.511, Brier 0.076; random forest had low recall (0.085); severity, syndrome type, viral load category, age, and geographic setting were the most informative predictors.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that interpretable machine‑learning models can stratify mortality risk in hantavirus infection, highlighting the need to prioritize sensitivity, calibration, and transparency over raw accuracy, and supports external validation of such frameworks in independent cohorts.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is rare but potentially fatal, requiring early risk identification. Methods: A retrospective supervised ML analysis of 10,000 global HFRS and HCPS records used logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost with extensive preprocessing and held‑out test evaluation. Results: Among 8,938 recoveries and 1,062 deaths (10.62% mortality), logistic regression achieved AUC 0.858, recall 0.741, precision 0.321; gradient boosting AUC 0.857, precision 0.511; random forest low recall 0.085; key predictors included severity, syndrome type, viral load, age, geography. Contribution: Shows interpretable ML can effectively stratify hantavirus mortality risk, emphasizing sensitivity, calibration, and transparency, and encourages external validation. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus Andes: cómo el cambio en el conocimiento nos lleva a un nuevo enfoque en las medidas de intervención para su abordaje. Andes hantavirus: how evolving knowledge is leading to a new approach to intervention measures

analysis.background: ANDV is the hantavirus of greatest relevance in Argentina and Chile because it is transmitted environmentally and also has intrinsic person‑to‑person transmissibility, posing a unique public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: A prospective cohort study in Chile (2008‑2022) analyzed viral RNA kinetics in plasma, leukocyte layer, gingival crevicular fluid and saliva of infected individuals.
analysis.results: Close contacts had a relative risk of 101.7 (95% CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) of infection during the pro‑dromic period; viral RNA was detectable up to day 22 post‑infection in multiple compartments, with 42% of samples containing infected cells and 88.9% infectivity in Vero E6 culture; the virus remains viable on stainless‑steel surfaces for up to five days, with an estimated half‑life of 23.6 h.
analysis.contribution: The evidence supports shifting from reactive measures to comprehensive, One‑Health preventive strategies, informing the adoption of Selective Respiratory Isolation for close contacts and enhanced surveillance protocols.
analysis.limitations: Limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: ANDV is the most relevant hantavirus in Argentina and Chile due to its environmental and person‑to‑person transmission. Methods: A prospective Chilean cohort (2008‑2022) examined viral RNA kinetics in plasma, leukocytes, gingival fluid and saliva. Results: Close contacts faced a relative risk of 101.7 (95% CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) during the pro‑dromic phase; viral RNA persisted up to day 22, with 42% of samples showing infected cells and 88.9% infectivity in culture; the virus stays viable on steel up to five days (half‑life 23.6 h). Contribution: Highlights need for proactive, One‑Health preventive measures and validates Selective Respiratory Isolation and updated surveillance. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care.
analysis.methods: The article addresses eleven practical ICU‑management questions, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system; no specific study design, sample size, or patient cohort is reported.
analysis.results: Recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA‑ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence.
analysis.contribution: Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology‑guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO‑capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.
analysis.limitations: Only an expert‑opinion review is presented; no primary data, sample size, or outcome measures are reported, and the evidence is limited to the abstract and partial text.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS due to Andes virus causes rapid respiratory and circulatory failure needing prompt critical care. Methods: The authors answer eleven ICU‑management questions based on Chilean clinical experience; no formal study design is described. Results: They provide guidance on recognition, diagnostics, haemodynamic monitoring, fluid/vasoactive support, respiratory strategies, VA‑ECMO referral, daily care, recovery, pitfalls, and low‑evidence therapies. Contribution: With no proven antiviral, patient survival depends on early suspicion, physiology‑guided support, and swift transfer to ECMO‑capable centers. Limitations: The work is an expert‑opinion review lacking primary data, sample details, or quantitative outcomes.

title: Unmasking Hantavirus: Insights into Pathogenesis, Clinical Manifestations and Next Generation Therapies

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure, prompting review of its impact.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers hantavirus history, global health burden, virology, morphology, replication cycle, reservoir hosts, transmission dynamics, and evaluates supportive interventions, antiviral agents, clinical management, and preventive measures.
analysis.current_state: Hantaviruses cause two severe clinical syndromes—Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) and hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS)—with high morbidity and mortality, and their immunopathology and diagnostic approaches are summarized.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps persist in early diagnosis, effective antiviral therapies, vaccine development, well‑designed clinical trials, and comprehensive global surveillance.
analysis.future_research: Continued scientific investigation combined with strong public‑health initiatives is required to address these gaps and improve patient outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an emerging zoonosis linked to rodent exposure, prompting review of its impact. Main directions: The review covers hantavirus history, global health burden, virology, morphology, replication cycle, reservoir hosts, transmission dynamics, and evaluates supportive interventions, antiviral agents, clinical management, and preventive measures. Current state: Hantaviruses cause two severe clinical syndromes—HPS and HFRS—with high morbidity and mortality, and their immunopathology and diagnostic approaches are summarized. Gaps: Key gaps persist in early diagnosis, effective antiviral therapies, vaccine development, well‑designed clinical trials, and comprehensive global surveillance. Future research: Continued scientific investigation combined with strong public‑health initiatives is required to address these gaps and improve patient outcomes.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease.
analysis.methods: A pan‑America Orthohantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed from an existing Sin Nombre primer‑probe set for use in human and rodent surveillance.
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection between 25 (Blue River virus) and 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction; similar limits were achieved for diverse North and Central/South American viruses, and the assay performed as well or better than a commercial assay for North American hantaviruses but not for South American ones, detecting diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens.
analysis.contribution: The assay shows strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent‑centered field studies.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; sample size, location, host details, and other methodological specifics are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Methods: A pan‑America Orthohantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed from an existing Sin Nombre primer‑probe set for use in human and rodent surveillance. Results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World Orthohantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection between 25 (Blue River virus) and 28,000 (Bayou virus) copies/reaction; similar limits were achieved for diverse North and Central/South American viruses, and the assay performed as well or better than a commercial assay for North American hantaviruses but not for South American ones, detecting diverse hantaviruses from rodent and human specimens. Contribution: The assay shows strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent‑centered field studies. Limitations: Only the abstract is available; sample size, location, host details, and other methodological specifics are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact (A1).
analysis.methods: The authors applied immunoinformatics to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine, analyzing Gn/Gc glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV for B‑cell and T‑cell epitopes, assessing allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage, and constructing two vaccine candidates incorporating β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants (A6,A7,A8,A9).
analysis.results: Molecular docking suggested potential compatibility of the constructs with TLR4, and in silico immune simulations predicted robust, long‑lasting humoral and cellular responses with memory cell persistence exceeding one year (A10,A11,A12).
analysis.contribution: The findings provide a rational framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccines (A13).
analysis.limitations: The study is limited to abstract‑only, in silico analyses; docking and immune simulation results require experimental confirmation (A10).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat with major health impact. Methods: Immunoinformatics was used to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine by analyzing Gn/Gc from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV, evaluating epitopes, and building two constructs with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein adjuvants. Results: Docking indicated potential TLR4 interaction and simulations forecast robust, durable humoral and cellular immunity with memory >1 year. Contribution: Provides a rational framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum hantavirus vaccines. Limitations: Abstract‑only, in silico work; predictions need experimental validation.

title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality, expanding distribution, and potential for international spread, prompting a review of their risks.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on how ecological disruption, climate change, urbanization, and global mobility raise hantavirus threats in mass‑gathering contexts such as religious events, refugee camps, cruise ships, and sports venues.
analysis.current_state: Evidence shows that transmission is mainly via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, though the extent of human‑to‑human spread remains uncertain.
analysis.gaps: Controversies persist regarding limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic infection, and the lack of mass‑gathering‑specific surveillance and diagnostic frameworks.
analysis.future_research: Enhanced preparedness should integrate One Health surveillance, ecological and genomic monitoring, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response mechanisms.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonoses with high mortality and expanding reach, driving a focused review. Main directions: Ecological change, climate variability, urbanization, and global mobility heighten hantavirus risks at mass gatherings like religious festivals, refugee settlements, cruise ships, and sporting events. Current state: Transmission is primarily through inhaled aerosolized rodent excreta, while human‑to‑human spread is uncertain. Gaps: Ongoing debates about limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, asymptomatic cases, and insufficient mass‑gathering‑specific diagnostics and surveillance. Future research: Implement One Health approaches, ecological and genomic surveillance, AI‑based epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyse spatial, temporal and population distribution of HFRS cases in Shaanxi from January 2004 to December 2023.
analysis.results: 34,265 HFRS cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, geographically concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, with incidence fluctuating markedly and a primary peak from October to January; the proportion of cases in >60‑year‑olds increased 150.94% (from 11.68% to 29.31%) while the 15‑60‑year‑old proportion decreased.
analysis.contribution: The 20‑year surveillance shows a significant shift toward older age groups, suggesting the need to adjust prevention measures and consider age‑expanded vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; detailed methods, case definitions and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas. Methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyse spatial, temporal and population distribution of HFRS cases in Shaanxi from January 2004 to December 2023. Results: 34,265 cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain, with incidence fluctuating markedly and a primary peak October‑January; >60‑year‑old cases rose 150.94% (11.68%→29.31%) while 15‑60‑year‑old cases declined. Contribution: The 20‑year data highlight an age shift, informing adjusted control measures and suggesting age‑expanded vaccination. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; detailed methods and analyses are not reported.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets—monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells—during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge shows these cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine release correlating with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: The precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined.
analysis.future_research: Future studies should longitudinally map immune cell phenotypes and cytokine networks to identify therapeutic targets that balance viral clearance with limiting immunopathology.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV). Main directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets—monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells—during HTNV infection. Current state: Current knowledge shows these cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine release correlating with disease severity. Gaps: The precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined. Future research: Future studies should longitudinally map immune cell phenotypes and cytokine networks to identify therapeutic targets that balance viral clearance with limiting immunopathology.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease where rodents are the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure (A1). Recent 2026 updates underscore the ongoing public‑health relevance of reservoir‑driven transmission (A13).
analysis.methods: The study develops a stochastic delay differential SIR–SIR model incorporating Brownian perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects to capture incubation, survival, and environmental uncertainty (A2, A4). Qualitative properties such as positivity, boundedness, feasibility, and well‑posedness are established, and disease‑free and endemic equilibria with deterministic and stochastic reproduction numbers are derived (A5, A6, A7). Numerical simulations employ Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite difference (SNSFD) methods (A8).
analysis.results: Analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise via spillover from infected rodents (A9). Stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote disease extinction (A10). Numerical simulations confirm consistency across methods for small time steps and demonstrate superior positivity preservation and stability of the SNSFD scheme under larger steps and stronger perturbations (A11, A12).
analysis.contribution: The model offers a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing hantavirus transmission risk and highlights that controlling infection within the rodent reservoir is the most effective strategy for reducing persistence and limiting human spillover (A14, A15). The SNSFD method’s stability makes it suitable for simulating stochastic epidemic systems with delays (A16).
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease where rodents are the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure; recent 2026 updates underscore its public‑health relevance. Methods: A stochastic delay differential SIR–SIR model incorporating Brownian perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects was developed; qualitative properties, equilibria, reproduction numbers, and numerical simulations using Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and SNSFD methods were performed. Results: Persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human infections arise via spillover; stochastic perturbations lower the reproduction threshold and can promote extinction; SNSFD preserves positivity and shows superior stability. Contribution: The model provides a rigorous framework for assessing hantavirus transmission risk and emphasizes reservoir control as the key strategy; SNSFD is recommended for simulating stochastic epidemic systems with delays. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne orthohantaviruses causing severe renal or cardiopulmonary syndromes (A1) and the 2026 Andes virus cluster on a cruise ship highlighted how modern travel can amplify a rare zoonosis (A3).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on ANDV’s limited person‑to‑person transmission (A5), tiered field‑ready diagnostics and evacuation strategies (A8), and the need for integrated One Health surveillance and maritime health governance (A9).
analysis.current_state: Old‑world hantaviruses cause HFRS while New‑world strains like ANDV cause HPS/HCPS (A1); ANDV uniquely transmits between humans under close contact (A5); infection presents with endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, and rapid organ failure (A7); no curative antivirals or licensed vaccines exist, so early risk recognition and laboratory confirmation are essential (A8).
analysis.gaps: Evidence on ANDV person‑to‑person spread remains limited to close‑contact settings (A5); the review’s literature window (2019‑2026) may miss earlier data (A4); and systematic maritime preparedness standards are lacking (A9).
analysis.future_research: Develop and validate rapid point‑of‑care diagnostics for field use (A8), conduct longitudinal studies on ANDV transmission dynamics in travel settings (A5), and establish standardized One Health surveillance and legal frameworks for maritime outbreak response (A9).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are globally distributed rodent‑borne pathogens causing severe renal or cardiopulmonary disease, and the 2026 Andes virus cruise‑ship cluster showed travel can magnify a rare zoonosis. Main directions: The review examines ANDV’s limited person‑to‑person spread, tiered diagnostics and evacuation, and calls for One Health maritime surveillance. Current state: Old‑world hantaviruses cause HFRS, New‑world strains like ANDV cause HPS/HCPS, with unique human transmission, severe endothelial dysfunction, and no approved antivirals or vaccines, relying on early detection. Gaps: Limited data on ANDV transmission beyond close contact, a literature window that may omit earlier studies, and absent standardized maritime health governance. Future research: Validate rapid field diagnostics, study ANDV transmission in travel contexts, and create integrated One Health surveillance and legal frameworks for shipboard outbreak preparedness.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health.
analysis.methods: The study uses a photo‑activatable magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) for fluorescence detection; activation requires UV irradiation and target RNA, and exonuclease III drives the walking process to release a trigger strand that initiates CHA.
analysis.results: The platform shows excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑, and triple‑base mismatches, achieves a detection limit of 30 fM with a linear range from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶ pM, and works with human serum specimens.
analysis.contribution: The work introduces a spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker strategy for ultrasensitive RNA detection, offering potential for early viral diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed experimental design, sample size, and validation data are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health. Methods: A photo‑activatable magnetic 3D DNA walker combined with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) and exonuclease III propulsion was used for UV‑controlled fluorescence detection of target RNA. Results: The system discriminates single‑ to triple‑base mismatches, detects DBSV RNA down to 30 fM across a 10⁻¹‑10⁶ pM linear range, and is validated in human serum. Contribution: This novel, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker approach provides a highly sensitive tool for early hantavirus diagnosis and field surveillance. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methods, sample numbers, and broader validation are not reported.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Mortality Risk Stratification in Hantavirus Infection: A Global Study Across Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential for timely triage and resource allocation.
analysis.methods: A retrospective supervised learning analysis was performed on 10,000 global patient records of HFRS and HCPS, including demographic, clinical, epidemiological and treatment variables; mortality was the binary outcome; preprocessing removed identifiers, handled missing data, encoded categories, selected features and corrected class imbalance; logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost models were trained and compared on a held‑out test set using ROC‑AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1‑score and Brier score; SHAP was planned for model interpretation.
analysis.results: The cohort comprised 8,938 recoveries and 1,062 deaths (mortality 10.62%). Logistic regression achieved the highest discrimination (ROC‑AUC 0.858) and recall (0.741) but modest precision (0.321) and weaker calibration (Brier 0.119). Gradient boosting showed comparable AUC (0.857) with better precision (0.511) and calibration (Brier 0.076). Random forest performed poorly with low recall (0.085). Severity, syndrome type, viral load category, age and geographic setting were the most informative predictors.
analysis.contribution: The findings demonstrate that interpretable machine‑learning models can stratify mortality risk in hantavirus infection, emphasizing sensitivity, calibration and transparency for clinical deployment and supporting external validation in independent cohorts.
analysis.limitations: Specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential. Methods: A retrospective supervised learning analysis on 10,000 global HFRS and HCPS records used demographic, clinical, epidemiological and treatment variables; mortality was the binary outcome; logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were trained with preprocessing and class‑imbalance correction, evaluated on a held‑out test set with ROC‑AUC, precision, recall, F1 and Brier score; SHAP was planned for interpretation. Results: The cohort had 8,938 recoveries and 1,062 deaths (mortality 10.62%). Logistic regression achieved ROC‑AUC 0.858 and recall 0.741 (precision 0.321, Brier 0.119); gradient boosting had AUC 0.857, precision 0.511, Brier 0.076; random forest showed low recall 0.085. Severity, syndrome type, viral load, age and geography were top predictors. Contribution: The study shows interpretable ML can stratify hantavirus mortality risk, prioritizing sensitivity, calibration and transparency, and supports external validation. Limitations: Specific limitations are not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Hantavirus Andes: cómo el cambio en el conocimiento nos lleva a un nuevo enfoque en las medidas de intervención para su abordaje. Andes hantavirus: how evolving knowledge is leading to a new approach to intervention measures

analysis.background: ANDV is the most important hantavirus in Argentina and Chile, notable for environmental exposure and confirmed person‑to‑person transmission, creating a unique public‑health challenge.
analysis.methods: This narrative review examined literature from 2020‑2026 on salivary/respiratory transmission, viral persistence, environmental stability and surveillance protocols for ANDV in Argentina.
analysis.results: The 2018‑19 outbreak showed a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts during the prodrome (F23); viral RNA persisted to day 22 in plasma, leukocytes, gingival fluid and saliva, with 88.9 % infectivity in culture (F33); antigens were identified in respiratory epithelium and saliva, supporting droplet and salivary spread (F28‑F31); ANDV remained viable on stainless steel up to five days (half‑life 23.6 h) (F34‑F36).
analysis.contribution: The synthesis supports proactive, One‑Health preventive measures and validates selective respiratory isolation for close contacts, guiding clinical and public‑health policy.
analysis.limitations: The article is a non‑systematic review; primary data are limited to a few outbreak and cohort studies, and detailed methods of cited work are not provided.

analysis.summary_en: Background: ANDV is the most important hantavirus in Argentina and Chile, notable for environmental exposure and confirmed person‑to‑person transmission, creating a unique public‑health challenge. Methods: This narrative review examined literature from 2020‑2026 on salivary/respiratory transmission, viral persistence, environmental stability and surveillance protocols for ANDV in Argentina. Results: The 2018‑19 outbreak showed a relative risk of 101.7 (95 % CI 13.76‑751.86; p < 0.0001) for close contacts during the prodrome; viral RNA persisted to day 22 in plasma, leukocytes, gingival fluid and saliva with 88.9 % infectivity; antigens were found in respiratory epithelium and saliva, supporting droplet and salivary spread; ANDV remained viable on stainless steel up to five days (half‑life 23.6 h). Contribution: The synthesis supports proactive, One‑Health preventive measures and validates selective respiratory isolation for close contacts, guiding clinical and public‑health policy. Limitations: The article is a non‑systematic review; primary data are limited to a few outbreak and cohort studies, and detailed methods of cited work are not provided.

title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care.
analysis.methods: The article addresses eleven practical ICU‑management questions, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system (narrative/expert‑opinion format).

title: Coping Equilibrium and Stability Margins: A Predictive Stability Control Architecture for Critical Biological Systems Demonstrated in Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS)

analysis.background: The study addresses the problem of abrupt transitions from compensated physiological states to irreversible collapse in critical diseases, noting that current clinical decision‑making is reactive and often detects catastrophic events only after a critical stability boundary has been crossed.
analysis.methods: The authors introduce the Ruin Horizon Framework (RHF), a conceptual systems‑theoretic architecture that models host physiology as a dynamically coupled regulatory system with finite resilience, adaptive capacity, and stability margins (A4–A7).
analysis.results: No empirical results are reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.contribution: The authors propose that, if validated prospectively, RHF could provide a generalizable systems‑level foundation for predictive stability monitoring across rapidly deteriorating critical illnesses (A15).
analysis.limitations: The manuscript does not disclose the proprietary mathematical implementation of RHF and is limited to a conceptual abstraction intended to stimulate discussion; the evidence is limited to the abstract only (A13–A14).

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease.
analysis.methods: The study designed a pan‑America orth hantavirus rRT‑PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) by adapting a Sin Nombre virus primer‑probe set for use in human and rodent surveillance.
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, the assay detected all New World orth hantaviruses causing human disease with limits of detection ranging from 25 copies/reaction (Blue River virus) to 28,000 copies/reaction (Bayou virus).
analysis.contribution: The authors conclude the assay detected New World orth hantaviruses in rodent and human samples across the United States and Central/South America, showing strong potential for diagnostic use in clinical labs and for surveillance research.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed methods, validation data, and field performance are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are negative-sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease. Methods: A pan‑America orth hantavirus rRT‑PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed by adapting a Sin Nombre virus primer‑probe set for human and rodent surveillance. Results: The assay detected all New World orth hantaviruses with limits of detection from 25 to 28,000 copies/reaction using synthetic RNA. Contribution: It detected viruses in rodent and human samples across the Americas, indicating strong potential for clinical diagnostics and surveillance. Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed methodology and field validation are not reported.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact.
analysis.methods: Immunoinformatics was applied to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine by analyzing Gn/Gc glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV for B‑cell and T‑cell epitopes, assessing allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage, constructing two candidates with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants, and performing physicochemical, structural stability, TLR4 docking and in silico immune‑simulation analyses.
analysis.results: Molecular docking suggested plausible ectodomain compatibility with TLR4; immune simulations predicted robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses, high antibody production and memory cell persistence exceeding one year.
analysis.contribution: The work offers a rational framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccines.
analysis.limitations: Findings are derived solely from computational analyses presented in an abstract; experimental validation of docking and immunogenicity is lacking.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat with no FDA‑approved vaccine. Methods: Immunoinformatics was used to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine targeting Gn/Gc from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV, evaluating epitopes, safety, conservation, population coverage, constructing two adjuvanted candidates, and performing docking and immune‑simulation analyses. Results: Docking indicated potential TLR4 interaction; simulations forecast robust, balanced humoral and cellular immunity with memory lasting over a year. Contribution: Provides a rational framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum hantavirus vaccines. title: Emerging hantavirus risks in mass gatherings: epidemiology, diagnostic challenges, and outbreak preparedness.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens of increasing global public health concern due to high mortality, expanding ecological distribution, and potential for international dissemination.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on epidemiology, transmission uncertainty, diagnostic and surveillance challenges, and preparedness strategies for hantavirus infections in mass gathering settings such as religious events, refugee settlements, cruise tourism, sporting events, and temporary accommodations.
analysis.current_state: Transmission is primarily via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, yet controversies remain regarding limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic infections.
analysis.gaps: Diagnostic limitations, underreporting, insufficient environmental surveillance, and lack of mass‑gathering‑specific preparedness frameworks, especially in resource‑limited settings, hinder effective risk assessment.
analysis.future_research: Strengthening proactive preparedness through integrated One Health approaches, ecological surveillance, genomic monitoring, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems is essential, underscoring the urgent need for multidisciplinary research and evidence‑based policy development.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens of increasing global public health concern due to high mortality, expanding ecological distribution, and potential for international dissemination. Main directions: The review focuses on epidemiology, transmission uncertainty, diagnostic and surveillance challenges, and preparedness strategies for hantavirus infections in mass gathering settings such as religious events, refugee settlements, cruise tourism, sporting events, and temporary accommodations. Current state: Transmission is primarily via inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta, yet controversies remain regarding limited interpersonal transmission, environmental persistence, and asymptomatic infections. Gaps: Diagnostic limitations, underreporting, insufficient environmental surveillance, and lack of mass‑gathering‑specific preparedness frameworks, especially in resource‑limited settings, hinder effective risk assessment. Future research: Strengthening proactive preparedness through integrated One Health approaches, ecological surveillance, genomic monitoring, AI‑driven epidemic intelligence, and coordinated international response systems is essential, underscoring the urgent need for multidisciplinary research and evidence‑based policy development.

title: Epidemiology and changes in age distribution of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Shaanxi, China, from 2004 to 2023.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a serious viral disease in mainland China, and Shaanxi Province is one of the most severely affected areas.
analysis.methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods were used to analyze the spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS cases in Shaanxi Province from January 2004 to December 2023.
analysis.results: A total of 34,265 HFRS human cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported; cases were geographically concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain; the local incidence fluctuated markedly over the past 20 years with a primary peak from October to January; the proportion of cases in the 15‑60 year age group showed a decreasing trend, while the proportion in the >60 year group increased by 150.94% (from 11.68% to 29.31%).
analysis.contribution: The 20‑year surveillance shows a significant rise in elderly HFRS cases, suggesting vaccine coverage limitations and providing data to adjust prevention, control, and consider age‑expanded vaccination strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; detailed methods, case definitions, and statistical analyses are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a serious viral disease in mainland China, with Shaanxi Province among the most severely affected areas. Methods: Descriptive epidemiological methods analyzed spatial, temporal, and population distribution of HFRS in Shaanxi from Jan 2004 to Dec 2023. Results: 34,265 cases (25,737 males, 8,528 females) were reported, concentrated in the Guanzhong Plain; incidence fluctuated markedly with a peak Oct‑Jan; the 15‑60 yr proportion decreased, while >60 yr cases rose 150.94% (11.68% to 29.31%). Contribution: The surveillance highlights a rise in elderly cases, implying vaccine coverage gaps and informing adjusted prevention and age‑expanded vaccination strategies. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; detailed methods and analyses are not reported.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets—monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells—during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge highlights that these immune cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine/chemokine release correlating with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: The precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined, limiting targeted therapeutic strategies.
analysis.future_research: Future work should integrate longitudinal clinical and mechanistic studies to delineate the balance between protective and pathogenic immune responses, guiding therapeutic target identification.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV). Main directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets—monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells—during HTNV infection. Current state: Current knowledge highlights that these immune cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine/chemokine release correlating with disease severity. Gaps: The precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined, limiting targeted therapeutic strategies. Future research: Future work should integrate longitudinal clinical and mechanistic studies to delineate the balance between protective and pathogenic immune responses, guiding therapeutic target identification.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure (A1).
analysis.methods: The study formulates an SIR‑SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations, extends it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects, establishes qualitative properties, and conducts numerical simulations using Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite difference (SNSFD) methods (A2, A3, A4, A8).
analysis.results: Analysis indicates hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human cases arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote extinction; simulations confirm these findings and show the SNSFD scheme preserves positivity and offers superior stability at larger time steps (A9, A10, A11, A12).
analysis.contribution: The work provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing hantavirus risk and underscores that controlling infection in the rodent reservoir is the most effective public‑health strategy; it also validates the SNSFD method as a robust tool for stochastic epidemic models with delays (A14, A15, A16).
analysis.limitations: The paper presents only theoretical modeling and numerical simulations without empirical validation; no explicit limitations are reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonosis with human spillover risk (A1). Methods: An SIR‑SIR model with stochastic Brownian perturbations, discrete delays, and delay‑survival effects was built and analyzed, using Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and SNSFD simulations (A2, A3, A4, A8). Results: Persistence is driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human infection follows spillover, and stochastic/delay effects can lower reproduction thresholds and aid extinction; SNSFD maintains positivity and stability (A9, A10, A11, A12). Contribution: Offers a rigorous framework for hantavirus risk assessment and highlights reservoir control as key, while demonstrating SNSFD’s computational advantages (A14, A15, A16). Limitations: Relies solely on theoretical and numerical work without empirical data; specific limitations not reported.

title: Hantavirus Cluster Linked to Cruise Ship Travel: A Comprehensive Review of a Looming Global Public Health Concern.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause severe renal and pulmonary syndromes; Andes virus can transmit person‑to‑person, and a 2026 cruise‑ship cluster highlighted travel‑linked risk.
analysis.main_directions: Environmental spillover, limited human transmission, maritime outbreak preparedness, and One Health surveillance.
analysis.current_state: The MV Hondius incident confirmed Andes virus spread on board, underscoring the absence of antivirals or vaccines and reliance on tiered diagnostics.
analysis.gaps: Limited knowledge of person‑to‑person dynamics, lack of therapeutics, insufficient maritime health governance, and inadequate crew mental‑health safeguards.
analysis.future_research: Study transmission mechanisms, develop antivirals/vaccines, improve rapid diagnostics, strengthen One Health maritime surveillance, and codify crew protections.

title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that poses a potential threat to human health, and current PCR‑based detection methods for related hantaviruses may yield false‑negative results.
analysis.methods: The authors engineered a light‑controllable fluorescence platform using a photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker combined with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA); detection requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA, with exonuclease III‑driven walking releasing a trigger that initiates the CHA cycle.
analysis.results: The system displayed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, and achieved a DBSV‑RNA detection limit of 30 fM with a linear range from 10⁻¹ to 10⁶ pM; applicability was confirmed using human serum specimens.
analysis.contribution: This dual‑amplification strategy introduces a novel, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker approach for ultrasensitive RNA detection, offering considerable potential for early hantavirus diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed experimental conditions, reproducibility data, and broader field validation are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus threatening human health, and existing PCR assays risk false negatives. Methods: A light‑controllable fluorescence platform was built using a photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly, requiring UV activation and target RNA, with Exo III‑driven walking to trigger CHA. Results: The assay showed excellent selectivity, detecting single‑ to triple‑base mismatches, and reached a detection limit of 30 fM for DBSV RNA with a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM; it was validated in human serum. Contribution: This novel dual‑amplification strategy demonstrates a spatiotemporally controllable approach for ultrasensitive viral RNA detection, valuable for early diagnosis and field monitoring. Limitations: Only the abstract is provided, so full methodological details and broader validation are not reported.
