title: Global Epidemiology and Emerging Trends of Hantavirus Infection: A One Health Perspective

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS).
analysis.main_directions: The review highlights that hantavirus epidemiology is driven by interactions among reservoir hosts, climate variability, urbanization, deforestation and other environmental changes, and it synthesizes findings into thematic areas such as global epidemiology, reservoir ecology, environmental determinants, surveillance strategies and prevention approaches.
analysis.current_state: Approximately 150,000–200,000 HFRS cases occur annually, predominantly in China; Europe experiences recurrent Puumala‑virus nephropathia epidemica, while the Americas face HCPS with 30–40% case‑fatality; climatic factors (temperature, precipitation, extreme events) influence rodent populations and transmission; integrated ecological‑epidemiological surveillance has improved outbreak prediction and preparedness.
analysis.gaps: There is uncertainty about how ongoing climate change and habitat modification will reshape future hantavirus emergence, and current diagnostic capacity and coordinated One‑Health surveillance remain limited.
analysis.future_research: Future work should strengthen One‑Health surveillance networks, expand ecological monitoring of rodent reservoirs, improve diagnostic tools, and promote interdisciplinary collaboration to better anticipate and mitigate emerging hantavirus threats.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing HFRS and HCPS. Main directions: Their epidemiology is shaped by host‑environment interactions, climate change, urbanization and deforestation, organized into themes of global epidemiology, reservoir ecology, environmental drivers, surveillance and prevention. Current state: 150‑200 k HFRS cases occur yearly (mainly China); Europe sees Puumala‑virus outbreaks; the Americas face HCPS with 30‑40% fatality; climate factors affect rodent dynamics; integrated surveillance improves prediction. Gaps: Uncertainty remains on future climate‑driven emergence and diagnostic/surveillance capacity is insufficient. Future research: Strengthen One‑Health surveillance, expand ecological monitoring, enhance diagnostics, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: Computational design and population-level evaluation of a multi-epitope Andes virus vaccine candidate

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and remains an important target for vaccine development.
analysis.methods: The study presents an in‑silico multi‑epitope ANDV vaccine design using class‑I and class‑II peptide–HLA prediction, reduction of overlapping predictions to non‑redundant regions, sequence‑conservation analysis, human‑proteome comparison, and genotype‑based population‑coverage modeling.
analysis.results: A candidate combining selected T‑cell components with secondary B‑cell‑directed elements was generated and computationally characterized across these analytical dimensions; no quantitative efficacy data are reported.
analysis.contribution: The work provides an openly accessible computational resource for further vaccine design, teaching, independent scrutiny, and future experimental investigation.
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is available; no experimental validation or detailed quantitative results are presented.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, making vaccine development a priority. Methods: The authors used in‑silico design integrating class‑I/II peptide–HLA predictions, redundancy reduction, conservation analysis, human proteome comparison, and genotype‑based population‑coverage modeling to create a multi‑epitope vaccine candidate. Results: A candidate combining selected T‑cell epitopes with secondary B‑cell elements was generated and computationally characterized; no quantitative efficacy data were reported. Contribution: The study offers an openly accessible computational resource for further vaccine design, education, and future experimental work. Limitations: Only an abstract is available, with no experimental validation or detailed results.

title: Raw peptide-HLA prediction data supporting the computational design and population-level evaluation of a multi-epitope Andes virus vaccine candidate

analysis.background: The work supports a computational effort to design a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Andes virus, a hantavirus of public‑health relevance.
analysis.methods: The study used large‑scale peptide–HLA binding predictions (342,430 class‑I and 64,680 class‑II rows) and then reduced these tables to non‑redundant candidate regions, evaluating them with conservation analysis, human‑proteome comparison, and genotype‑based population‑coverage modeling; location, host, and sample details are not reported.
analysis.results: The raw dataset contains 342,430 class‑I and 64,680 class‑II peptide–allele prediction rows; derived candidate regions and population‑coverage metrics are reported in the associated manuscript and code, but specific quantitative outcomes are not provided in the supplied evidence.
analysis.contribution: The dataset and accompanying analysis code enable reproducible computational vaccine design and population‑level assessment for Andes virus, facilitating further research and potential vaccine development.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract‑level information is available; detailed experimental validation, immunogenicity data, and full methodological specifics are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The work supports a computational effort to design a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Andes virus, a hantavirus of public‑health relevance. Methods: Large‑scale peptide–HLA predictions (342,430 class‑I and 64,680 class‑II rows) were reduced to non‑redundant candidate regions and evaluated via conservation, human‑proteome comparison, and genotype‑based population‑coverage modeling; location, host, and sample details are not reported. Results: The raw dataset includes the stated prediction rows; derived candidate regions and coverage metrics are described in the associated release, but specific quantitative results are absent. Contribution: Provides reproducible data and code for computational vaccine design and population‑level evaluation of an Andes virus candidate. Limitations: Only abstract‑level data are provided; experimental validation and detailed methods are not reported.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Mortality Risk Stratification in Hantavirus Infection: A Global Study Across Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential for timely triage and resource allocation (A1).
analysis.methods: A retrospective supervised learning analysis was performed on 10,000 global hantavirus patient records (A4) with mortality as the binary outcome (A5); logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models were trained and evaluated on a held‑out test set (A7); preprocessing steps included identifier removal, missing‑value handling, encoding, feature selection, and class‑imbalance correction (A6); the cohort comprised 8,938 recovered and 1,062 deceased cases (mortality 10.62%) with both HFRS and HCPS presentations (A9).
analysis.results: Logistic regression achieved the highest discrimination (ROC‑AUC 0.858) and recall (0.741) but modest precision (0.321) and Brier score 0.119 (A10); gradient boosting showed comparable AUC (0.857) with better precision (0.511) and calibration (Brier 0.076) (A11); random forest performed poorly for mortality detection (recall 0.085) (A12); severity, syndrome type, viral load category, age, and geographic setting were the most informative predictors (A14).
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that mortality risk in hantavirus infection can be modeled with routine clinical and epidemiological features, emphasizing sensitivity, calibration, and transparency for clinical deployment (A15), and supports interpretable ML as a practical framework for early risk stratification and external validation (A16).
analysis.limitations: The paper does not report explicit limitations in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is rare but potentially fatal, requiring early risk identification (A1). Methods: Retrospective analysis of 10,000 global cases (mortality outcome) using logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost with extensive preprocessing; cohort included 8,938 recoveries and 1,062 deaths (A4,A5,A7,A9). Results: Logistic regression had ROC‑AUC 0.858, recall 0.741, precision 0.321; gradient boosting similar AUC 0.857 with precision 0.511; random forest low recall 0.085; key predictors were severity, syndrome type, viral load, age, geography (A10,A11,A12,A14). Contribution: Shows interpretable ML can stratify hantavirus mortality risk, prioritizing sensitivity and transparency, and provides a framework for validation (A15,A16). Limitations: No explicit limitations reported.

title: Hantavirus: comprender el reservorio para prevenir la enfermedad Hantavirus: Understanding the Reservoir to Prevent the Disease

analysis.background: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in humans is the final step of a complex chain linking environment, wildlife reservoirs, the virus, and human activities, and understanding this chain is essential for prevention. (A1‑A3)
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Massive bamboo (Chusquea culeou) flowering in Patagonia triggers exceptional increases in Oligoryzomys longicaudatus populations and their dispersal toward rural houses (F14‑F16), but subsequent flowering events have produced weaker rodent responses and no rise in human cases (F18‑F19). Peridomestic rural structures concentrate the reservoir and double the probability of capturing an infected rodent compared with wild habitats (F23). Adult male long‑tailed mice show higher infection prevalence, likely due to aggressive horizontal transmission (F31).
analysis.contribution: The article highlights that real‑time ecological monitoring and coordinated inter‑institutional actions enable timely risk communication and targeted preventive measures at the human‑rodent interface (F20, F34‑F36).
analysis.limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS results from a chain linking environment, rodent reservoirs, virus, and human activity, making reservoir understanding vital (A1‑A3). Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Bamboo flowering in Patagonia caused huge spikes in O. longicaudatus numbers and rural dispersal (F14‑F16), yet later blooms gave modest rodent responses and no human cases (F18‑F19); peridomestic settings double capture odds of infected rodents (F23); adult male mice have higher infection rates (F31). Contribution: Real‑time ecological monitoring and coordinated institutional response allow timely risk communication and focused prevention at the rodent‑human interface (F20, F34‑F36). Limitations: not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease, and their diversity complicates surveillance and diagnostics.
analysis.methods: A pan‑America Orthohantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was developed from an existing Sin Nombre primer‑probe set for use in human and rodent surveillance.
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World hantaviruses that cause human disease with limits of detection between 25 and 28,000 copies/reaction; it also detected diverse hantaviruses from North, Central, and South America within similar limits and performed as well or better than a commercial assay for North American viruses but not for South American viruses.
analysis.contribution: The assay has strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent field studies, detecting hantaviruses in both rodent and human samples across the United States and Central/South America.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, posing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact (A1). No FDA‑approved vaccine exists (A2), and the viral surface glycoprotein (GP) is a key vaccine target but is highly variable across species (A3, A4). Epitope‑based vaccines are proposed as a promising alternative (A5).
analysis.methods: The authors used immunoinformatics to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine, integrating B‑cell and T‑cell epitope prediction, antigenicity scoring, IFN‑γ induction, conservation analysis, and population‑coverage assessment (A6). GP sequences from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, and ANDV were analyzed (A7) and predicted epitopes were screened for allergenicity, toxicity, conservation, and coverage (A8). Two constructs with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants were evaluated for physicochemical properties, structural stability, and immunogenicity (A9); molecular docking screened ectodomain compatibility with TLR4 (A10).
analysis.results: In silico immune simulations indicated robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses with memory cell persistence exceeding one year (A11, A12). Docking suggested potential interaction with TLR4, though experimental validation is pending (A10).
analysis.contribution: The study provides a rational framework for designing broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope vaccines against genetically diverse hantaviruses, supporting pre‑clinical development of universal hantavirus vaccines (A13).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on computational analyses; experimental confirmation of immunogenicity and TLR4 interaction is required (A10). The evidence is limited to the abstract, lacking detailed methods or empirical data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause severe disease and lack an FDA‑approved vaccine; GP variability hampers conventional approaches, prompting epitope‑based strategies (A1‑A5). Methods: Immunoinformatics integrated B‑ and T‑cell epitope prediction, antigenicity, IFN‑γ potential, conservation, and population coverage on GP sequences from four hantaviruses, with two adjuvanted constructs evaluated for stability and docking to TLR4 (A6‑A10). Results: Simulations predicted robust, long‑lasting humoral and cellular immunity with memory >1 year, and docking suggested possible TLR4 interaction (A11‑A12). Contribution: Offers a computational framework for universal hantavirus vaccine design, guiding pre‑clinical development (A13). Limitations: Conclusions are purely in silico; experimental validation is needed and only abstract data are available (A10).

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure, representing a continuing public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: The study formulates an SIR‑SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations and extends it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; qualitative properties (positivity, boundedness, feasibility, well‑posedness) are proved and numerical simulations are run using Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite‑difference (SNSFD) methods.
analysis.results: Analysis indicates hantavirus persistence is primarily driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote disease extinction; simulations support these findings and show SNSFD preserves positivity and offers superior stability at larger time steps.
analysis.contribution: The work provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing hantavirus risk and underscores that controlling infection within the rodent reservoir is the most effective strategy to reduce disease persistence and limit human spillover.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease where humans acquire infection via spillover from rodent reservoirs, posing ongoing public‑health risk. Methods: An SIR‑SIR model linking rodent and human populations was built, incorporating Brownian noise, discrete delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; model properties were proved and simulations performed with Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and SNSFD schemes. Results: Persistence is driven mainly by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human cases arise from spillover, and stochastic perturbations/delay‑survival can lower the reproduction threshold and promote extinction; SNSFD maintains positivity and stability at larger steps. Contribution: Provides a rigorous framework for hantavirus risk assessment and highlights rodent‑reservoir control as key to reducing human spillover. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Ecological and Individual-Level Factors Associated With Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome Notifications and in-Hospital Mortality Among Hospitalized Patients in Chile, 2005-2022.

analysis.background: HCPS, a severe zoonotic disease caused by Andes virus, imposes a significant public‑health burden in Chile (A1).
analysis.methods: Two complementary analyses were performed: an ecological negative binomial mixed‑effects model of district‑level notifications (2005‑2022) with predictors such as male population rate, urbanization, density, season and burned area (A5); and a logistic mixed‑effects model of hospitalized patients (2010‑2020) assessing age, sex, indigenous affiliation, hospital stay length and surgical interventions (A6).
analysis.results: A total of 886 cases were reported across 187 districts (average 49.2 cases/yr) (A7). Notifications increased with higher male population rates and burned area, and decreased with urbanization and density (A8). Among 462 hospitalized patients, in‑hospital case‑fatality was 19.7 % (A9); older age, female sex and indigenous affiliation raised mortality risk (A10), as did shorter stays and more surgeries (A11).
analysis.contribution: The study identifies forest‑fire activity as a novel ecological risk indicator for HCPS notifications (A12) and highlights disproportionate mortality among older, female, and indigenous patients, informing targeted surveillance and One‑Health interventions (A13).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on abstract information; detailed methods, sample characteristics, and full statistical results are not reported (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS, a severe zoonotic disease caused by Andes virus, imposes a significant public‑health burden in Chile. Methods: An ecological negative binomial mixed‑effects model of district notifications (2005‑2022) and a logistic mixed‑effects model of hospitalized patients (2010‑2020) were used, incorporating demographic, environmental and clinical predictors. Results: 886 cases were reported (average 49.2 yr⁻¹); notifications rose with male population rate and burned area, fell with urbanization and density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, in‑hospital mortality was 19.7 %; higher risk was linked to older age, female sex, indigenous affiliation, shorter stay and more surgeries. Contribution: Forest‑fire activity emerges as a novel ecological risk indicator, and mortality is concentrated in older, female, indigenous groups, guiding targeted surveillance and One‑Health actions. Limitations: Only abstract data are available, so detailed methods and full results are not reported.

title: Global Epidemiology and Emerging Trends of Hantavirus Infection: A One Health Perspective

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), motivating a review of their global impact.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on how interactions among reservoir hosts, environmental conditions, climatic variability, and human activities drive hantavirus epidemiology.
analysis.current_state: Approximately 150 000–200 000 HFRS cases occur annually worldwide, mainly in China; Europe experiences recurrent Puumala virus outbreaks, while the Americas face HCPS with 30‑40% case‑fatality rates.
analysis.gaps: There is a need to strengthen One Health surveillance, expand ecological monitoring, improve diagnostic capacity, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration to address current knowledge gaps.
analysis.future_research: Expanding integrated surveillance systems that combine ecological, environmental, and epidemiological data will enhance outbreak prediction and preparedness.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens causing HFRS and HCPS, prompting a global review. Main directions: The review examines how reservoir hosts, environmental conditions, climate variability, and human activities shape transmission. Current state: 150‑200k HFRS cases occur yearly, chiefly in China; Europe sees Puumala virus outbreaks, and the Americas confront HCPS with 30‑40% fatality. Gaps: Insufficient One Health surveillance, ecological monitoring, and diagnostic capacity limit preparedness. Future research: Integrated surveillance merging ecological, environmental, and epidemiological data should be expanded to improve outbreak prediction and response.

analysis.results: The resulting candidate combines selected T‑cell components with secondary B‑cell‑directed elements and is characterized computationally across these analytical dimensions.
analysis.contribution: The work provides an openly accessible research resource for further computational study, teaching, independent scrutiny, and future experimental investigation.

Results: The candidate merges selected T‑cell epitopes with B‑cell elements and is fully characterized computationally. Contribution: The study offers an openly accessible resource for computational research, education, and future experimental work. Limitations: Only the abstract is provided; experimental validation and detailed methods are not reported.

title: Clinical Features, Mechanisms, and Renal Outcomes of Hantavirus-Associated Kidney Injury: A Narrative Review

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an underrecognized infectious cause of acute kidney injury, with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) defining its dominant renal phenotype and accounting for an estimated 150,000–200,000 cases annually.
analysis.main_directions: The review integrates mechanisms such as integrin receptor tropism, endothelial glycocalyx degradation, IL‑6 trans‑signaling, immune‑checkpoint dynamics, and coagulation disturbances, while addressing viral species, clinical phenotypes, supportive care, and long‑term renal outcomes.
analysis.current_state: Complete functional renal recovery is common, yet normalization of serum creatinine does not always reflect full physiologic recovery; subsets of patients exhibit persistent proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, or tubular dysfunction, especially with severe strains like Hantaan and Dobrava‑Belgrade.
analysis.gaps: The prevalence, predictors, and clinical impact of chronic renal sequelae remain uncertain, and evidence for targeted therapeutic interventions beyond supportive care is limited.
analysis.future_research: Prospective cohort studies, biomarker‑driven risk stratification, and interventional trials focusing on endothelial protection, immune modulation, and long‑term follow‑up are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an underrecognized cause of AKI, with HFRS as its dominant renal phenotype and 150‑200k annual cases. Main directions: The review covers mechanisms (integrin tropism, glycocalyx loss, IL‑6, immune checkpoints, coagulation), viral species, supportive management, and long‑term outcomes. Current state: Most patients regain renal function, but serum creatinine normalization may mask persistent proteinuria, hematuria, hypertension, or tubular dysfunction, especially with severe strains. Gaps: The extent and predictors of chronic renal sequelae are unclear, and targeted therapies are lacking. Future research: Prospective cohorts, biomarker‑based risk stratification, and trials of endothelial and immune‑targeted therapies are required.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Mortality Risk Stratification in Hantavirus Infection: A Global Study Across Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is a rare but potentially fatal zoonosis, and early identification of patients at highest risk of death is essential for timely triage and resource allocation.
analysis.methods: A retrospective supervised learning study used a global hantavirus epidemiology dataset of 10,000 patient records, including demographic, clinical, epidemiological, and treatment variables, with mortality as the binary outcome. Data preprocessing involved identifier removal, missing‑value handling, categorical and symptom encoding, feature selection, and class‑imbalance correction. Logistic regression, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models were trained and compared on a held‑out test set using ROC‑AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, F1‑score, and Brier score, and interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations.
analysis.results: Logistic regression achieved the highest discrimination (ROC‑AUC 0.858) and recall for mortality (0.741) but modest precision (0.321) and weaker calibration (Brier 0.119). Gradient boosting had comparable discrimination (AUC 0.857) with better precision (0.511) and calibration (Brier 0.076). Random forest performed poorly for mortality detection (recall 0.085). The cohort comprised 8,938 recovered and 1,062 deceased cases (mortality 10.62 %), with 6,460 HFRS (64.6 %) and 3,540 HCPS (35.4 %) cases. Severity, syndrome type, viral load category, age, and geographic setting were the most informative predictors.
analysis.contribution: The study demonstrates that routine clinical and epidemiological features can be used to model mortality risk in hantavirus infection with interpretable machine‑learning methods, supporting early risk stratification and informing resource allocation. It highlights the importance of sensitivity, calibration, and transparency over accuracy alone for clinical deployment and suggests external validation in independent cohorts.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease, and their diversity complicates surveillance and diagnostics.
analysis.methods: Starting from an existing rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set for Sin Nombre virus, the authors developed a pan‑American orth hantavirus real‑time PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) for both human and rodent surveillance (study design described in A5).
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World orth hantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection from 25 copies/reaction (Blue River virus) to 28,000 copies/reaction (Bayou virus); it also detected diverse viruses from North, Central and South America with similar limits and performed as well as or better than a commercial assay for North American strains.
analysis.contribution: The assay provides a broadly reactive diagnostic tool suitable for North American clinical laboratories and for rodent‑based surveillance and research across the Americas.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; detailed validation data, sample sizes, and field performance are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses causing severe human disease, and their diversity hinders surveillance and diagnostics. Methods: A pan‑American rRT‑PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was built from a Sin Nombre virus primer set for human and rodent surveillance (A5). Results: The assay detected all New World hantaviruses with limits of 25–28,000 copies/reaction, identified diverse strains from the Americas, and matched or exceeded a commercial assay for North American viruses (A6‑A8). Contribution: It offers a broadly reactive diagnostic for clinical labs and rodent surveillance across the Americas (A4, A10). Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; detailed validation and field performance are not reported.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact.
analysis.methods: Immunoinformatics workflow integrated B‑cell and T‑cell epitope prediction on glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, and ANDV; predicted epitopes were filtered for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage; two multi‑epitope constructs using β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 as adjuvants were evaluated for physicochemical properties, structural stability, molecular docking to TLR4, and in silico immune simulation.
analysis.results: Docking suggested plausible TLR4 interaction; immune simulations predicted robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses, high antibody production and memory cell persistence exceeding one year.
analysis.contribution: Provides a rational framework for designing broad‑spectrum multi‑epitope vaccines against genetically diverse hantaviruses, guiding pre‑clinical development of universal vaccine candidates.
analysis.limitations: Findings are based solely on in silico analyses; experimental confirmation is required and only an abstract is available.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat with major health impact. Methods: Immunoinformatics screened glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV, ANDV for B‑ and T‑cell epitopes, filtered them for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage, and built two multi‑epitope constructs with β‑defensin or 50S ribosomal protein L7/L12 adjuvants, assessing physicochemical traits, docking to TLR4, and immune simulation. Results: Docking indicated potential TLR4 interaction; simulations forecast robust, balanced humoral and cellular immunity with antibody levels and memory cells lasting >1 year. Contribution: Offers a rational design framework for broad‑spectrum hantavirus vaccines, supporting pre‑clinical development of universal candidates. Limitations: Conclusions derive only from computational work; experimental validation is lacking and the paper provides only an abstract.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets (monocytes, macrophages, DCs, NK cells, neutrophils, T and B cells) during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge highlights that these cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine/chemokine release correlating with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: The precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined.
analysis.future_research: Future studies should longitudinally map immune cell phenotypes, identify therapeutic targets that balance antiviral responses with limiting immunopathology, and integrate clinical and mechanistic data.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus. Main directions: The review examines dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets during HTNV infection. Current state: These cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine/chemokine release correlating with disease severity. Gaps: Precise temporal dynamics and mechanistic links between protective immunity and tissue damage remain poorly defined. Future research: Longitudinal mapping of immune phenotypes and identification of therapeutic targets that balance antiviral responses with limiting immunopathology are needed.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease in which rodents serve as the primary reservoir and humans acquire infection through spillover exposure. (A1)
analysis.methods: The study formulates an SIR‑SIR transmission framework for interacting rodent and human populations, extends it with Brownian stochastic perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects, and solves it numerically using Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and stochastic nonstandard finite difference (SNSFD) methods. (A2,A3,A4,A8)
analysis.results: Model analysis indicates that hantavirus persistence is primarily driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects can lower the effective reproduction threshold and promote extinction; the SNSFD scheme preserves positivity and shows superior stability for larger time steps. (A9,A10,A12)
analysis.contribution: The stochastic delay model offers a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for public‑health risk assessment of rodent‑driven hantavirus spillover and highlights reservoir control as the most effective mitigation strategy; additionally, SNSFD is presented as a robust computational approach for stochastic epidemic systems with delays. (A14,A15)
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonosis with human spillover risk (A1). Methods: An SIR‑SIR model with stochastic Brownian noise, discrete delays, and delay‑survival effects was built and solved using Euler‑Maruyama, stochastic Runge‑Kutta, and SNSFD methods (A2,A3,A4,A8). Results: Persistence is driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, human cases stem from spillover; stochasticity and delays can lower the reproduction threshold and aid extinction; SNSFD maintains positivity and stability (A9,A10,A12). Contribution: Provides a rigorous framework for assessing hantavirus spillover risk and underscores reservoir control; SNSFD is a valuable tool for stochastic delayed epidemic modeling (A14,A15). Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: Ecological and Individual-Level Factors Associated With Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome Notifications and in-Hospital Mortality Among Hospitalized Patients in Chile, 2005-2022.

analysis.background: HCPS is a severe zoonotic disease caused by Andes virus that imposes a significant public‑health burden in Chile (A1) and knowledge gaps remain about its ecological drivers and mortality determinants (A2).
analysis.methods: Two complementary analyses were performed: an ecological negative‑binomial mixed‑effects model of district‑level notifications (2005‑2022) with demographic and burned‑area predictors (A5), and a logistic mixed‑effects model of hospitalized patients (2010‑2020) with individual risk factors (A6); the overall approach is described in the methods overview (A4).
analysis.results: A total of 886 HCPS cases were reported across 187 districts (average 49.2 cases/yr) (A7); notifications increased with higher male population rates and burned area and decreased with urbanization and population density (A8). Among 462 hospitalized patients, in‑hospital case‑fatality was 19.7% (A9); older age, female sex, indigenous affiliation, shorter hospital stay and more surgical interventions were each associated with higher mortality (A10, A11).
analysis.contribution: The study identifies forest‑fire activity as a novel, actionable ecological risk indicator and highlights older, female, and indigenous groups as disproportionately affected by in‑hospital mortality, informing targeted surveillance and One‑Health strategies (A12, A13).
analysis.limitations: Findings are based on abstract‑only information; detailed methods, full dataset, and causal inference cannot be assessed (abstract_only).

analysis.summary_en: Background: HCPS caused by Andes virus is a severe zoonotic disease with major public‑health impact in Chile. Methods: An ecological negative‑binomial mixed‑effects model examined district notifications (2005‑2022) using demographic and fire‑related predictors, and a logistic mixed‑effects model assessed hospitalized patients (2010‑2020) with individual risk factors. Results: 886 cases were reported in 187 districts (mean 49.2 yr⁻¹); notifications rose with male population proportion and burned area and fell with urbanization and density. Among 462 hospitalized patients, in‑hospital mortality was 19.7%; higher age, female sex, indigenous affiliation, shorter stay and more surgeries increased death risk. Contribution: Identifies forest‑fire activity as a novel ecological risk indicator and pinpoints vulnerable demographic groups, guiding targeted surveillance and One‑Health interventions. Limitations: Findings are based on abstract data only; detailed methods and causal inference are not provided.

title: Global Epidemiology and Emerging Trends of Hantavirus Infection: A One Health Perspective

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic pathogens responsible for Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) and Hantavirus Cardiopulmonary Syndrome (HCPS), motivating a review of their global impact.
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on interactions among reservoir hosts, environmental conditions, climate variability, and human activities, and evaluates One Health approaches for surveillance and prevention.
analysis.current_state: Approximately 150 000–200 000 HFRS cases occur annually worldwide, chiefly in China; Europe experiences recurrent Puumala virus outbreaks, while the Americas face HCPS with 30‑40 % case‑fatality, and climatic and environmental drivers are widely recognized.
analysis.gaps: There is uncertainty about how ongoing climate change and ecosystem modifications will reshape hantavirus transmission and emergence patterns.
analysis.future_research: Strengthening One Health surveillance, expanding ecological monitoring, improving diagnostic capacity, and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration are essential next steps.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne zoonotic viruses causing HFRS and HCPS, prompting a review of their global impact. Main directions: The review examines how reservoir hosts, climate variability, land‑use change, and human activities shape transmission and discusses One Health surveillance and prevention. Current state: Annually 150 000–200 000 HFRS cases occur, mainly in China, with Europe facing Puumala virus outbreaks and the Americas experiencing HCPS with 30‑40 % mortality; climatic and environmental factors are recognized drivers. Gaps: Uncertainty remains about how ongoing climate change and ecosystem alterations will modify future hantavirus emergence. Future research: Strengthening One Health surveillance, expanding ecological monitoring, improving diagnostics, and fostering interdisciplinary collaboration are recommended.

title: Computational design and population-level evaluation of a multi-epitope Andes virus vaccine candidate

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and remains an important target for vaccine development.
analysis.methods: The study presents an in‑silico multi‑epitope ANDV vaccine design, integrating class‑I and class‑II peptide–HLA prediction, reduction of overlapping predictions to non‑redundant regions, sequence‑conservation analysis, human‑proteome comparison, and genotype‑based population‑coverage modeling.
analysis.results: The resulting candidate combines selected T‑cell components with secondary B‑cell‑directed elements and is characterized computationally across these analytical dimensions; no quantitative efficacy data are reported.
analysis.contribution: The work provides an openly accessible computational vaccine candidate and methodological resource for further computational study, teaching, independent scrutiny, and future experimental investigation.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract information is available; no experimental validation, quantitative results, or detailed methodological data are reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome and is a priority for vaccine development. Methods: An in‑silico multi‑epitope vaccine was designed using class‑I/II peptide–HLA predictions, redundancy reduction, conservation analysis, human‑proteome comparison, and population‑coverage modeling. Results: The final construct merges selected T‑cell epitopes with secondary B‑cell elements and was computationally characterized; no quantitative efficacy data are provided. Contribution: The study offers an openly accessible computational vaccine candidate and framework for further computational, educational, and experimental work. Limitations: Only abstract data are available; no experimental validation or detailed results are reported.

title: ANDVOR: Andes Virus Open Research Vaccine computational research package

analysis.background: The release addresses the need for vaccine development against Andes virus, a hantavirus of public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: The package provides an in‑silico vaccine design workflow, including a candidate peptide sequence, peptide‑HLA binding predictions, analysis code, and provenance metadata; no laboratory, animal, or clinical validation is reported.
analysis.results: Derived computational results and a raw peptide‑HLA prediction dataset are supplied, but quantitative outcomes are not detailed in the abstract.
analysis.contribution: The release offers an open, reproducible computational resource that can accelerate Andes virus vaccine research and facilitate downstream experimental testing.
analysis.limitations: No experimental validation is included; only abstract‑level information is available, limiting insight into detailed methods, performance metrics, or real‑world efficacy.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The work targets vaccine development for Andes virus, a hantavirus of public‑health relevance. Methods: An open computational package delivers an in‑silico candidate sequence, peptide‑HLA predictions, analysis code, and reproducibility metadata, without laboratory, animal, or clinical validation. Results: The release includes derived computational outputs and a raw peptide‑HLA dataset, though quantitative details are absent. Contribution: Provides a transparent, reusable resource to support Andes virus vaccine design and future experimental work. Limitations: Lacks experimental validation and detailed methodological data; only abstract information is provided.

title: Clinical Features, Mechanisms, and Renal Outcomes of Hantavirus-Associated Kidney Injury: A Narrative Review

analysis.background: Hantavirus infection is an underrecognized cause of acute kidney injury, with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) as its dominant renal phenotype.
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes data on viral tropism, endothelial glycocalyx damage, IL‑6 trans‑signaling, immune‑checkpoint dynamics, coagulation disturbances, biomarker‑based risk stratification, and long‑term renal sequelae.
analysis.current_state: In most endemic regions, patients develop KDIGO stage 2–3 AKI, but mortality and irreversible renal failure are rare when supportive care is available.
analysis.gaps: Persistent microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, or subtle tubular dysfunction can remain in a subset of survivors, indicating incomplete physiologic recovery and limited long‑term data.
analysis.future_research: Prospective longitudinal cohorts are needed to define the prevalence, predictors, and clinical impact of chronic renal abnormalities after hantavirus infection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus infection is an underrecognized cause of acute kidney injury, with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome as its dominant renal phenotype. Main directions: The review synthesizes data on viral tropism, endothelial glycocalyx damage, IL-6 trans-signaling, immune-checkpoint dynamics, coagulation disturbances, biomarker risk stratification, and long-term renal sequelae. Current state: In most endemic regions, patients develop KDIGO stage 2-3 AKI, but mortality and irreversible renal failure are rare with supportive care. Gaps: Persistent microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, or subtle tubular dysfunction can remain in some survivors, showing incomplete recovery and limited long-term data. Future research: Prospective longitudinal cohorts are needed to define prevalence, predictors, and impact of chronic renal abnormalities after hantavirus infection.

title: Detection of new world hantaviruses by a broadly reactive rRT-PCR assay.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses are negative‑sense RNA viruses that persistently infect rodents and can cause severe human disease, and their diversity complicates surveillance and diagnostics.
analysis.methods: Starting from a Sin Nombre virus rRT‑PCR primer‑probe set, the authors developed a pan‑American Orthohantavirus assay (HantAmeriQ) intended for both human and rodent surveillance (A5).
analysis.results: Using synthetic RNA, HantAmeriQ detected all New World hantaviruses known to cause human disease with limits of detection from 25 copies/reaction (Blue River virus) to 28,000 copies/reaction (Bayou virus) and identified diverse viruses from North, Central and South America (A6, A7).
analysis.contribution: The assay demonstrates strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical laboratories and for surveillance and research in rodent‑focused field studies across the Americas (A10).
analysis.limitations: Only an abstract is provided; detailed validation data, sample sizes, and field performance metrics are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses causing severe human disease, and their diversity hampers surveillance. Methods: A pan‑American rRT‑PCR assay (HantAmeriQ) was built from a Sin Nombre virus primer set for human and rodent surveillance (A5). Results: The assay detected all New World hantaviruses with limits of detection ranging from 25 to 28,000 copies/reaction and identified diverse viruses across the Americas (A6, A7). Contribution: It shows strong potential for diagnostic use in North American clinical labs and for rodent‑based surveillance and research (A10). Limitations: Only an abstract is available; detailed performance data and sample numbers are not reported.

title: Broad-Spectrum Multi-Epitope Design Targeting Conserved Hantavirus Glycoproteins (Gn/Gc): Chimeric Antigen Engineering and Structural Mapping.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, representing a high‑risk zoonotic threat with substantial global health impact.
analysis.methods: The authors applied immunoinformatics to design a universal multi‑epitope vaccine, analyzing Gn/Gc glycoproteins from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV, predicting B‑ and T‑cell epitopes, assessing allergenicity, toxicity, conservation and population coverage, and constructing two adjuvanted vaccine candidates evaluated for physicochemical properties, structural stability, molecular docking with TLR4, and in silico immune simulations.
analysis.results: Molecular docking suggested potential interaction with TLR4, and immune‑simulation predicted robust, balanced humoral and cellular responses with memory cell persistence exceeding one year.
analysis.contribution: The work offers a rational framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum, multi‑epitope hantavirus vaccines targeting genetically diverse strains.
analysis.limitations: Findings are derived solely from computational analyses presented in an abstract; experimental validation of docking and immunogenicity is lacking.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses cause HFRS and HPS, a high‑risk zoonotic threat. Methods: Immunoinformatics was used to design multi‑epitope vaccine constructs targeting Gn/Gc from SEOV, PUUV, SNV and ANDV, with epitope prediction, safety assessment, docking to TLR4, and immune‑simulation. Results: Docking indicated possible TLR4 interaction, and simulations forecast robust, balanced humoral and cellular immunity with memory >1 year. Contribution: Provides a framework for pre‑clinical development of broad‑spectrum hantavirus vaccines. Limitations: Conclusions are based only on in silico data from an abstract; experimental confirmation is required.

title: The role of immune cells in Hantaan-induced hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.

analysis.background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV).
analysis.main_directions: The review focuses on dynamic changes, phenotypic alterations, and functional profiles of immune subsets—monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, NK cells, neutrophils, T cells, and B cells—during HTNV infection.
analysis.current_state: Current knowledge highlights that these immune cells are essential for viral clearance yet also contribute to immunopathology, with cytokine/chemokine levels correlating with disease severity.
analysis.gaps: There is a lack of comprehensive, stage‑specific data on immune cell dynamics and functional states, limiting understanding of the balance between protection and tissue damage.
analysis.future_research: Future studies should longitudinally profile immune subsets and cytokine networks to identify therapeutic targets that modulate protective immunity while reducing immunopathology.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a severe zoonotic disease mainly caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV). Gaps: There is a lack of comprehensive, stage‑specific data on immune cell dynamics and functional states, limiting understanding of the balance between protection and tissue damage. Future research: Future studies should longitudinally profile immune subsets and cytokine networks to identify therapeutic targets that modulate protective immunity while reducing immunopathology.

title: Public health risk assessment of rodent-driven hantavirus spillover in Europe using a stochastic delay model.

analysis.background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease transmitted to humans via spillover, posing ongoing public health risk in Europe.
analysis.methods: The authors develop a stochastic delay differential SIR–SIR model for interacting rodent and human populations, incorporating Brownian perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; they derive qualitative properties, equilibria, reproduction numbers, extinction and persistence conditions, and perform numerical simulations with Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and SNSFD methods.
analysis.results: Analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote extinction; simulations confirm consistency across methods for small steps and superior stability of SNSFD for larger steps.
analysis.contribution: The model provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing rodent‑driven hantavirus spillover risk and highlights reservoir control as the most effective strategy; the SNSFD method offers a stable computational tool for stochastic epidemic systems with delays.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonotic disease transmitted to humans via spillover, posing ongoing public health risk in Europe. Methods: The authors develop a stochastic delay differential SIR–SIR model for interacting rodent and human populations, incorporating Brownian perturbations, discrete time delays, and exponential delay‑survival effects; they derive qualitative properties, equilibria, reproduction numbers, extinction and persistence conditions, and perform numerical simulations with Euler–Maruyama, stochastic Runge–Kutta, and SNSFD methods. Results: Analysis shows hantavirus persistence is mainly driven by rodent‑to‑rodent transmission, while human infections arise from spillover; stochastic perturbations and delay‑survival effects lower the effective reproduction threshold and can promote extinction; simulations confirm consistency across methods for small steps and superior stability of SNSFD for larger steps. Contribution: The model provides a mathematically rigorous, biologically realistic framework for assessing rodent‑driven hantavirus spillover risk and highlights reservoir control as the most effective strategy; the SNSFD method offers a stable computational tool for stochastic epidemic systems with delays. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
